# Writing modules in Python

Every stage of an X-SCAPE event (hard process, energy loss, hadronization, soft particlization, afterburner, writer, hydro, ...) can be a Python class. You subclass the C++ base class and override the method JETSCAPE calls; the framework then creates, copies, calls and writes your module exactly as it would a C++ one, next to the C++ modules of the run. Use this to prototype a new physics module, to wrap a model that lives in Python, or to tap the event at a stage the standard output does not cover. Because the bindings keep the C++ names and argument order, a working Python module ports to C++ line by line, and a C++ module ports to Python the same way.

Python modules need no compiler: they run with the [production container](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/install/container/index.md) and the [Mac wheel](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/install/mac/index.md) as they are, against the compiled X-SCAPE inside. The examples on this page are in `python_modules/` of the copied examples (`xscape-examples DEST`), or in the repository under [`contribs/PyJetscape/example/python_modules/`](https://github.com/jhputschke/js-contrib/tree/main/contribs/PyJetscape/example/python_modules).

## How JETSCAPE calls a module

| when                           | method                                      |                                             |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `Init()`                       | `InitTask()`                                | once; read your XML parameters here         |
| every event                    | `ExecuteTask()`                             | gun, sampler, afterburner: the event's work |
| every event, energy loss       | `DoEnergyLoss(deltaT, time, Q2, pIn, pOut)` | once per parton per time step               |
| every event, jet hadronization | `DoHadronization(shower, hOut, pOut)`       | once per event, all showers at once         |
| end of every event             | `ClearTask()`                               | drop per-event state                        |
| `Finish()`                     | `FinishTask()`                              | once; close files                           |

Override only what you need: a method you leave out does what the C++ base class does. Call the base explicitly when you extend it, e.g. `core.SoftParticlization.ClearTask(self)`.

## The base classes

All are in `jetscape.pyjetscape_core` (below `core`).

| stage               | base class               | override                                                                     | gets / gives                                                                                                                    |
| ------------------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| initial state       | `InitialState`           | `ExecuteTask` (+ `GetNcoll`, `GetNpart`, `SampleABinaryCollisionPoint`)      | `set_entropy_density_from_numpy`, `set_num_of_binary_collisions_from_numpy`                                                     |
| hard process        | `HardProcess`            | `ExecuteTask` (+ `GetSigmaGen`, `GetSigmaErr`, `GetPtHat`, `GetEventWeight`) | `self.AddParton(...)`, `self.AddHadron(...)`                                                                                    |
| pre-equilibrium     | `PreequilibriumDynamics` | `InitializePreequilibrium`, `EvolvePreequilibrium`                           | `set_e_numpy`, `set_utau_numpy`, ...                                                                                            |
| hydro               | `FluidDynamics`          | `InitializeHydro`, `EvolveHydro`                                             | `store_fluid_cells_from_numpy`, the freeze-out surface ([example](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/python/fno/index.md)) |
| energy loss         | `JetEnergyLoss`          | `DoEnergyLoss(deltaT, time, Q2, pIn, pOut)`                                  | the parton in `pIn`; the partons at `time` out                                                                                  |
| jet hadronization   | `Hadronization`          | `DoHadronization(shower, hOut, pOut)`                                        | one list of final partons per shower; hadrons out                                                                               |
| soft particlization | `SoftParticlization`     | `ExecuteTask`                                                                | `self.GetHydroHyperSurface()`; `self.set_hadron_list([[Hadron, ...], ...])`                                                     |
| afterburner         | `Afterburner`            | `ExecuteTask`, `GetCurrentHadronList`                                        | `self.GatherAfterburnerHadrons()`                                                                                               |
| writer              | `JetScapeWriter`         | `GetStatus`, `Write(obj)`, `WriteEvent`                                      | every `Parton`, `PartonShower`, `Hadron` the tasks write; `self.GetHeader()`                                                    |
| liquefier           | `LiquefierBase`          | `smearing_kernel(tau, x, y, eta, droplet)`                                   | `[j^tau, j^x, j^y, j^eta]`                                                                                                      |
| shower growth       | `PartonShowerGenerator`  | `DoShower(jloss)`                                                            |                                                                                                                                 |

[`toy_modules.py`](https://github.com/jhputschke/js-contrib/blob/main/contribs/PyJetscape/example/python_modules/toy_modules.py) has one template per stage in the plain binding style (`ToyGun`, `ToySplit`, `ToyHadronizer`, `ToySampler`, `ToyAfterburner`, `ToyWriter`); [`toy_modules_pythonic.py`](https://github.com/jhputschke/js-contrib/blob/main/contribs/PyJetscape/example/python_modules/toy_modules_pythonic.py) has the same in the Pythonic style used below. The toys are not physics; they show the interface.

## A worked example: an energy-loss module

Three Python modules make a complete jet event: a gun that fires two back-to-back 40 GeV gluons, an energy-loss module that splits every parton above `e_min` into two halves once `time >= t_split`, and a hadronizer that turns every final parton into a π⁺. The classes are those of `toy_modules_pythonic.py`.

my_modules.py

```python
import jetscape as js
from jetscape import pyjetscape_core as core


@js.module("CustomModuleToyGunV2", section="Hard")
class ToyGunV2(core.HardProcess):
    """Two back-to-back gluons of E (GeV) along x."""

    xml_parameters = {"E": 40.0}

    def ExecuteTask(self):
        position = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)
        ini = js.JetScapeSignalManager.Instance().GetInitialStatePointer()
        if ini is not None and ini.GetNcoll() > 0:
            position = ini.sample_binary_collision_point()        # (t, x, y, z)
        for sign in (+1, -1):
            self.AddParton(js.make_parton(21, (self.E, sign * self.E, 0.0, 0.0), position))

    def GetSigmaGen(self):
        return 1.0


@js.module("CustomModuleToySplitV2", section="Eloss")
class ToySplitV2(core.JetEnergyLoss):
    """A parton above e_min splits into two halves at t >= t_split."""

    xml_parameters = {"t_split": 1.0, "e_min": 30.0}

    def DoEnergyLoss(self, deltaT, time, Q2, pIn, pOut):
        p = pIn[0]
        if time >= self.t_split and p.e() > self.e_min:
            E, px, py, pz = p.momentum
            return [js.make_parton(p.pid(), (E / 2, px / 2, s * 1.0, pz / 2),
                                   position=p.position) for s in (+1, -1)]


@js.module("CustomModuleToyHadronizerV2")
class ToyHadronizerV2(core.Hadronization):
    """Every final parton becomes a pi+ with its momentum and position."""

    def DoHadronization(self, shower, hOut, pOut):
        return [js.make_hadron(211, p.momentum, p.position, stat=1)
                for partons in shower for p in partons]
```

What the pieces do:

- **`@js.module(name, section)`** registers the class in JETSCAPE's module factory, so an XML can name it, and turns `xml_parameters` into XML parameters (next sections). Inside the module they are plain attributes: `self.E`, `self.t_split`, `self.e_min`.
- **`DoEnergyLoss` returns the partons at `time`.** Returning `None` (here, below `e_min` or before `t_split`) lets the parton go on unchanged; returning two partons makes a splitting vertex.
- **`DoHadronization` returns the hadrons.** `js.make_parton` / `js.make_hadron` take the momentum as `(E, px, py, pz)` and the position as `(t, x, y, z)`.

The run builds the pipeline by hand: the energy-loss and hadronization *managers* and their containers are made in Python and the modules put inside, as the XML would do.

run_my_modules.py

```python
import numpy as np
import jetscape as js
from jetscape import paths
from jetscape import pyjetscape_core as core
from my_modules import ToyGunV2, ToySplitV2, ToyHadronizerV2

eloss_manager = core.JetEnergyLossManager()   # copies `eloss` once per shower
eloss = core.JetEnergyLoss()                  # the per-shower container (deltaT, maxT)
eloss.Add(ToySplitV2())                       # modules in order (Matter before LBT)
eloss_manager.Add(eloss)

hadronization_manager = core.HadronizationManager()
hadronization = core.Hadronization()
hadronization.Add(ToyHadronizerV2())
hadronization_manager.Add(hadronization)

tasks = [ToyGunV2(), eloss_manager, hadronization_manager]     # pipeline order
main_xml = paths.xscape_root() / "config" / "jetscape_main.xml"

with js.per_event(main_xml, "my_user.xml", tasks=tasks) as driver:
    for i in driver.events():
        fp = driver.energy_loss_manager.final_parton_array()
        had = driver.hadronization_manager.hadron_array()
        print(f"event {i}: {len(fp)} final partons, E = {fp['E'].sum():.1f} GeV;",
              f"{len(had)} hadrons, pT = {np.hypot(had.p[:, 1], had.p[:, 2]).round(2)}")
```

my_user.xml

```xml
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<jetscape>
  <nEvents>3</nEvents>
  <vlevel>0</vlevel>
  <Random><seed>1</seed></Random>
  <enableAutomaticTaskListDetermination> false </enableAutomaticTaskListDetermination>
  <Eloss>
    <deltaT>0.1</deltaT>
    <maxT>2</maxT>
  </Eloss>
</jetscape>
```

```console
$ python run_my_modules.py
event 0: 4 final partons, E = 80.0 GeV; 4 hadrons, pT = [20.02 20.02 20.02 20.02]
event 1: 4 final partons, E = 80.0 GeV; 4 hadrons, pT = [20.02 20.02 20.02 20.02]
event 2: 4 final partons, E = 80.0 GeV; 4 hadrons, pT = [20.02 20.02 20.02 20.02]
```

Each 40 GeV gluon split once into two 20 GeV halves with ±1 GeV along y. Now set a parameter from the user XML: add

```xml
    <CustomModuleToySplitV2><e_min>50</e_min></CustomModuleToySplitV2>
```

inside `<Eloss>`. The 40 GeV gluons stay below `e_min`, nothing splits, and every event prints `2 final partons ... 2 hadrons, pT = [40. 40.]`.

### The same modules named in the XML

With the automatic task list (the default), the user XML names the modules, and X-SCAPE builds the managers itself. Import the module file so the decorators register the classes, then run:

my_user_xml.xml

```xml
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<jetscape>
  <nEvents>3</nEvents>
  <vlevel>0</vlevel>
  <Random><seed>1</seed></Random>
  <Hard>
    <CustomModuleToyGunV2><E>50</E></CustomModuleToyGunV2>
  </Hard>
  <Eloss>
    <deltaT>0.1</deltaT>
    <maxT>2</maxT>
    <CustomModuleToySplitV2><e_min>30</e_min></CustomModuleToySplitV2>
  </Eloss>
  <JetHadronization><name>CustomModuleToyHadronizerV2</name></JetHadronization>
</jetscape>
```

```python
import jetscape as js
from jetscape import paths
import my_modules  # noqa: F401  (the decorators register the modules)

main_xml = paths.xscape_root() / "config" / "jetscape_main.xml"
with js.per_event(main_xml, "my_user_xml.xml") as driver:
    print([type(t).__name__ for t in driver.GetTaskList()])
    # ['ToyGunV2', 'JetEnergyLossManager', 'HadronizationManager']
    for i in driver.events():
        fp = driver.energy_loss_manager.final_parton_array()
        print(i, len(fp), fp["E"].sum())          # 4 partons, 100 GeV: E is 50 here
```

C++ and Python modules mix freely in both styles: replace `ToyGunV2` by `<Hard><PythiaGun>`, or put your energy-loss module after `<Matter>` in `<Eloss>`.

## Named in the XML or built by hand

|            | named in the XML                                                     | built by hand                                                                                     |
| ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| user XML   | `<enableAutomaticTaskListDetermination>` true (the default)          | false                                                                                             |
| the module | registered (`@js.module` or `register_module`), named in its section | an object you `Add()`                                                                             |
| managers   | made by X-SCAPE                                                      | `JetEnergyLossManager` / `JetEnergyLoss`, `HadronizationManager` / `Hadronization` made in Python |
| examples   | `run_from_xml.py` + `user_from_xml.xml`                              | `run_by_hand.py` (plain bindings), `run_by_hand_pythonic.py` (\`--style old                       |

**Names.** Every XML section accepts a module whose element name contains `CustomModule`: `<Hard><CustomModuleMyGun>`, `<Eloss><CustomModuleMyLoss>`, `<SoftParticlization><CustomModuleMySampler>`, `<Afterburner><CustomModuleMyAfterburner>`. Jet hadronization takes it as text: `<JetHadronization><name>CustomModuleMyHadronizer</name>`. A module that does not contain `CustomModule` in its name is never created from the XML.

**Every user-XML tag needs a default in the main XML.** At `Init()`, X-SCAPE compares every tag of the user XML with `config/jetscape_main.xml` and **stops the process** (`exit`) on a tag the main XML lacks: your module's name and each of its parameters. For a C++ module that means adding default blocks to `jetscape_main.xml` (js-contrib's [README](https://github.com/jhputschke/js-contrib/blob/main/README.md#xml-configuration-requirements-for-new-modules) explains it). A Python module needs no edit: registering it gives the defaults, and `Init()` adds `<section><name>defaults</name>` to the main XML **in memory** (the file is not changed).

- With `@js.module`, the defaults are `xml_parameters` (int, float, str or bool). Before your `InitTask` runs, each is read into `self.<key>` from `[section, name, key]`: the user XML's value, else the default, converted to the default's type (`bool`: `0`, `false`, `off`, `no` are false).

- With the plain call, give the defaults as XML text and read them yourself in `InitTask`, as a C++ module does:

  ```python
  class ToyGun(core.HardProcess):
      def InitTask(self):
          self.e = self.get_xml_element_double(["Hard", "CustomModuleToyGun", "E"], False)

  core.register_module("CustomModuleToyGun", ToyGun, section="Hard", defaults="<E>40</E>")
  ```

`get_xml_element_int` and `get_xml_element_text` work alike; with `True` a missing element raises.

- `core.registered_modules()` lists the factory (the build's C++ modules and the Python ones), `core.unregister_module(name)` removes a Python one.

A module built by hand needs no registration, but register it anyway if it reads XML parameters: without the main-XML default, setting them in the user XML stops the run.

## Energy loss in detail

`DoEnergyLoss(deltaT, time, Q2, pIn, pOut)` is called for every parton of every shower at every time step up to `<Eloss><maxT>`, in steps of `<Eloss><deltaT>` (fm/c).

- **`time`** is the end of the step. **`Q2`** is what the framework passes: the parton's pT, not a virtuality; the virtuality is `pIn[0].virtuality()`.

- **`pIn`** is a list with this step's parton, the C++ object itself: `p.set_stat(...)` changes it in place. It is valid during the call only; do not keep it.

- **The output** (appended to `pOut`, or returned as a list):

  | output         | the shower                                                   |
  | -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
  | empty / `None` | the parton (as changed) goes on unchanged into the next step |
  | one parton     | it replaces the parton (no new vertex)                       |
  | two or more    | a vertex at `time`; each parton is a new branch              |

  Partons with the liquefier's statuses (droplet −11, miss −13, negative −17) and non-partons (photons, leptons) do not go on. Return a list *or* append, not both (`ValueError`).

  - **Several modules** in `<Eloss>` (Matter then LBT, or yours after Matter) are called in turn on the same lists, as in C++. Leave alone a parton another module handles (`p.GetController()`, `pOut` already filled).
  - **The medium:** `self.GetHydroCell(t, x, y, z)` returns a `FluidCellInfo` (`temperature`, `energy_density`, `pressure`, `vx`, `vy`, `vz`, ...), or `None` without a hydro.
  - **Copies:** the energy-loss manager copies the module once per shower at the start of each event with `Clone()` and drops the copies at the end. The default copy runs the C++ copy constructor and copies the instance attributes *shallowly*; `__init__` and `InitTask` are not called on copies. Override `Clone` for state that must not be shared between showers:

  ```python
  def Clone(self):
      copy = core.JetEnergyLoss.Clone(self)   # the default copy
      copy.history = []                       # one list per shower
      return copy
  ```

## The other stages

- **Jet hadronization**, `DoHadronization(shower, hOut, pOut)`: once per event, after the energy loss. `shower` is a list with one list of final partons per shower. Return (or append to `hOut`) the hadrons, or a tuple `(hadrons, partons)` for partons you leave unhadronized; for hadrons alone return a list, not a tuple. `self.GetHydroHyperSurface(T)` and `self.GetHydroCell(...)` give the medium.
- **Soft particlization**, `ExecuteTask()`: `self.GetHydroHyperSurface()` is the freeze-out surface (a list of `SurfaceCellInfo`); store hadrons with `self.set_hadron_list(samples)`, a list of oversamples, each a list of `Hadron`s.
- **Afterburner**, `ExecuteTask()` and `GetCurrentHadronList()`: `self.GatherAfterburnerHadrons()` gives per oversample the soft hadrons, plus the jet hadrons when `<Afterburner><include_fragmentation_hadrons>` is 1.
- **Writer**, `GetStatus()` and `Write(obj)` (+ `WriteEvent()`): per event the header is filled (`self.GetHeader().GetSigmaGen()`, ...), then `Write` receives the hard partons, per shower the initiating `Parton` and the `PartonShower`, then the jet `Hadron`s. Add a writer with `driver.Add(writer)` before `Init()`, also in XML mode. The C++ ASCII writer comes from `core.create_module("JetScapeWriterAscii")` + `core.set_writer_output_file(w, name)`, and `core.JetScapeReaderAscii(name)` reads its file back.
- **Initial state, pre-equilibrium, hydro, liquefier**: examples in `example/inspect_bulk_info.py` (`GaussianIC`), `python/jetscape/fno_hydro.py` ([PyFNOHydro](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/python/fno/index.md)), `python/jetscape/surface_replay.py`, FastHydro's `hydro.py` and `initial_state.py` ([FastHydro](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/python/fasthydro/index.md)).

## Particles and lists

- `js.make_parton(pid, momentum, position=(0, 0, 0, 0), stat=0, label=0, color=0, anti_color=0)`, `js.make_hadron(pid, momentum, position, stat, label, mass=None)` and `js.make_photon(...)` take momentum `(E, px, py, pz)` and position `(t, x, y, z)`. The bound constructors keep C++'s order: `core.Parton(label, pid, stat, p, x)` with `p = core.FourVector(px, py, pz, E)` and `x = core.FourVector(x, y, z, t)`.
- Getters and setters as in C++: `pid()`, `pstat()`, `e()`, `px()`, `pt()`, `eta()`, `p_in()`, `x_in()`, `set_stat()`, `set_form_time()`, `set_color()`, ...; and `p.momentum`, `p.position`.
- A particle's `x()`, `y()`, `z()`, `t()` are its **position**; a parton's virtuality is `virtuality()`, set with `set_t()`.
- Lists C++ passes by reference arrive as Python lists: the inputs are the C++ objects (valid during the call), the outputs are copied back into C++ after the call.

## Random numbers

- **`self.rng`** (Pythonic layer) is a numpy `Generator` seeded from the module's own C++ engine on first use: reproducible with `<Random><seed>`, with its own stream for each per-shower copy. Use it in `InitTask` or later; before the XML is loaded it raises.
- **`self.GetMt19937Generator()`** is the engine itself, as in C++: `g()` is the next 32-bit draw, `g.uniform()` a draw in \[0, 1).

The engines are seeded from the seed and the module's task number. Adding a Python module shifts the task numbers, and so the random streams, of the tasks created after it, exactly as adding a C++ module does.

## Checking a module against C++

Run the C++ module and your Python version with the same seed and compare the output files, as [`tests/equivalence_driver.py`](https://github.com/jhputschke/js-contrib/blob/main/contribs/PyJetscape/tests/equivalence_driver.py) does. For identical random numbers the Python version must create the same tasks in the same order; a Python module that holds a C++ module of its own gives it its task number back with `core.next_task_number()` / `core.set_next_task_number()` (see `PyMatter` there). Run each configuration in its own process: JETSCAPE keeps the XML, the seed and the module registry in process-wide singletons. Checked this way, a Python module handing each step to C++ Matter gives byte-identical hadrons to the C++ run, and a Python writer writes the same lines as the C++ one.

## Cost

A call into a Python energy-loss module costs about 1.4 µs on top of the module's own work: on a GB10, 715,438 calls in 500 events of a 100 GeV gluon in vacuum took 3.70 s through a Python module that hands each step to C++ Matter, against 2.72 s for Matter alone. A module written in Python costs what its Python code costs on top of that, per parton and time step. Python modules run in one thread (each call takes the GIL).

## Pitfalls

| symptom                                                              | cause                                                                                                                       |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `User XML tag <X> is unrecognized` and the run stops                 | the module or a parameter is not registered (`@js.module` / `register_module` with `section=` and defaults) before `Init()` |
| a module named in the XML never runs                                 | its name does not contain `CustomModule`                                                                                    |
| `AttributeError: module 'jetscape' has no attribute 'JetEnergyLoss'` | most bound classes are in `jetscape.pyjetscape_core`, not re-exported by `jetscape`                                         |
| a parton's `t()` is not its virtuality                               | `t()` is the position time; use `virtuality()`                                                                              |
| state shared between showers                                         | the default `Clone()` copies attributes shallowly; override `Clone`                                                         |
| a liquefier attached from Python is gone                             | C++ keeps only a weak reference; keep the Python object alive                                                               |
| `undefined symbol ... iColoredHadronization` on import               | X-SCAPE built without `-DUSE_3DGlauber=ON`                                                                                  |
| `all 256 slots for Python modules are taken`                         | more than 256 registered Python modules in one process                                                                      |

## Next steps

- [Live PyTorch FNO hydro](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/python/fno/index.md): a complete Python hydro module backed by a neural network.
- [The Pythonic interface](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/python/pythonic/index.md): reading what your module produced.
- The full reference: PyJetscape's [README, *Writing modules in Python*](https://github.com/jhputschke/js-contrib/blob/main/contribs/PyJetscape/README.md#writing-modules-in-python) and [`example/python_modules/README.md`](https://github.com/jhputschke/js-contrib/blob/main/contribs/PyJetscape/example/python_modules/README.md).

# Live PyTorch FNO hydro

`PyFNOHydro` is a hydro module written in Python and backed by a PyTorch Fourier neural operator (FNO). It takes the initial condition from the pre-equilibrium stage, predicts the whole space-time evolution of the medium in one forward pass, stores it in X-SCAPE's evolution history and builds the freeze-out surface, so Matter, LBT and iSS run on the prediction exactly as they would on MUSIC. Use it to test a surrogate model against the full event: jet quenching and hadron observables on the predicted medium, side by side with MUSIC. Because the model can be a live `torch.nn.Module`, you can do this in the same Python session in which you train it, with no export step. The method and the 2+1D models are described in [Phys. Rev. C 113, 014904 (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1103/jsh8-6tm7) (arXiv:2507.23598).

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    IS["initial state<br/>(e.g. TrentoInitial)"] --> PE["pre-equilibrium<br/>(e.g. NullPreDynamics)"]
    PE --> F["PyFNOHydro"]
    F --> J["Matter, LBT<br/>(read the medium)"]
    F --> S["iSS<br/>(freeze-out surface)"]
```

Inside `EvolveHydro()`, `PyFNOHydro`:

1. takes the pre-equilibrium energy density and flow (`e`, `ux`, `uy`) and rebins them (nearest neighbour) onto the FNO grid: 3 features `(e, vx, vy)` or 4 `(e, T, vx, vy)`;
1. repeats that frame `ntau` times along the time axis and, for a 3-feature model, multiplies the energy density by τ₀ (the models are trained on e·τ);
1. calls the model on a tensor of shape `(1, n_features, nx, ny, ntau)`, under `torch.no_grad()`; the model must return the same shape;
1. prepends the τ₀ frame, divides by τ again, and stores the `ntau + 1` frames as a boost-invariant evolution starting at τ₀ (the pre-equilibrium module's end time);
1. finds the freeze-out surface at the configured temperature.

## Three ways to give it a model

```python
import torch                                   # always before jetscape
from jetscape.fno_hydro import PyFNOHydro

# 1. a JIT-traced TorchScript file (the format the C++ FnoHydro reads)
hydro = PyFNOHydro("models/traced.pt", config)

# 2. your model class plus a checkpoint (state_dict, or a dict with "model_state_dict")
from my_model import FNOModel
net = FNOModel(modes=12, width=20)
hydro = PyFNOHydro((net, "checkpoints/epoch50.pt"), config)

# 3. a live model object, used as it is: no serialisation
hydro = PyFNOHydro(net, config)
```

### The live model (approach 3)

Approach 3 is what makes the module useful while you develop a model. `PyFNOHydro` keeps a reference to *your* `nn.Module`, not a copy, so a model you have just trained, or are still training, runs inside a full X-SCAPE event:

```python
import torch                                   # (1) before jetscape
import torch.nn as nn
from jetscape import create_module
from jetscape.fno_hydro import PyFNOHydro, fno_config_from_xml
from jetscape.run_jetscape import run_manual
from jetscape.utils import bulk_info_to_numpy

net = ...                                      # your nn.Module, e.g. the FNO you are training:
                                               # (1, F, nx, ny, ntau) -> (1, F, nx, ny, ntau)

user_xml = "jetscape_user_fno.xml"             # a user XML with a <Hydro><FNO> block
config = fno_config_from_xml(user_xml, device="mps")      # "cpu", "cuda" or "mps"
hydro = PyFNOHydro(net, config)                # (2) sets net.eval()

modules = [create_module("TrentoInitial"), create_module("NullPreDynamics"), hydro]
run_manual("jetscape_main.xml", user_xml, modules, n_events=1)

evo = bulk_info_to_numpy(hydro.get_bulk_info(), n_features=4)  # (ntau+1, nx, ny, [e, T, vx, vy])
surface = hydro.get_surface_cells()                             # what iSS samples
```

Run it from the X-SCAPE build directory (or inside a [`js.JobDir`](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/python/pythonic/#running-events)): TrentoInitial and the other C++ modules read their tables from there. `run_manual` takes a pipeline built in Python; the user XML must set `<enableAutomaticTaskListDetermination>false</enableAutomaticTaskListDetermination>`. FnoHydro's [`config/jetscape_user_root_bulk_test.xml`](https://github.com/jhputschke/js-contrib/blob/main/contribs/FnoHydro/config/jetscape_user_root_bulk_test.xml) is such a file, with a Trento initial state and a `<Hydro><FNO>` block. For jet energy loss and hadronization on the predicted medium, add the managers by hand as on [Writing modules in Python](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/python/modules/#a-worked-example-an-energy-loss-module), with `create_module("Matter")` and `create_module("ColorlessHadronization")` inside them, or use `js.per_event(..., tasks=[...])` to read each event's results.

Pitfalls of the live model

- **Import `torch` before `jetscape`.** PyTorch and the compiled extension each load an OpenMP runtime, and the one initialised second can crash the process. On macOS `import jetscape` imports torch first if it is installed; on Linux torch is otherwise only loaded when `PyFNOHydro` is constructed, after the extension. Put `import torch` at the top.
- **`PyFNOHydro` calls `net.eval()`** when it is constructed. If you continue training the same object, call `net.train()` for the training steps and `net.eval()` again before the next event.
- **The grid must be the model's.** `nx`, `ny`, `ntau`, `x_min`, `y_min`, `dtau` and `n_features` must match what the model was trained on; nothing checks this for you. `dx = -2 x_min / nx`.
- **The model runs on `config["device"]`**, and `PyFNOHydro` moves your model there (`net.to(device)` moves the object itself, not a copy).
- **A pre-equilibrium module is required** before `PyFNOHydro` (`NullPreDynamics` will do); τ₀ is its end time, not a config key.
- **The evolution is 2+1D, boost-invariant.** Higher-dimensional models need their own module (see [FastHydro](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/python/fasthydro/index.md) for a 3+1D Python hydro).
- The log line `Unrecognized hydro module id:PyFNOHydro` is a harmless warning.
- One forward pass per event runs with the GIL held; the heavy work is inside torch.

## The grid configuration

The `config` dict gives the FNO grid:

```python
config = dict(
    nx=60, ny=60, ntau=59,          # required
    n_features=3,                   # required: 3 or 4
    x_min=-15.0, y_min=-15.0,       # required [fm]
    dtau=0.1,                       # required [fm/c]
    T_freeze=0.136,                 # required: freeze-out temperature [GeV]
    neta=1, deta=0.0,               # optional
    tau_normalise=True,             # optional: the model predicts e*tau (default for 3 features)
    device="cpu",                   # optional: "cpu", "cuda", "mps"
)
```

Instead of a dict, keep the grid in the user XML, next to the run: `fno_config_from_xml(user_xml, device=...)` parses the `<Hydro><FNO>` block before the run, and `config=None` lets `PyFNOHydro` read the same block from the loaded XML in `InitializeHydro()`, as the C++ module does:

```xml
<Hydro>
  <FNO>
    <model_file>models/traced_JS3.7_10k_3feat_fno_model_cpu_40_60_59bins.pt</model_file>
    <n_features>3</n_features>
    <freezeout_temperature>0.136</freezeout_temperature>
    <nx>60</nx>
    <ny>60</ny>
    <neta>1</neta>
    <ntau>59</ntau>
    <x_min>-15.0</x_min>
    <y_min>-15.0</y_min>
    <dtau>0.1</dtau>
    <deta>0</deta>
  </FNO>
</Hydro>
```

X-SCAPE's `config/jetscape_main.xml` (branch `contrib`) has the defaults of this block, so a user XML may carry it. `PyFNOHydro` takes the model from its constructor, not from `<model_file>`.

## Try it: `python_fno_test.py`

[`example/python_fno_test.py`](https://github.com/jhputschke/js-contrib/blob/main/contribs/PyJetscape/example/python_fno_test.py) runs TrentoInitial → NullPreDynamics → `PyFNOHydro` with a traced model, prints the stored grid, the evolution as numpy and torch tensors and the number of surface cells, and saves `python_fno_test_bulk.png` (energy-density slices). Put the model file into `contribs/FnoHydro/models/` or pass `--model`:

```bash
cd X-SCAPE/build_gpu
python ../external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape/example/python_fno_test.py \
  --model ../external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/FnoHydro/models/traced_JS3.7_10k_3feat_fno_model_cpu_40_60_59bins.pt \
  --events 1 --device cpu
```

`--config-source dict|python-xml|jetscape-xml` picks one of the three configuration routes above, `--user` another user XML (default: FnoHydro's `config/jetscape_user_root_bulk_test.xml`), `--no-plots` skips matplotlib.

PyTorch is not part of the [container](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/install/container/index.md) or the [Mac wheel](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/install/mac/index.md) environment; install it there, or use the `js_fno` conda environment of a [source build](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/install/source/index.md), which has it.

## Utilities: the evolution as arrays and tensors

`jetscape.utils` converts between X-SCAPE's evolution history and numpy / torch:

```python
from jetscape.utils import (bulk_info_to_numpy, bulk_info_to_tensor,
                            numpy_to_bulk_info, tensor_to_bulk_info, rebin_preeq_to_fno_grid)

info = hydro.get_bulk_info()                               # EvolutionHistory, any hydro module
arr = bulk_info_to_numpy(info, n_features=4)               # (ntau, nx, ny, 4): e, T, vx, vy; float32
t = bulk_info_to_tensor(info, n_features=4, device="cpu")  # (1, 4, nx, ny, ntau), the FNO layout

tensor_to_bulk_info(t, hydro)                              # back into a FluidDynamics module
fno_input = rebin_preeq_to_fno_grid(preeq, ini, nx_fno, ny_fno, x_min_fno, y_min_fno,
                                    dx_fno, dy_fno, n_features=3)   # (3, nx, ny, 1)
```

`bulk_info_to_numpy` reads the transverse slice (2+1D). For a 3+1D evolution, e.g. from MUSIC, `info.to_numpy_full(n_features)` returns `(ntau, nx, ny, neta, n_features)` with the columns `e, T, vx, vy, vz, s`. The production writers store MUSIC's evolution directly in the HDF5 layout the FNO training reads ([below](#training-data-from-the-productions)).

## The C++ FnoHydro (LibTorch)

For runs without Python in the loop, the [FnoHydro contrib](https://github.com/jhputschke/js-contrib/tree/main/contribs/FnoHydro) is the same idea in C++: a `FluidDynamics` module registered as `FnoHydro` that loads a traced TorchScript model with LibTorch and runs it on the pre-equilibrium output. It reads the model file and the grid from the same `<Hydro><FNO>` block (`<model_file>`, `nx`, `ny`, `ntau`, ...), so a traced model and its XML work in both; the freeze-out temperature it takes from `<Hydro><MUSIC><freezeout_temperature>`. It needs LibTorch (about 2 GB) and ROOT at build time:

```bash
cmake .. -DUSE_MUSIC=ON -DUSE_ISS=ON -DUSE_JS_CONTRIB=ON -DUSE_JS_FNO_HYDRO=ON \
  -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="$(python -c 'import torch; print(torch.utils.cmake_prefix_path)')"
make -j FnoModule
```

It is not built in the container or the Mac wheel. The contrib also holds `FnoRooIn` (replays a stored evolution from ROOT) and the ROOT bulk writers of the original training pipeline; see its [README](https://github.com/jhputschke/js-contrib/blob/main/contribs/FnoHydro/README.md).

## Where the models come from

The trained models are not in js-contrib, because they are too large for git (about 1.5 GB each). They are published with the paper on **Zenodo**, [record 16647726](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.16647726), together with the training data in ROOT format:

| Model file                                                                      | What it is                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `traced_JS3.7_10k_3feat_fno_model_cpu_40_60_59bins.pt`                          | traced, 3 features, 60 × 60, 59 time steps, 40–60 % centrality; the default of `python_fno_test.py` |
| `traced_JS3.7_10k_3feat_fno_model_cpu_0_10_59bins.pt`                           | the same for 0–10 %                                                                                 |
| `traced_JS3.7_2k_3feat_fno_model_cpu_4types_59bins.pt`                          | traced, trained on four event types                                                                 |
| `model_10K_central.pt`, `model_10K_peripheral.pt`, `model_500_of_four_types.pt` | the untraced models of the paper (central, peripheral, four event types)                            |

```bash
mkdir -p models && cd models
curl -L -o traced_JS3.7_10k_3feat_fno_model_cpu_40_60_59bins.pt \
  "https://zenodo.org/records/16647726/files/traced_JS3.7_10k_3feat_fno_model_cpu_40_60_59bins.pt?download=1"
```

In the future, trained models and training data will also be shared on the OSDF, next to the production outputs; see [Data on the OSDF](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/run/osdf/index.md).

## Training data from the productions

A model is only as good as its training set, and js-contrib's productions write it directly in the HDF5 layout of the FNO4d training code (`/arr` of shape `(nevents, 4, nx, ny, neta, ntau)` with `e, vx, vy, vz`, plus the grid as attributes), with no ROOT step in between:

- **Hydro only:** `prod_AuAu_0_10` writes one MUSIC evolution per event (`H5BulkWriter`).
- **Jet + medium pairs:** `prod_AuAu_0_10_jet` runs the two-stage hydro: MUSIC_1 evolves the background, Matter + LBT lose energy in it, and MUSIC_2 evolves the **same** initial condition with the lost energy deposited. Each event is written as a pair: `arr` (with the jet), `arr_bg` (without), the droplets that were deposited (`source/droplets`) and the parton shower (`shower/`). `arr - arr_bg` is the jet's effect alone, the target of a deposition model. How to run it, also on clusters: [Au+Au jets (two stages)](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/run/auau-jet/index.md).
- **FastHydro** writes the same pair layout with a fast PyTorch solver, for large samples: [FastHydro](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/python/fasthydro/index.md).

## Next steps

- [Writing modules in Python](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/python/modules/index.md): the module interface `PyFNOHydro` is built on.
- [FastHydro](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/python/fasthydro/index.md): a 3+1D hydro solver in PyTorch with the jet-deposition workflow.
- [Au+Au jets (two stages)](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/run/auau-jet/index.md): the GPU production of training pairs.

# FastHydro

FastHydro runs X-SCAPE's real jet energy-loss chain, **Matter + LBT → CausalLiquefier → droplets**, on top of a fast 3+1D finite-volume hydro solver in Milne coordinates written in PyTorch, with an MC-Glauber initial state. For each event it gives back a **pair**: the medium without the jet and the medium with the jet's lost energy deposited, both from the identical initial condition. That pair is what jet-deposition FNO studies and wake analyses need, and the cost per event makes large samples practical on a CPU, a CUDA GPU or Apple's MPS. On the same initial condition the solver agrees with MUSIC to about 0.3 % (relative L2 of the energy density at freeze-out). For production-grade pairs with MUSIC itself, use the [two-stage Au+Au production](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/run/auau-jet/index.md); FastHydro writes the same file layout.

The solver and the initial state are FNO4d's `fast_data`, vendored unchanged under `python/fast_data/`. FastHydro itself is the glue that makes them X-SCAPE modules.

## Requirements

- An X-SCAPE build (branch `contrib`) with PyJetscape: `-DUSE_JS_CONTRIB=ON -DUSE_JS_PYJETSCAPE=ON` ([source build](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/install/source/index.md)). FastHydro is pure Python: it compiles nothing and needs no CMake option of its own.
- **The Python that `pyjetscape_core` was built with**, with numpy, scipy, h5py, hdf5plugin, pyyaml, and PyTorch ≥ 2.0 for the solver. The `js_fno` conda environment has all of them and installs FastHydro as an editable package. PyTorch is not in the production container.

```bash
pip install -e external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/FastHydro          # from the X-SCAPE root
# or without installing:
export PYTHONPATH=$PWD/external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/FastHydro/python:$PYTHONPATH
```

The example scripts find their own paths, so they also run from a checkout without the install.

## The pipeline

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    IS["FastGlauberInitialState"] --> H["PythiaGun or PGun"] --> P["NullPreDynamics"]
    P --> BG["FastHydro('bg')<br/>background leg, no source"]
    BG --> E["JetEnergyLossManager: Matter, LBT<br/>+ CausalLiquefier"]
    E --> D["DropletBridge<br/>droplets -> the jet leg's source"]
    D --> JET["FastHydro('jet')<br/>same initial condition, with the source"]
```

This is X-SCAPE's two-stage hydro (`config/jetscape_user_twostagehydro.xml`, `examples/custom_examples/TwoStagesHydro.cc`) with FastHydro in place of MUSIC. Four things in it are fixed:

- **NullPreDynamics is mandatory.** X-SCAPE requires a pre-equilibrium stage for every hydro except MUSIC and Brick. (The log then shows a harmless `Unrecognized hydro module id` warning.)
- **Matter before LBT.** Matter hands over to LBT at `Q0`; `<Eloss><mutex>ON</mutex>` arbitrates.
- **The background leg comes first.** X-SCAPE registers only the first `FluidDynamics` as *the* hydro, so Matter, LBT and the liquefier see the background and the jet leg is invisible to them. That is the two-stage semantics: the shower is quenched by the undisturbed medium, and its deposit goes into the second leg. The coupling is one-way.
- **The deposit is computed in Python.** FastHydro deposits the droplets with `fast_data`'s `CausalLiquefierSource`; the C++ `CausalLiquefier` is used only as the droplet container. There is no double counting.

## Configuration: an XML and a YAML

Two files, for two readers:

| file                                        | read by                  | holds                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `config/jetscape_user_fasthydro.xml`        | X-SCAPE (C++)            | `<IS>`, `<Preequilibrium>`, `<Hard>`, `<Eloss>`, `<Liquefier>` |
| `config/fasthydro_twostage.yaml`, top level | the solver (`fast_data`) | grid, EoS, transport, τ axis, deposit scheme, device, dtype    |
| the same YAML, section `fasthydro:`         | FastHydro's adapters     | hard-scattering vertices, shower storage, `bulk_info` storage  |

The solver settings cannot go into the XML: X-SCAPE stops on any user-XML tag that `jetscape_main.xml` lacks. Three quantities appear in both files, and `build_two_stage()` **refuses to run** if they disagree:

| quantity          | XML                                 | YAML        | rule                            |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------- | ----------- | ------------------------------- |
| grid              | `<IS><grid_max_*>`, `<grid_step_*>` | `grid:`     | must agree (`grid_max = n·d/2`) |
| hydro start       | `<Preequilibrium><taus>`            | `time.tau0` | must agree                      |
| energy-loss start | `<Eloss><tStart>`                   |             | must not precede `time.tau0`    |

The liquefier's deposit parameters (`tau_delay`, `time_relax`, `d_diff`, `width_delta`, and the `frame` of the diffusion, `bjorken` by default or `lab`; X-SCAPE's `fluid` frame is not supported by FastHydro yet and is refused; see [The physics](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/about/physics/#5-energymomentum-deposition-the-causalliquefier)) live only in `<Liquefier><CausalLiquefier>`; FastHydro reads them from the C++ object and records them in the output (`liquefier_frame` among them). Any YAML key can be overridden on the command line with `--set`, routed by its prefix: `--set time.choose_ntau=41` (solver), `--set fasthydro.hard_vertex.mode=centre` (adapters), `--set transport.mode=israel_stewart`.

**Where the hard scatterings happen** is `fasthydro.hard_vertex.mode`: `ncoll` (default, the smeared binary-collision density, what a hard process follows), `ncoll_mc`, `npart` or `centre` (every vertex at the origin).

PGun ignores the vertex

X-SCAPE's `PGun` overwrites the sampled vertex with the origin, so with PGun every shower starts at (0, 0, 0) whatever `hard_vertex.mode` says. `PythiaGun` uses the vertex and is the default here.

## Running

Run from the X-SCAPE build directory; the framework resolves several paths relative to it.

```bash
cd $XSCAPE_BUILD
C=../external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/FastHydro
export OMP_WAIT_POLICY=passive OMP_NUM_THREADS=8    # idle OpenMP threads otherwise spin

# 0. smoke test: hydro only, then check the medium queries against the stored grid
python $C/example/run_hydro_only.py --config $C/config/fasthydro_twostage.yaml

# 1. the real thing: background leg, Matter + LBT, jet leg -> one HDF5 file
python $C/example/run_two_stage.py \
    --config   $C/config/fasthydro_twostage.yaml \
    --user-xml $C/config/jetscape_user_fasthydro.xml \
    --main-xml ../config/jetscape_main.xml \
    --events 1 --out out/pair.h5 --dump-droplets out/run.droplets.npz

# 2. replay the same shower through other solver settings: no X-SCAPE, no Matter/LBT
python $C/example/run_replay.py --droplets out/run.droplets.npz \
    --config $C/config/fasthydro_twostage.yaml \
    --set transport.mode=israel_stewart --out out/pair_visc.h5
```

- **Give `--out` an `.h5` name.** It writes the FNO4d HDF5 layout, one event at a time, so the memory is one pair however many events you ask for. An `.npz` name writes plain arrays of one pair, for a quick look only.
- **The replay** reads the droplet dump (small, numpy only) and runs both legs again, so it works on a machine without h5py or an X-SCAPE build. It answers "what does the same jet do in a different medium": the shower responds to the medium it crosses, so a live run on a viscous background gives a different jet, while a replay keeps the deposit fixed.
- `run.device` in the YAML (or `--set run.device=cuda`) picks `cpu`, `cuda` or `mps`; MPS runs in float32. CPU runs are slower and bitwise reproducible.

For the wake notebook, one command makes both legs (ideal and viscous, the second replayed from the first's droplets), about a minute per leg on Apple MPS:

```bash
python $C/example/make_wake_data.py                      # -> out_wake/wake_{ideal,visc}.h5
python $C/example/make_wake_data.py --medium realistic   # dN_ch/deta about 650
```

It finds or downloads the EoS table it needs (`--no-download` refuses the network, `--dry-run` prints what it would do).

## Soft particlization: hadrons from one leg

FastHydro has no surface code of its own: when iSS finds no surface, X-SCAPE builds one from the stored evolution (Cornelius, in C++). **One run particlizes one leg**, chosen with `<SoftParticlization><hydro_id>`; `run_particlize.py` sets it:

```bash
cd $XSCAPE_BUILD
C=../external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/FastHydro
python $C/example/run_particlize.py --leg jet --events 10 --out-dir out_particlize
python $C/example/run_particlize.py --leg bg  --events 10 --out-dir out_particlize --oversample 200
python $C/example/delta_spectra.py --out-dir out_particlize --npz out_particlize/delta.npz
```

An event's initial condition depends only on the seed and the event index, so event *k* of the background run is the background of event *k* of the jet run; both record the initial condition's hash, and `delta_spectra.py` refuses to pair events whose hashes differ. It prints every (jet − background) difference with its compound-Poisson error: the wake's tens of GeV sit on about 10⁴ GeV of bulk, so the background's sampling noise decides how many oversamples a signal needs.

The driver refuses settings that cannot give a meaningful surface: frames zeroed after freeze-out (`output.zero_after_freezeout` / `stop_at_freezeout` must be off), and an EoS whose hadron list iSS does not decay. Use `eos.kind: hotqcd` (MUSIC EOS 9, the UrQMD list, decayed by iSS); `hotqcd_smash` (EOS 91) needs SMASH as an afterburner.

Checked with Israel–Stewart (η/s = 0.08), 2 central events × 200 oversamples, mid-rapidity:

|                       | FastHydro + iSS  | PHENIX 0–5 %        |
| --------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------- |
| dN_ch/dη              | 637              | ~650–690            |
| dN/dy π⁺, K⁺, p       | 292, 56, 17.4    | ~286, ~49, ~18      |
| ⟨p_T⟩ π⁺, K⁺, p [GeV] | 0.51, 0.74, 1.03 | ~0.45, ~0.67, ~0.95 |

⟨p_T⟩ is about 10 % harder than data: there is no δf and no hadronic cascade. The surface conserves entropy (98 % of the hydro's total at τ₀ on an ideal run).

## Comparison with MUSIC, and the 0–10 % tune

`notebooks/bulk_vs_music.ipynb` compares FastHydro's hadrons with 3D MC-Glauber + MUSIC + iSS, 0–10 % Au+Au (`example/make_bulk_comparison_data.py` makes its inputs). On 25 events per model:

- **The initial state alone is close.** Against MUSIC with FastHydro's transport and no δf, FastHydro's multiplicity is 9 % lower, ⟨p_T⟩ 3–4 % softer for every species, and the dN/dη shape agrees to 1 % in width.
- **Transport matters more.** MUSIC's calibrated bulk viscosity and δf add 23 % multiplicity and lower ⟨p_T⟩ by 7–13 %.
- **The tune.** τ₀ = 0.5 fm/c, `target_T` = 0.418, η/s = 0.08, ζ/s = 0.12, b ∈ [0, 4.7] fm matches calibrated MUSIC in dN_ch/dη at mid-rapidity (−1 %) and in π and K ⟨p_T⟩ (+1.5 %, −0.6 %). Protons stay about 7 % soft and dN/dη 7–9 % wide at |η| ≈ 3.

The tune comes as two configuration pairs on the same medium:

| pair                                                   | for                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `config/AuAu_FastHydro_tune_0_10_particles.{yaml,xml}` | spectra: iSS on one leg, every frame kept                 |
| `config/AuAu_FastHydro_tune_0_10_wake.{yaml,xml}`      | jet-wake pairs (`arr`, `arr_bg`, `source/`), parton level |

```bash
python $C/example/run_particlize.py --leg bg --events 25 --oversample 100 --set run.device=cuda \
    --config $C/config/AuAu_FastHydro_tune_0_10_particles.yaml \
    --user-xml $C/config/AuAu_FastHydro_tune_0_10_particles.xml
python $C/example/make_wake_data.py --medium tune_0_10 --legs visc --device cuda
python $C/example/make_hadron_wake_data.py --medium tune_0_10 --device cuda
```

On this medium use only the viscous leg for wake runs: the "ideal" leg drops the tuned shear and bulk viscosity.

## Output format

The file is FNO4d's HDF5 layout, written with `fast_data`'s own writer, so every FNO4d reader loads it:

```text
arr               (N, 4, nx, ny, neta, ntau) f4   the JET leg   [e, vx, vy, vz]
arr_bg            (N, 4, nx, ny, neta, ntau) f4   the background leg
source/S          (N, 4, nx, ny, neta, ntau) f4   what was injected (contravariant Milne)
source/droplets   (M, 8) f8                       tau, x, y, eta, E, px, py, pz
source/offsets    (N+1,) i8                       per-event slices into droplets
shower/partons, shower/vertices, shower/initiators, and their offsets
ntau_freezeout[_bg], tau_freezeout[_bg]           per leg
diag/                                             per-event scalars: n_droplets, ic_sha256, ...
```

- `e` is in GeV/fm³, `vx, vy, vz` are Cartesian lab velocities; attributes record the full resolved configuration as JSON.
- **`arr` is the jet leg**, following `fast_data`'s convention: `arr` together with `source/S` is what a deposition FNO consumes. `arr_bg` is the same initial condition without the jet.
- **`arr` is not `arr_bg + S`.** The fluid keeps responding after the last droplet has fired, and the response spreads far beyond the cells the source touched. That propagating difference, the wake, is the physics.
- **The shower** costs about 9 kB per event against 5.5 MB for the hydro pair, and is stored by default (`fasthydro.store_showers: false` turns it off). Shower positions are Cartesian `(x, y, z, t)` and live on the partons; X-SCAPE's vertices carry only a time.

Read a pair with `PairBrowser`:

```python
from fasthydro.browse import PairBrowser

p = PairBrowser("out_wake/wake_ideal.h5")
p.summary()                          # IC identical, first differing frame, deposit, freeze-out
p.diff(0, k)                         # e(jet) - e(background), event 0, frame k
p.source_at(0, tau)                  # where the jet was, from the droplet table
par, ver, ini = p.showers(0)         # the shower graph of event 0
start, tip, alive = p.shower_at(0, 3.0)   # the shower as it stands at t = 3 fm/c
```

`PairBrowser` also opens the MUSIC pair files of the [Au+Au jet production](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/run/auau-jet/index.md), which use this layout. Two diagnostics are worth reading after every run: the energy of droplets that would deposit after the end of the τ window (often 20 % or more with a short window; fix with a longer `time.choose_ntau` or a smaller `tau_delay`), and the count of medium queries outside the grid (a grid too small silently removes quenching).

## Notebooks

| notebook                        |                                                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `notebooks/jet_wake.ipynb`      | the wake in the medium: Mach cone, damping, broadening, Mach angle (inputs: `make_wake_data.py`)                                                 |
| `notebooks/hadron_wake.ipynb`   | the wake in the hadrons: Δφ and (Δη, Δφ) maps with significance, the near-side excess, the momentum balance (inputs: `make_hadron_wake_data.py`) |
| `notebooks/bulk_vs_music.ipynb` | bulk observables against 3D MC-Glauber + MUSIC, 0–10 % (inputs: `make_bulk_comparison_data.py`)                                                  |

## Limitations

- **Soft hadrons only, ideal Cooper–Frye.** The viscous stresses are stored as zero, so iSS applies no δf (exact for ideal runs, an approximation for viscous ones). The jet's surviving partons are not hadronized.
- **No hadronic afterburner** in the default build; iSS decays the resonances itself.
- **The η edges are open**: analyse at mid-rapidity.
- **The surface lattice is coarser than the hydro grid** (twice the spacing in the shipped XML) to keep the surface finder affordable.
- **Bulk viscosity is untested upstream**, and the non-conformal viscous sector has no analytic benchmark.

## Tests

```bash
pytest tests -q
FAST_DATA_FULL_SELFTEST=1 pytest tests/test_fast_data_selftests.py   # the solver's physics gates
```

Tests that need `pyjetscape_core` skip cleanly without a build. Among them: zero droplets give a jet leg equal to the background bit for bit, four-momentum is conserved to 1e-10, and the Python deposit kernel matches the real C++ one.

The full documentation, with every measurement and design decision: [`contribs/FastHydro/README.md`](https://github.com/jhputschke/js-contrib/blob/main/contribs/FastHydro/README.md).
