### Nested views with awkward

`to_awkward()` makes a nested view of the same arrays, with four-vector kinematics. `by_unit=True` nests the bulk as **events × oversamples × hadrons**.

`js.select` picks species, by their names in the [particle](https://github.com/scikit-hep/particle) package (`"pi+"`, `["K+", "K-"]`, `["p", "p~"]`) or by class (`"charged"`, `"meson"`, `"baryon"`, `"strange"`). It returns a mask of the same nesting, so `b[js.select(b, "charged")]` keeps the charged hadrons of every oversample. For decayed hadrons, as here, `"charged"` picks exactly the stable charged hadrons (and leptons) of `hadrons_h5.CHARGED`, the list all the analysis tools use. `ak.num` and `ak.sum` count along an axis, and the mean over the oversamples of an event (`axis=1`) is that event's average:

```python
b = bulk.to_awkward(by_unit=True)                   # events x oversamples x hadrons
j = jet.to_awkward()                                # events x hadrons
per_event = lambda counts: np.round(ak.to_numpy(ak.mean(counts, axis=1)), 1).tolist()

print("bulk hadrons per oversample:", per_event(ak.num(b, axis=2)))
for label, names in [("pi+-", ["pi+", "pi-"]), ("K+-", ["K+", "K-"]), ("p, pbar", ["p", "p~"])]:
    print(f"  {label:8s}", per_event(ak.sum(js.select(b, names), axis=2)))
ch = b[js.select(b, "charged")]                     # the charged bulk hadrons
print("charged at |eta| < 0.5:", per_event(ak.sum(abs(ch.eta) < 0.5, axis=2)))
j_ch = j[js.select(j, "charged")]
print("jet hadrons per event:", ak.num(j).tolist(), "| charged:", ak.num(j_ch).tolist())
```

```
bulk hadrons per oversample: [425.0, 321.1, 325.9]
```

```
  pi+-     [191.6, 144.6, 146.8]
  K+-      [34.2, 25.5, 26.2]
  p, pbar  [16.8, 12.8, 12.9]
charged at |eta| < 0.5: [27.5, 19.3, 22.1]
jet hadrons per event: [116, 171, 136] | charged: [56, 78, 56]
```

Pions dominate the bulk: they are the lightest hadrons, and many come from the decays of heavier resonances. The multiplicity differs strongly from event to event, which reflects the geometry and the strings of each collision (compare with `npart` and `strings` above).

### `$dN/d\eta$` and `$p_T$` spectra

Now as histograms, with [hist](https://hist.readthedocs.io) and `Weight` storage, which keeps the statistical errors. Each bulk hadron is weighted by `$1/N_\text{oversamples}$`, so the yields are **per oversample**, that is per collision. The errors are the sampling errors of the oversamples only: the three collisions are three different events, not three measurements of one.

```python
import hist
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import mplhep as mh

n_os = ak.num(b, axis=1).to_numpy()                 # oversamples per event (100)
flat = lambda a: ak.to_numpy(ak.flatten(a, axis=None))

h_eta = (hist.Hist.new.Integer(0, len(b), name="event", label="event")
         .Reg(40, -5, 5, name="eta", label=r"$\eta$").Weight())
for e in range(len(b)):
    h_eta.fill(event=e, eta=flat(ch[e].eta), weight=1.0 / n_os[e])

PT = hist.axis.Regular(16, 0, 4, name="pt", label=r"$p_T$ [GeV]")
h_bulk = hist.Hist(PT, storage=hist.storage.Weight())
h_jet = hist.Hist(PT, storage=hist.storage.Weight())
for e in range(len(b)):
    h_bulk.fill(pt=flat(ch[e].pt[abs(ch[e].eta) < 1]), weight=1.0 / (n_os[e] * len(b) * 2.0))
    h_jet.fill(pt=flat(j_ch[e].pt[abs(j_ch[e].eta) < 1]), weight=1.0 / (len(b) * 2.0))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
w_eta = h_eta.axes["eta"].widths[0]
for e in range(len(b)):
    mh.histplot(h_eta[e, :] / w_eta, ax=ax[0], flow="none",
                label=f"event {e}: npart {base.npart[e]}, {base.strings[e]} strings")
ax[0].set(ylabel=r"$dN_{ch}/d\eta$ per oversample", title="charged bulk hadrons, O+O 200 GeV")
ax[0].legend(fontsize=8)
mh.histplot(h_bulk / PT.widths, ax=ax[1], flow="none", label="bulk (iSS)")
mh.histplot(h_jet / PT.widths, ax=ax[1], flow="none", label="jet hadrons (iColored)")
ax[1].set(yscale="log", ylabel=r"$dN_{ch}/dp_T\,d\eta$ per event [GeV$^{-1}$]",
          title=r"charged hadrons, $|\eta| < 1$, mean of the 3 events")
ax[1].legend()
fig.tight_layout()
```

**What to notice.**

- **Each collision has its own `$dN/d\eta$`.** The heights differ by up to a factor 1.4, and the shapes are lumpy and asymmetric: the strings break the boost invariance along the beam, so an event can have more hadrons on one side. Smooth, symmetric distributions appear only after averaging over many events (tutorial 05). The 100 oversamples reduce the sampling noise, not these event-by-event fluctuations: they all come from the same fluid.
- **The bulk dominates at low `$p_T$`, the jet at high `$p_T$`.** The bulk spectrum falls about exponentially, as for a thermal source moving with the flow. The jet hadrons fall much more slowly and take over above about 1 GeV. Below 1 GeV they are still about half as many as the bulk hadrons: iColoredHadronization strings the jet partons together with the remnants of the two colliding nucleons, and those strings make soft hadrons too. In a small system like O+O, the hard scattering is a sizable part of the whole event.

## 4. Change one setting: the shear viscosity

Now a physics question. How does the friction of the plasma, its shear viscosity, change what comes out? The relevant quantity is the ratio of the shear viscosity to the entropy density, `$\eta/s$`. Strongly coupled theories suggest a lower bound near `$1/4\pi \approx 0.08$`, and the QGP is thought to be close to it: it is the most nearly perfect fluid known.

In this XML, `$\eta/s$` depends on the temperature: it is smallest at a *kink* temperature `$T_k$` = 206 MeV and rises linearly on both sides,

`$\frac{\eta}{s}(T) = \left(\frac{\eta}{s}\right)_k + a_{\pm}\,(T - T_k),$`

with `$a_\pm = \pm 1.999$` GeV`$^{-1}$`. We raise `$(\eta/s)_k$` from 0.108 to 0.30, which shifts the whole curve up by 0.19, and change **nothing else**:

```python
KINK = "Hydro/MUSIC/shear_viscosity_3_at_kink"
tree = ET.parse(BASE_XML)
tree.getroot().find(KINK).text = "0.30"
ETA_XML = OUT / "oo_eta030.xml"
tree.write(ETA_XML)

def eta_over_s(T, xml_path):
    """MUSIC's eta/s(T) for T_dependent_Shear_to_S_ratio 3, from the XML's settings."""
    m = ET.parse(xml_path).getroot().find("Hydro/MUSIC")
    f = lambda tag: float(m.findtext(tag))
    kink, Tk = f("shear_viscosity_3_at_kink"), f("shear_viscosity_3_T_kink_in_GeV")
    slope = np.where(T < Tk, f("shear_viscosity_3_low_T_slope_in_GeV"),
                     f("shear_viscosity_3_high_T_slope_in_GeV"))
    return np.maximum(kink + slope * (T - Tk), 1e-3)

T = np.linspace(0.15, 0.40, 200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 3.5))
ax.plot(T * 1000, eta_over_s(T, BASE_XML), label=r"$(\eta/s)_k$ = 0.108 (the XML)")
ax.plot(T * 1000, eta_over_s(T, ETA_XML), label=r"$(\eta/s)_k$ = 0.30")
ax.axhline(1 / (4 * np.pi), color="0.5", ls=":", label=r"$1/4\pi$")
ax.set(xlabel="T [MeV]", ylabel=r"$\eta/s$", ylim=(0, None))
ax.legend(fontsize=9);
```

What should change? Right after the collision the fluid expands fastest along the beam. Shear viscosity resists this anisotropic expansion: it lowers the pressure along the beam and raises it in the transverse plane. More viscous fluid therefore pushes outward harder, builds up more *radial flow*, and its hadrons come out with larger `$p_T$`. Viscosity also produces entropy, so a little more multiplicity is expected.

### Making the comparison fair

With three events, the differences between collisions (up to a factor 1.4 in multiplicity) are far larger than the effect we look for. So we compare **the same three collisions**, once with each value. We run the new XML with the same seed. The modules before the hydro then draw the same random numbers: the same nucleons, strings and hard scattering. MUSIC itself has no random numbers. Any difference in the fluid then comes from `$\eta/s$` alone.

This only works when the change keeps the list of modules. The modules take their random numbers from engines seeded from the one seed, in the order of the task list. A module added or removed can change what the others receive, and the events stop matching (exercise 2). We check that the inputs agree, event by event:

```python
eta = run(ETA_XML, "oo_eta030")
inputs = ["pthat", "npart", "ncoll", "strings", "b", "E sources [GeV]", "iSS seed"]
same = (base[inputs] == eta[inputs]).all()
print("identical in both runs:", same.to_dict())
pd.concat({"eta/s 0.108": base[inputs], "eta/s 0.30": eta[inputs]}, axis=1).round(2)
```

```
oo_eta030: 3 events in 20 s; modules: MCGlauber -> PythiaGun (IsrManager, MCGlauberGenString) -> NullPreDynamics -> MUSIC -> JLossManager (JetEnergyLoss) -> HadronizationManager (Hadronization) -> iSS
identical in both runs: {'pthat': True, 'npart': True, 'ncoll': True, 'strings': True, 'b': True, 'E sources [GeV]': True, 'iSS seed': True}
```

The hard scattering, the geometry, the energy MUSIC received from the strings and remnants, and even the seed iSS sampled with: all identical. The two runs differ in the fluid only.

### The fluid

The freeze-out surface needs no sampling, so its numbers carry no statistical error. The table compares its lifetime, its number of cells and the mean transverse flow on it, each cell weighted by the fluid that crosses it. The figure shows, on the left, a cut through event 0's surface at `$y \approx 0$`, `$\eta_s \approx 0$`, colored by the flow `$u^x$` (positive outward on the right, negative on the left), and on the right the distribution of the transverse flow `$u_T$` over the whole surface, for both runs:

```python
fluid = pd.DataFrame({
    "tau_max 0.108": base.tau_max, "tau_max 0.30": eta.tau_max,
    "<u_T> 0.108": base.flow_uT, "<u_T> 0.30": eta.flow_uT,
    "<u_T> ratio": eta.flow_uT / base.flow_uT,
    "cells ratio": eta.cells / base.cells,
})
display(fluid.round(3))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.8))
cut = np.load(OUT / "oo_base_surface.npz")["event0"]          # tau, x, u^x of the cells
sc = ax[0].scatter(cut[:, 1], cut[:, 0], c=cut[:, 2], s=5, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-0.6, vmax=0.6)
fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax[0], label=r"flow $u^x$")
ax[0].set(xlabel="x [fm]", ylabel=r"$\tau$ [fm/c]",
          title=r"event 0: the freeze-out surface at $y, \eta_s \approx 0$")
UT = hist.axis.Regular(40, 0, 1, name="uT", label=r"transverse flow $u_T$ on the surface")
for name, label in [("oo_base", r"$(\eta/s)_k$ = 0.108"), ("oo_eta030", r"$(\eta/s)_k$ = 0.30")]:
    with np.load(OUT / f"{name}_surface.npz") as f:
        w = sum(f[f"event{e}_uT"] for e in range(3))           # the 3 events, weighted cells
    mh.histplot(w / w.sum(), UT.edges, ax=ax[1], label=label)
ax[1].set(ylabel="fraction of the fluid", title="all 3 events")
ax[1].legend()
fig.tight_layout()
```

|       | tau_max 0.108 | tau_max 0.30 | \<u_T> 0.108 | \<u_T> 0.30 | \<u_T> ratio | cells ratio |
| ----- | ------------- | ------------ | ------------ | ----------- | ------------ | ----------- |
| event |               |              |              |             |              |             |
| 0     | 4.293         | 4.230        | 0.177        | 0.194       | 1.099        | 1.010       |

| 2     | 4.079         | 4.040        | 0.199        | 0.216       | 1.083        | 1.006       |

**What to notice.**

- **The surface has the shape of a fireball.** The fluid's edge stays near `$|x| \approx 3.3$` fm until `$\tau \approx 3$` fm/c, then the cold region eats its way in, and the middle freezes out last, at `$\tau \approx 4.3$` fm/c. The flow points outward everywhere (red on the right, blue on the left). On the edge it grows with time, up to `$u^x \approx 0.5$`; toward the middle it falls to zero.
- **The more viscous fluid flows faster.** Its `$u_T$` distribution is shifted slightly up, and the mean transverse flow on the surface is higher by 8–10 % in every event, with the same initial state. The lifetime and the number of cells change by about 1 % only.
- **About a fifth of the fluid has no transverse flow.** That is the spike at `$u_T = 0$`: fluid that is already below 150 MeV when the hydro starts, mostly far forward and backward along the beam. It freezes out at once, before any flow builds up.

### The hadrons

The bulk hadrons are sampled, so their averages have errors. With 100 oversamples per event, the error of the mean `$p_T$` is about 1 %:

```python
def bulk_summary(name):
    """dNch/deta at |eta| < 0.5 and mean pT of the charged bulk hadrons at |eta| < 1, per event."""
    a = js.HadronArray.from_h5(OUT / f"{name}_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5").to_awkward(by_unit=True)
    c = a[js.select(a, "charged")]
    rows = []
    for e in range(len(c)):
        n = len(c[e])
        mid = flat(abs(c[e].eta) < 0.5).sum()
        pt = flat(c[e].pt[abs(c[e].eta) < 1])
        rows.append({"dNch/deta": mid / n, "error": np.sqrt(mid) / n,
                     "<pT>": pt.mean(), "<pT> error": pt.std() / np.sqrt(len(pt))})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

hb, he = bulk_summary("oo_base"), bulk_summary("oo_eta030")
change = pd.DataFrame({
    "dNch/deta change [%]": 100 * (he["dNch/deta"] / hb["dNch/deta"] - 1),
    "in errors": (he["dNch/deta"] - hb["dNch/deta"]) / np.hypot(he["error"], hb["error"]),
    "<pT> change [%]": 100 * (he["<pT>"] / hb["<pT>"] - 1),
    "in errors ": (he["<pT>"] - hb["<pT>"]) / np.hypot(he["<pT> error"], hb["<pT> error"]),
})
pd.concat({"eta/s 0.108": hb, "eta/s 0.30": he, "0.30 vs 0.108": change}, axis=1).round(3)
```

|     | eta/s 0.108 |       |       |            | eta/s 0.30 |       |       |            | 0.30 vs 0.108        |           |                 |           |
| --- | ----------- | ----- | ----- | ---------- | ---------- | ----- | ----- | ---------- | -------------------- | --------- | --------------- | --------- |
|     | dNch/deta   | error | <pT>  | <pT> error | dNch/deta  | error | <pT>  | <pT> error | dNch/deta change [%] | in errors | <pT> change [%] | in errors |
| 0   | 27.46       | 0.524 | 0.424 | 0.004      | 27.94      | 0.529 | 0.444 | 0.004      | 1.748                | 0.645     | 4.674           | 3.763     |
| 1   | 19.32       | 0.440 | 0.401 | 0.004      | 19.94      | 0.447 | 0.421 | 0.004      | 3.209                | 0.990     | 5.071           | 3.523     |
| 2   | 22.06       | 0.470 | 0.420 | 0.004      | 22.35      | 0.473 | 0.432 | 0.004      | 1.315                | 0.435     | 2.910           | 2.143     |

```python
def bulk_pt(name):
    """The charged bulk pT spectrum at |eta| < 1, per event and oversample, of all events."""
    a = js.HadronArray.from_h5(OUT / f"{name}_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5").to_awkward(by_unit=True)
    c = a[js.select(a, "charged")]
    h = hist.Hist(PT, storage=hist.storage.Weight())
    for e in range(len(c)):
        h.fill(pt=flat(c[e].pt[abs(c[e].eta) < 1]), weight=1.0 / (len(c[e]) * len(c) * 2.0))
    return h / PT.widths

s_base, s_eta = bulk_pt("oo_base"), bulk_pt("oo_eta030")
v1, v0 = s_eta.values(), s_base.values()
filled = (v0 > 0) & (v1 > 0)                         # bins with hadrons in both runs
ratio = np.where(filled, v1 / np.where(filled, v0, 1), np.nan)
rel = s_eta.variances() / np.where(filled, v1, 1) ** 2 + s_base.variances() / np.where(filled, v0, 1) ** 2
ratio_err = np.where(filled, ratio * np.sqrt(rel), 0)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
mh.histplot(s_base, ax=ax[0], flow="none", label=r"$(\eta/s)_k$ = 0.108")
mh.histplot(s_eta, ax=ax[0], flow="none", label=r"$(\eta/s)_k$ = 0.30")
ax[0].set(yscale="log", ylabel=r"$dN_{ch}/dp_T\,d\eta$ per event [GeV$^{-1}$]",
          title=r"charged bulk hadrons, $|\eta| < 1$, the same 3 events")
ax[0].legend()
mh.histplot(ratio, PT.edges, yerr=ratio_err, ax=ax[1], histtype="errorbar", flow="none")
ax[1].axhline(1, color="0.5", lw=0.8)
ax[1].set(xlabel=PT.label, ylabel="0.30 / 0.108", xlim=(0, 2.5), ylim=(0.5, 2), title="ratio")
fig.tight_layout()
```

**What to notice.**

- **The mean `$p_T$` rises in each event,** by 3–5 %, two to four times the error of the difference. The multiplicity rises too, but only by 1–3 %, within about one error per event.
- **The ratio of the spectra rises with `$p_T$`.** Below 0.5 GeV the two runs agree; above, the more viscous fluid gives more hadrons, up to about 25 % more near 1–1.5 GeV: a flatter, *harder* spectrum. This is the stronger radial flow of the surface, now in the hadrons. The viscous correction `$\delta f$` that iSS adds to the hadrons' momentum distribution grows with `$\eta/s$` too, and also shapes the spectrum. Above about 1.5 GeV the errors are large: there are few bulk hadrons there.

This is how `$\eta/s$` is constrained in practice: its effects on spectra and flow are compared over many events, with everything else fixed, and fitted to data. The famous signature is the *elliptic flow* `$v_2$`, which viscosity damps. In central O+O collisions `$v_2$` comes from fluctuations and is small, so measuring it needs many more events than three.

## 5. Without the notebook

The same run, as a script, is the example the notebook started from. In your copy of the examples (`xscape-examples` makes one; in a checkout it is `contribs/PyJetscape/example/pythonic/`):

```
python oo_workflow.py --xml <this folder>/out/02_first_events/oo_eta030.xml --outdir out_eta030
python oo_workflow.py --events 10 --seed 3 --outdir out_oo_s3
```

It writes the same two kinds of hadron files. And X-SCAPE runs a user XML without Python at all, with its own executable. On a Mac, the wheel's `xscape-run` copies both XMLs into a run directory, makes their paths absolute, links the tables and checks the XML before it starts:

```
xscape-run -w ~/xscape/runs/oo -u <this folder>/out/02_first_events/oo_base.xml
```

Then X-SCAPE's own writers decide what is stored, and this XML switches them all off: set, for example, `<JetScapeWriterFinalStateHadronsAscii> on </JetScapeWriterFinalStateHadronsAscii>` in a copy. In a source build the script behind `xscape-run` is `X-SCAPE/examples/run_in_workdir.sh`. Details: [Your first event](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/run/first-event/#the-same-xml-without-python-xscape-run).

### Check your result

Your numbers come from your own run of X-SCAPE. With the same build they are the ones shown, bit for bit. Another GPU, or MUSIC on the CPU, changes them slightly, and another build of PYTHIA or 3dMCGlauber can give other collisions altogether. The check allows for that: the comparison must be fair and show the same physics everywhere, and the numbers must match where the collisions do:

```python
import json
exp = json.load(open("expected/02_first_events.json"))
# on any setup: a fair comparison, and the physics
assert same.all(), "the two runs must have the same inputs"
assert (eta.flow_uT > base.flow_uT).all() and (he["<pT>"] > hb["<pT>"]).all()
# the same collisions as shown here (seed 7), unless your build of PYTHIA or 3dMCGlauber differs
if np.allclose(base.pthat, exp["pthat"], rtol=1e-6):
    assert (base.npart.tolist(), base.ncoll.tolist()) == (exp["npart"], exp["ncoll"])
    np.testing.assert_allclose(base.cells, exp["cells"], rtol=0.02)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(hb["dNch/deta"], exp["dNch_deta"], rtol=0.1)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(hb["<pT>"], exp["mean_pt"], rtol=0.03)
else:
    print("Your collisions differ from the ones shown (another build): only the physics was checked.")
print("All checks pass.")
```

```
All checks pass.
```

## Exercises

1. **Another setting.** Switch the bulk viscosity off (`bulk_viscosity_3_max` 0), or lower `$(\eta/s)_k$` to 0.08, and compare with the first run the same way. Which way does the mean `$p_T$` move?
1. **Removing a module.** Delete the `<Lbt>` element from a copy of `oo_base.xml` (so that only MATTER acts on the jets) and run it. Compare the inputs table with the first run: which events are still the same collisions? How would you switch LBT off and keep the events? (Look at `<in_vac>` in the XML.)
1. **The jets.** In `oo_base_partons.npz` and `oo_eta030_partons.npz`, compare the recoils and holes of each event. Does the jet lose more energy in the more viscous fluid? Think about which medium property the energy loss reads (temperature, flow) before you look.
1. **More events.** Run 10 events with each `$\eta/s$` (edit `nEvents`, or use `oo_workflow.py`) and compare the mean `$p_T$` averaged over events, with the event-to-event spread as its error.

# 03 · The production scripts

**Time:** 45 minutes · **Needs:** X-SCAPE (the production container, the Mac wheel or a source build) · **Data:** `auau_stats` and `auau_pair_mini`: a few job records (kB) and one table; the notebook makes its own job (about 0.7 GB in `out/`)

Tutorial 02 ran events from a Python loop. For physics you need thousands of events, made the same way, recorded so that they can be checked, combined and shared. That is what the *production scripts* do. This tutorial runs one real production job, a central Au+Au collision with two jets, through both stages, and looks at every file each step writes:

- the driver `run_prod_jet.py`, its user XML and its options;
- seeds, and why a seed is a set of collisions;
- stage 2: hadronization with `hadronize.py`, and the ROOT conversion;
- `$\hat p_T$` windows and their cross sections, hadrons made in the job, correlated sampling;
- how many jobs make a campaign, how it is watched, and how its files are shared on the OSDF.

The job is a small copy of the one behind the data set `auau_pair_mini` of tutorials 04, 06 and 07, and the last section shows the recipe of all the tutorial data.

Reference pages: [Running the productions](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/run/), [Au+Au jets](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/run/auau-jet/), [Clusters, GPUs and monitoring](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/run/clusters/), [Data on the OSDF](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/run/osdf/).

> **Work in progress: examples, not vetted physics.** The tutorials show how to run the simulation and use its outputs. The data sets are small, so the statistics are low, and the analyses have not been checked to the standard of a publication: treat every number and figure as an illustration, not as a physics result.

> **The outputs shown** were produced on an Apple Silicon Mac, in the environment the xscape wheel 0.2.0 is built in, with the hydro on the GPU through Metal.

## 1. Jobs and campaigns

A **production** is a folder of ready-made scripts for one physics setup. Its **driver** runs one **job**: one seed, N events, one set of output files. A **campaign** is many jobs of the same setup, each with its own seed, run side by side on one or many GPUs. Every production works this way:

| production           | physics                                                                          | driver               |
| -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| `prod_AuAu_0_10`     | 0–10 % Au+Au at 200 GeV, hydro only                                              | `run_prod.py`        |
| `prod_AuAu_0_10_jet` | the same medium with a jet, whose lost energy flows back into a second hydro run | `run_prod_jet.py`    |
| `prod_OO_isr`        | O+O at 200 GeV with initial-state radiation (tutorial 02's chain)                | `run_prod_oo_isr.py` |

We use the main production, `prod_AuAu_0_10_jet`. Its folder holds the driver, the stage-2 scripts and `run_jobs.sh` for campaigns. In the container and the Mac wheel the scripts sit in a read-only place, which is fine: they write only into the output directory we give them. The helper `script` runs one of them with this notebook's Python, in a process of its own, and shortens the paths in what it prints:

```python
import json, re, shutil, subprocess, sys, time
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from jetscape import paths

EX = paths.examples_dir()                      # the examples: the productions and their XMLs
PROD = EX / "prod_AuAu_0_10_jet"
OUT = Path("out/03_production").resolve()      # this tutorial's files (out/ is git-ignored)
JOB = OUT / "AuAu"                             # the job's output directory
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
for old in [JOB, OUT / "demo"]:                # a second run of the notebook starts afresh
    shutil.rmtree(old, ignore_errors=True)

SHORT = [(str(JOB), "out/03_production/AuAu"), (str(OUT), "out/03_production"),
         (str(PROD), "<prod>"), (str(EX), "<examples>"), (str(paths.build_dir()), "<build>"),
         (str(paths.xscape_root()), "<X-SCAPE>")]

def tidy(text):
    """This machine's paths -> short names."""
    for long, short in SHORT:
        text = text.replace(long, short)
    return text

def script(name, *args, log=None):
    """Run a script of the production folder in a new process -> (its output, seconds).
    The full output also goes to the file `log`, if given."""
    t0 = time.time()
    done = subprocess.run([sys.executable, PROD / name, *map(str, args)], cwd=OUT, text=True,
                          stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT)
    if log:
        Path(log).write_text(done.stdout)
    if done.returncode != 0:
        print(tidy(done.stdout[-3000:]))
        raise RuntimeError(f"{name} failed")
    return tidy(done.stdout), time.time() - t0

print(sorted(p.name for p in PROD.iterdir() if p.suffix in (".py", ".sh")))
```

```

```

```python
    return m.group(0).rstrip()

            "--seed", "--outdir"]:
```

## 2. The user XML and the job XML

The physics is in a **user XML**, as in tutorial 02. The production's template is `config/AuAu_MCGlauber_MUSIC_0_10_jet.xml`: the initial state, the hydro with its viscosities, Matter and LBT, the liquefier that turns the jet's lost energy into sources for the fluid. The driver takes it, or your own with `--user-xml my.xml`, and fills in what belongs to the job: the number of events, the seed, the hard process and its window, what to store. It checks the result and writes it next to the output, as `<stem>.xml`; the same text goes into the files (tutorial 04).

So, **to change the physics**, copy the template, edit the copy and pass it with `--user-xml`; **to change the job**, use the options. A dry run (`--dry-run`) checks everything, writes the job XML and prints the plan, without running an event. Here is our job, a small copy of the one behind `auau_pair_mini`:

```python
JOB_ARGS = ["--events", 2, "--reuse", 2, "--seed", 101, "--pthat-min", 30, "--pthat-max", 40,
            "--parton-ymax", 0.6, "--write-particlize", "both", "--outdir", JOB]
plan, _ = script("run_prod_jet.py", *JOB_ARGS, "--dry-run")
print(plan)
```

The first line is the plan: 2 events with seed 101, PYTHIA with `$\hat p_T$` 30–40 GeV and the leading parton at `$|y| < 0.6$`, one background for both jets (`reuse 2`), the jet's energy deposited in the fluid, and both freeze-out surfaces stored for hadronization. The output grid is the one the hydro history is stored on (tutorial 06). What did the driver change in the template? We compare the two XMLs element by element:

```python
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

def leaves(el, path=""):
    """{path: text} of every element without children."""
    out = {}
    for child in el:
        if not isinstance(child.tag, str):
            continue                                  # a comment
        p = f"{path}/{child.tag}"
        while p in out:
            p += "+"                                  # a repeated tag
        out.update(leaves(child, p) if len(child) else {p: (child.text or "").strip()})
    return out

template = leaves(ET.parse(EX / "config" / "AuAu_MCGlauber_MUSIC_0_10_jet.xml").getroot())
job_xml = leaves(ET.parse(JOB / "AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0101.xml").getroot())
changed = [(k, template.get(k, "(absent)"), job_xml.get(k, "(absent)"))
           for k in sorted(set(template) | set(job_xml)) if template.get(k) != job_xml.get(k)]
pd.DataFrame(changed, columns=["element", "template", "job"]).set_index("element")
```

| ----------------------------------- | -------- | ------- |
| element                             |          |         |

| /Hard/PythiaGun/pTHatMax            | 70       | 40.0    |
| /Hard/PythiaGun/pTHatMin            | 50       | 30.0    |
| /Hard/PythiaGun/partonYMax          | (absent) | 0.6     |

| /Hydro/MUSIC/freeze_out_surface     | 0        | 1       |

| /nEvents                            | 10       | 2       |
| /nReuseHydro                        | 1        | 2       |
| /setReuseHydro                      | false    | true    |

**What to notice.** Only the job changed: the number of events, the seed, the window and the parton cut of PYTHIA, the reuse of the background, and the freeze-out surface that the particlize file needs. Two technical switches come with them: `slim_bulk_info` (a smaller copy of the medium for the energy loss, with the same output) and the extra hard scatterings, off. Every physics setting is the template's. This is what makes the jobs of a campaign, and campaigns made months apart, comparable: each records its full XML, and you can check that the physics agrees (tutorial 04, section 7).

## 3. Seeds

`--seed S` sets X-SCAPE's `<Random><seed>`. Every random number of the job derives from it: the nucleons and strings of the initial state, PYTHIA's hard scattering, the energy loss. So **a seed is a set of collisions**: the same seed, XML and build give the same events, bit for bit. That is what you want to compare two settings on the same collisions (tutorial 02 did this with `$\eta/s$`), and exactly what you must avoid in a campaign meant to add statistics.

- **An explicit seed** (`--seed 101`) names the file (`..._seed0101.h5`) and reproduces it.
- **`--seed 0`** draws a new seed from the operating system's entropy, one that the *seed registry* has not seen, and records it in the files and the job record, so the job stays reproducible. The file is then named by the campaign and a job number (`AuAu_0_10_jet_<campaign>_0001.h5`). This is what campaigns use.
- **Not X-SCAPE's own seed 0.** In a plain X-SCAPE XML, seed 0 means "take the clock": PYTHIA then seeds itself from the time in seconds, so jobs started together get the same jets, and the seed is recorded nowhere. The drivers never pass 0 to X-SCAPE.
- **The seed registry** is `seeds_used.tsv` in the *parent* of the output directory: every job appends its seed, under a lock, and a seed used before is reported. Campaigns kept side by side in one directory share it. Our job writes to `out/03_production/AuAu`, so its registry is `out/03_production/seeds_used.tsv`.

## 4. Stage 1: hydro and jets

Now the job itself. The background (MUSIC_1) runs once; each of the two jets showers in it with Matter and LBT; the energy and momentum the jet loses becomes *droplets*, sources for a second hydro run with the same strings (MUSIC_2). One Au+Au jet event takes about 10–15 s on an Apple Silicon GPU, so the job takes well under a minute. Like `run_jobs.sh`, we keep the driver's output as `<stem>.log` in the output directory:

```python
STEM = "AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0101"
text, seconds = script("run_prod_jet.py", *JOB_ARGS, log=JOB / f"{STEM}.log")
for line in text.splitlines():
    if re.match(r"(PairH5Writer|ParticlizeH5Writer): event|\s+pTHat|restart", line):
        print(line)
print(f"stage 1: {seconds:.0f} s")
```

```

ParticlizeH5Writer: event 0: jet 1165243 cells, bg 1151293 cells, 49 final partons, bg_unit 0
```

Per event, the pair writer reports how many time frames each hydro leg has, how many droplets the jets deposited and how much energy they carried, and how many leading frames of the two legs are identical (before the first droplet arrives). The particlize writer reports the cells of each leg's freeze-out surface. The background (`bg`) is the same for both events: it was computed once.

The files of the job:

- **`<stem>.h5`**, the hydro **pair**: the jet leg and the background on the output grid. With a shared background it is stored once. This is the big one, and it is only needed for the hydro (tutorial 06) and for training the ML hydro.
- **`<stem>_particlize.h5`**: both freeze-out surfaces with their full viscous information, the final partons and the shower initiators: everything stage 2 needs, on its own.
- **`<stem>.xml`**: the job XML as run. **`<stem>.json`**: the **job record**, written at the end, below. **`<stem>.log`**: the driver's output.

### A seed is a set of collisions

The data set `auau_pair_mini` of tutorials 04, 06 and 07 was made with the same template, the same window and seed 101, but five jets per background (`--reuse 5`). A background is made once per `reuse` events, so its first two events should be ours (with the build the data were made with). The pair files record each event's `$\hat p_T$` and droplets (`diag/`):

**What to notice.** The first two events of the data set are our two events: the same hard scattering, the same 24 and 14 droplets with the same energy, the same hydro lifetimes. The other three events of the data set are the next jets on the same background. This is also how to extend a sample on purpose: same seed and settings, more events. And it is why two campaigns meant as independent statistics must never share seeds.

## 5. Stage 2: hadrons

`hadronize.py` turns one particlize file into hadrons, on the CPU, without MUSIC: iSS samples each stored freeze-out surface (the *bulk*), and PYTHIA fragments the stored final partons (the *jet fragments*). Since the surfaces are stored, stage 2 can be repeated any number of times, with more oversamples or other settings, without the expensive stage 1. The options we use:

- `--oversample 20`: iSS samples per surface. Productions use 100–500; we keep it small.
- `--n-frag 5`: PYTHIA fragmentations of each event's partons.
- `--correlated --common-seeds`: correlated sampling. Sample `$k$` of a jet event and sample `$k$` of its background use the same random numbers, addressed by the surface cell. Where the two surfaces agree, they give the same hadrons, so jet minus background, the jet's wake in hadrons, is far less noisy (tutorial 07).

Each unit (an event, or a background) gets its own seed, derived from the base seed (`--seed`, default 1), the particlize file's unique id, the tag and the unit, and recorded in the file. For a whole campaign, `run_hadronize.py` runs `hadronize.py` over a directory, several files at once, and skips files whose hadrons are complete.

```python
text, seconds = script("hadronize.py", JOB / f"{STEM}_particlize.h5", "--correlated",
                       "--common-seeds", "--oversample", 20, "--n-frag", 5,
                       log=JOB / f"{STEM}_hadronize.log")
for line in text.splitlines():
    if re.match(r"\s+(event|\d+ event|bulk_|jet_frag)", line):
        print(line)
print(f"stage 2: {seconds:.0f} s")
```

```
  2 event(s), tags bulk_jet, bulk_bg, jet_frag, iSS oversample 20, 5 fragmentation(s)/event, base seed 1, EOS 91 (SMASH list, decays: iSS, Breit-Wigner masses for the unstable daughters of channels closed at the pole masses; eta, Sigma0 stable), eCMforHadronization 200
  event 0, bulk_jet 169040 hadrons, bulk_bg (unit 0) 168432, jet_frag 36.6/sample
  event 1, bulk_jet 169041 hadrons, jet_frag 28.8/sample
  bulk_jet  -> out/03_production/AuAu/AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0101_hadrons_bulk_jet.h5 (10.2 MB)
  bulk_bg   -> out/03_production/AuAu/AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0101_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5 (4.6 MB)
  jet_frag  -> out/03_production/AuAu/AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0101_hadrons_jet_frag.h5 (0.2 MB)
stage 2: 8 s
```

Three hadron files, one per *tag*: `bulk_jet` (the jet event's fluid: the medium with the jet's wake), `bulk_bg` (the background's fluid) and `jet_frag` (the jet's own hadrons). What each holds, and the seeds:

```python
with h5py.File(JOB / f"{STEM}_particlize.h5") as f:
    uuid = f.attrs["file_uuid"]
rows = []
for tag in ["bulk_jet", "bulk_bg", "jet_frag"]:
    with h5py.File(JOB / f"{STEM}_hadrons_{tag}.h5") as f:
        u = f["units"]
        n = len(f["hadrons/pid"])
        rows.append({"tag": tag, "units (events)": u["event"][:].tolist(),
                     "samples per unit": u["n_samples"][:].tolist(),
                     "hadrons per sample": round(n / u["n_samples"][:].sum(), 1),
                     "seeds": u["seed"][:].tolist(),
                     "correlated": bool(f.attrs.get("correlated_sampling", False)),
                     "source_uuid matches": f.attrs["source_uuid"] == uuid})
hadrons = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("tag")
hadrons
```

|          | units (events) | samples per unit | hadrons per sample | seeds                  | correlated | source_uuid matches |
| -------- | -------------- | ---------------- | ------------------ | ---------------------- | ---------- | ------------------- |
| tag      |                |                  |                    |                        |            |                     |
| bulk_jet | [0, 1]         | [20, 20]         | 8452.0             | [12608650, 12608650]   | True       | True                |
| bulk_bg  | [0]            | [20]             | 8421.6             | [12608650]             | True       | True                |

**What to notice.**

- **One background unit for two events.** `bulk_bg` has a single unit: the background both jets shared. A jet event is `bulk_jet` + `jet_frag`; its background is `bulk_bg`'s unit `bg_unit` of the particlize file.
- **The common seeds.** Both `bulk_jet` units carry the seed of their background unit: that is `--common-seeds`. The jet fragments have their own seed per event.
- **About 8,400 hadrons per bulk sample** (all species, all rapidities: one central Au+Au collision), and a few tens per fragmentation of the jets.
- **`source_uuid`** ties each hadron file to its particlize file; the readers refuse mismatched files (tutorial 04).

## 7. `$\hat p_T$` windows and cross sections

The jet cross section falls steeply with `$p_T$`. A sample generated over one wide `$\hat p_T$` range would be almost all low-`$\hat p_T$` events. So the productions generate in **windows** of `$\hat p_T$` and weight each window by its cross section afterwards.

- `--pthat-min/--pthat-max` set one window (our job: 30–40 GeV).
- `--pthat-bins 10-20,20-30,30-50` runs K windows in one job, one PYTHIA per window with its own seed and cross section; event `$i$` uses window `$i \bmod K$`.
- `--jets-per-bin M` gives every background M jets in each window: `reuse` becomes `$K \times M$`, and the events per job must be a multiple of it. A background costs about as much as a jet leg, so sharing it saves nearly half the time.

PYTHIA estimates each window's cross section `$\sigma$` from the events it generates. With the parton cut (`--parton-ymax`) rejected events are regenerated, and `$\sigma$` is multiplied by the accepted fraction. Our job tried only 2 events, so its `$\sigma$` is a rough estimate; `auau_pair_mini` tried 6 for the same window:

```python
mini_record = json.loads(te.read_text("auau_pair_mini", f"{STEM}.json"))
for name, r in [("this job", record), ("auau_pair_mini", mini_record)]:
    print(f"{name:15s} sigma = {r['pthat_bin_sigma_gen_mb'][0]:.2e} mb from "
          f"{r['pthat_bin_n_tried'][0]} events tried, acceptance {r['pthat_bin_acceptance'][0]}")
```

```
this job        sigma = 1.33e-06 mb from 2 events tried, acceptance 1.0
auau_pair_mini  sigma = 2.09e-06 mb from 6 events tried, acceptance 0.8333
```

The two estimates of the same quantity differ by a factor 1.6: a single job's `$\sigma$` is noisy. A campaign combines the estimates of all its jobs. The data set `auau_stats` is a small campaign: 4 jobs of 30 events, three windows 10–20, 20–30 and 30–50 GeV, 2 jets per window per background. Each job recorded its own estimates, and the campaign file of `run_h5toROOT.py` holds the combination:

```python
per_job = []
for seed in [201, 202, 203, 204]:
    r = json.loads(te.read_text("auau_stats", f"AuAu_0_10_jet_stats_seed{seed:04d}.json"))
    per_job.append({"seed": seed, **{f"sigma {lo:.0f}-{hi:.0f} [mb]": s for (lo, hi), s in
                                     zip(r["pthat_bins"], r["pthat_bin_sigma_gen_mb"])},
                    "tried": r["pthat_bin_n_tried"], "reuse": r["reuse"], "wall_s": r["wall_s"]})
display(pd.DataFrame(per_job).set_index("seed").map(lambda v: f"{v:.2e}" if isinstance(v, float) and v < 0.1 else v))

with uproot.open(te.data("auau_stats", "stats_campaign.root")) as rf:
    windows = pd.DataFrame(rf["windows"].arrays(["pthat_lo", "pthat_hi", "sigma_mb", "sigma_err_mb",
                                                  "acceptance", "n_events", "weight_mb"], library="np"))
windows.map(lambda v: f"{v:.3g}")
```

|      | sigma 10-20 [mb] | sigma 20-30 [mb] | sigma 30-50 [mb] | tried        | reuse | wall_s |
| ---- | ---------------- | ---------------- | ---------------- | ------------ | ----- | ------ |
| seed |                  |                  |                  |              |       |        |
| 201  | 3.46e-03         | 4.97e-05         | 2.27e-06         | [19, 16, 15] | 6     | 327.8  |
| 202  | 2.37e-03         | 3.53e-05         | 2.13e-06         | [24, 20, 12] | 6     | 315.7  |
| 203  | 3.09e-03         | 3.95e-05         | 3.29e-06         | [14, 21, 12] | 6     | 377.7  |
| 204  | 2.69e-03         | 2.88e-05         | 2.65e-06         | [21, 24, 14] | 6     | 400.8  |

|     | pthat_lo | pthat_hi | sigma_mb | sigma_err_mb | acceptance | n_events | weight_mb |
| --- | -------- | -------- | -------- | ------------ | ---------- | -------- | --------- |
| 0   | 10       | 20       | 0.00285  | 0.000356     | 0.513      | 40       | 7.13e-05  |
| 1   | 20       | 30       | 3.73e-05 | 4.67e-06     | 0.494      | 40       | 9.33e-07  |
| 2   | 30       | 50       | 2.57e-06 | 2.95e-07     | 0.755      | 40       | 6.42e-08  |

**What to notice.**

- **The cross section falls by three orders of magnitude** from the 10–20 to the 30–50 GeV window, yet each window has 40 events. Generated over 10–50 GeV in one go, only about one event in a thousand would land in the 30–50 GeV window.
- **The jobs' estimates scatter by up to about 30 %** around the combined value: each job saw only 12–24 PYTHIA events per window. The combined value carries an error of 11–13 %.
- **`weight_mb` = `$\sigma$` / `n_events`** is the weight of one event of that window. A spectrum over all windows is the sum of the windows' histograms, each event weighted by its window's `weight_mb` (tutorial 05). Results for one window alone need no weights.

A dry run shows the plan of one such job. We give it `--seed 0` and a campaign name, as a campaign would: the seed is drawn from the operating system (yours will differ), the file is named by campaign and job number, and a dry run records nothing in the registry:

```python
plan, _ = script("run_prod_jet.py", "--events", 30, "--seed", 0, "--campaign", "demo",
                 "--pthat-bins", "10-20,20-30,30-50", "--jets-per-bin", 2, "--parton-ymax", 0.6,
                 "--hadrons-only", "--oversample", 10, "--n-frag", 10, "--no-x",
                 "--outdir", OUT / "demo", "--dry-run")
print(plan.splitlines()[0])
print([line.strip() for line in plan.splitlines() if line.strip().startswith("output")])
```

```
prod_AuAu_0_10_jet: 30 event(s), seed 693593494 (from OS entropy), campaign demo #1, grid_mode grid, PythiaGun pTHat windows 10-20, 20-30, 30-50 GeV, 2 jet(s) per window per background, partons |y| < 0.6 (leading), reuse 6, deposition on, freeze-out surface: bg+jet, particlize input: both, HADRONS ONLY (no pair or particlize file)
['output   out/03_production/demo/AuAu_0_10_jet_demo_0001_hadrons_{bulk_jet,bulk_bg,jet_frag}.h5 + *_primary.h5']
```

## 8. Hadrons in the job, and correlated sampling

That dry run also used **`--hadrons-only`**: iSS and the jet fragmentation run inside the GPU job, exactly as `hadronize.py` would (same code, settings and seeds), and the job writes only the hadron files and its record: no pair file, no particlize file, no stage 2. It suits campaigns with little oversampling, here 10 samples per jet event. The price: no surfaces, so no new samples later, and no hydro history. Measured on the GB10 (the [Au+Au jets](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/run/auau-jet/#hadrons-in-the-job-hadrons-only) page), it wrote 0.64 MB per event, against about 160 MB in two stages. `auau_stats` was made this way; its job record keeps the hadronization settings:

```python
r = json.loads(te.read_text("auau_stats", "AuAu_0_10_jet_stats_seed0201.json"))
print("hadrons_only:", r["hadrons_only"])
print("hadronize_settings:", r["hadronize_settings"])
```

```
hadrons_only: True
hadronize_settings: {'oversample': 10, 'oversample_bg': 'per-pthat-bin', 'n_frag': 10, 'keep_primaries': 'all', 'base_seed': 1, 'correlated': False}
```

`oversample_bg: per-pthat-bin` gives each background `$M \times$` `oversample` samples, as many as the `$M$` jet events of one window have together: the right balance for results per window. **Correlated sampling** (`--correlated`) works in the job as in stage 2; `auau_stats` did not use it, our job and `auau_pair_mini` did. Use it when the analysis is jet minus background, and analyse such files sample by sample (tutorial 07).

**Decide the hadron settings once per campaign.** The number of oversamples, the correlation, the precision (`--keep-bits-p/-x`) and the selection (`--eta-max`, `--charged`, `--no-x`) must be the same for every job: restarts skip complete files whatever settings made them.

## 9. From a job to a campaign

Nothing below runs in this notebook; each is a command for a terminal.

**`run_jobs.sh`** runs many jobs of one production, `-j P` at a time on one GPU, each in its own working directory:

```
cd <your copy of the examples>/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet
./run_jobs.sh [-j P] [--mps] [--stagger S] [--campaign NAME] NJOBS EVENTS_PER_JOB FIRST_SEED [OUTDIR] [driver options]

# 67 jobs x 15 events, new seeds, three windows, 5 jets per window per background
./run_jobs.sh -j 3 --campaign pth10-40_c1 67 15 0 ~/xscape/prod/AuAu_c1 \
    --pthat-bins 10-20,20-30,30-40 --jets-per-bin 5 --parton-ymax 0.6 --write-particlize both
```

- `FIRST_SEED 0` gives every job a new seed through `--seed 0` (a campaign); `FIRST_SEED 1` gives seeds 1, 2, ... (to reproduce files, or to compare settings on the same collisions).
- OUTDIR is the argument after FIRST_SEED; one campaign per OUTDIR. Every job leaves `<stem>.log`, `.json`, `.xml` there, and the campaign ends with `run_jobs.finished`.
- **Restart** with the same command: jobs whose `.json` says complete are skipped, the others are redone.
- On a Mac, split the cores between the jobs: `OMP_NUM_THREADS=5 OMP_WAIT_POLICY=passive ./run_jobs.sh -j 3 ...` on a 16-core M3 Max. On CUDA, `--mps` lets the jobs share the GPU.

**`utils/prodwizard.py`** plans a campaign before it runs: pick a preset (`auau_jet`, `auau_hadrons_only`, `oo_hadrons`, ...) and a machine (`mac_wheel`, `2x3090`, `slurm_a100`, ...), and it writes the launch command with the measured settings for that machine and estimates events per hour, duration, disk and memory. It checks the plan (events per job a multiple of windows × jets, memory, disk) and never starts jobs:

```
utils/prodwizard.py --preset auau_jet --machine mac_wheel --events 300     # xscape-prodwizard in the wheel
```

**`utils/jobmon.py`** watches a running or finished campaign from what the jobs write (logs, job records): jobs done, running and failed, events per hour, the time left, disk per event, and checks such as the deposition check, which flags the rare job whose jets deposited far less energy than the rest:

```
utils/jobmon.py ~/xscape/prod/AuAu_c1 --watch      # xscape-jobmon in the wheel
```

**On a cluster** with SLURM, `utils/slurm_prod_array.sh` runs a campaign as a job array in the production container: each array task gets one GPU and runs `P` jobs on it, all tasks sharing one seed registry. A GPU needs several jobs at once to stay busy, so one SLURM job per production job would waste it. Stage 2 runs on CPU nodes with `utils/slurm_hadronize.sh`:

```
SIF=$PWD/xscape_prod.sif CAMPAIGN=pth10-40_c2 NJOBS=40 EVENTS=15 \
  EXTRA_ARGS="--pthat-bins 10-20,20-30,30-40 --jets-per-bin 5 --parton-ymax 0.6 --write-particlize both" \
  sbatch --array=0-19 utils/slurm_prod_array.sh
```

The sizes per GPU type, the launch settings and a 12,000-event example are on [Clusters, GPUs and monitoring](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/run/clusters/).

## 10. Sharing the files on the OSDF

The tutorial data come from the **OSDF** (Open Science Data Federation), a network of data origins and caches. Reading is public: with pelicanfs in Python (`osdf://` URLs, tutorial 01), or over plain HTTPS. Writing to the namespace `osdf:///fno4hic` needs a login. `utils/remote_transfer/js_osdf.py` (`xscape-osdf` in the Mac wheel) moves whole productions or kinds of files:

```
./js_osdf.py login                                         # once: a link to log in from any browser
./js_osdf.py upload ~/xscape/prod/AuAu_c1 --what h5 --dry-run     # what would go
./js_osdf.py upload ~/xscape/prod/AuAu_c1 --what h5        # -> osdf:///fno4hic/AuAu_c1/
./js_osdf.py download AuAu_c1 --what root --to /scratch    # anyone, no login
```

- `--what` picks files by kind: `h5` (particlize and hadron files: everything an analysis needs), `root`, `pair` (the hydro, for the ML hydro), `all`.
- Incomplete files (an HDF5 file whose `complete` attribute is false, `*.part`) are left out. Each upload is checked: the size at the origin, and a CRC32C recorded in a manifest in the remote folder, which downloads (and `get_data.py`) check against.
- **Whatever is uploaded can be read by everyone.**
- **Uploaded files are never overwritten.** The OSDF caches keep a copy of a file for a long time, so a file replaced at the origin can still be served in its old version, and readers would get different data under one name. A changed data set is a new version under a new name instead: the tutorial data live under `tutorials/v2/`, and a change would become `v3`.

This notebook uploads nothing.

## 11. A worked example: how the tutorial data were made

The data sets of the tutorials were made by one script, `data_recipes/make_v2.sh` in this folder: each set is a function of a few production commands. Here are the two Au+Au sets:

```python
recipe = Path("data_recipes/make_v2.sh").read_text()
for name in ["pair_mini", "stats"]:
    print(re.search(rf"^{name}\(\) \{{.*?^\}}", recipe, re.M | re.S).group(0), "\n")
```

```
pair_mini() {
  local D="$OUT/AuAu_pair_mini"
  log "AuAu_pair_mini -> $D"
  (cd "$EX/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet" &&
   $PY run_prod_jet.py --events 5 --reuse 5 --seed 101 --pthat-min 30 --pthat-max 40 \
       --parton-ymax 0.6 --write-particlize both --outdir "$D" &&
   $PY hadronize.py "$D/AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0101_particlize.h5" \
       --correlated --common-seeds --oversample 200 --n-frag 20 &&
   $PY run_h5toROOT.py "$D" --writer uproot)
} 

stats() {
  local D="$OUT/AuAu_stats"
  log "AuAu_stats -> $D"
  (cd "$EX/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet" &&
   printf '%s\n' 201 202 203 204 | xargs -P "$JOBS" -I{} \
     $PY run_prod_jet.py --events 30 --seed {} --campaign stats \
       --pthat-bins 10-20,20-30,30-50 --jets-per-bin 2 --parton-ymax 0.6 \
       --hadrons-only --oversample 10 --n-frag 10 --no-x --outdir "$D" &&
   mkdir -p "$OUT/AuAu_stats_primaries" &&       # the undecayed hadrons (for an afterburner):
   mv "$D"/*_primary.h5 "$OUT/AuAu_stats_primaries/" &&   # not part of the set
   $PY run_h5toROOT.py "$D" --writer uproot -j "$JOBS")
}
```

**Read them with this tutorial in mind.**

- **`pair_mini`** is our job with five jets: `run_prod_jet.py --events 5 --reuse 5 --seed 101 ...`, then `hadronize.py --correlated --common-seeds --oversample 200 --n-frag 20` and `run_h5toROOT.py --writer uproot`. Its first two events are ours (section 4).
- **`stats`** is a campaign of four jobs with seeds 201–204, three windows and two jets per window per background, hadrons made in the job (`--hadrons-only`, 10 oversamples, no positions), started three at a time by `xargs -P` instead of `run_jobs.sh`. It moves the undecayed hadrons (`*_primary.h5`, kept for a later hadronic afterburner) out of the set, then writes the ROOT files and the campaign file.
- **Fixed seeds** make every set reproducible with the same build. The script's header states the machine and environment, and that uploaded sets are never overwritten.
- The last function, `upload`, sends each set with `js_osdf.py upload --what all --prefix tutorials/v2`.

### Check your result

Your job ran on your setup. Its collisions are fixed by the seed and the build: another GPU or MUSIC on the CPU changes the numbers slightly, another build of PYTHIA or 3dMCGlauber can give other collisions. The hadrons of stage 2 also depend on the particlize file's unique id, so they change with every run of stage 1. The check allows for both:

```python
exp = json.load(open("expected/03_production_scripts.json"))
assert record["events_written"] == exp["events"] and record["reuse"] == exp["reuse"] and record["seed"] == 101
assert hadrons["source_uuid matches"].all() and hadrons.loc["bulk_bg", "units (events)"] == [0]
assert set(hadrons.loc["bulk_jet", "seeds"]) == set(hadrons.loc["bulk_bg", "seeds"])   # common seeds
assert len(events) == 2 and 101 in reg["seed"].values
# the same collisions as shown here, unless your build of PYTHIA or 3dMCGlauber differs
if np.allclose(ours["pthat"], exp["pthat"], rtol=1e-6):
    np.testing.assert_allclose(ours["E_droplets"], exp["E_droplets"], rtol=0.1)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(hadrons.loc["bulk_jet", "hadrons per sample"], exp["bulk_jet_per_sample"], rtol=0.03)
else:
    print("Your collisions differ from the ones shown (another build): only the job's structure was checked.")
print("All checks pass.")
```

```
All checks pass.
```

## Exercises

1. **The null test.** Run one event with `--no-deposit` (and its own seed and output directory): MUSIC_2 then runs without the droplets, and the two legs must be identical. Check `diag/frames_identical` against `diag/ntau_jet` in the pair file. Why is this the first thing to run on a new machine or build?
1. **Stage 2 again.** Run `hadronize.py` on our particlize file once more, with `--tags jet_frag --seed 2 --force`. Which hadron file changes, and which seeds? Then without `--force`: what happens?
1. **A campaign's arithmetic.** With `--dry-run`, try `--events 20 --pthat-bins 10-20,20-30,30-40 --jets-per-bin 5`. What does the driver say, and why? Which numbers of events work?
1. **Plan a campaign.** Run `utils/prodwizard.py --list`, then a plan for 300 Au+Au events on your machine (`--preset auau_jet --machine mac_wheel --events 300`, or a cluster). How long would it take, and how much disk would it need?

# 04 · The files and their provenance

**Time:** 30 minutes · **Needs:** any setup · **Data:** `auau_pair_mini` (streamed: a few MB are read)

A production job writes several files, each for a different use. This tutorial opens every file of one job: a Au+Au collision with five jets. Along the way it shows what each stage of the simulation leaves behind, and where the job records how it was made: the seed, the physics settings, the software and the grid. Those records let you check that files belong together before you combine them.

Reference pages: [What a production writes](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/analysis/files/) and [The physics](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/about/physics/).

> **Work in progress: examples, not vetted physics.** The tutorials show how to run the simulation and use its outputs. The data sets are small, so the statistics are low, and the analyses have not been checked to the standard of a publication: treat every number and figure as an illustration, not as a physics result.

> **The outputs shown** were produced on an Apple Silicon Mac, in the environment the xscape wheel 0.2.0 is built in, with the hydro on the GPU through Metal.

```python
SET = "auau_pair_mini"
STEM = "AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0101"          # one job: one seed, one stem for all its files
```

## 1. One job, its files

A jet production runs in two stages:

1. **Stage 1, on the GPU** (`run_prod_jet.py`): the initial state, the hard scattering, the hydro of the background (MUSIC_1), the jet's energy loss in it (Matter + LBT), and the hydro again with the energy the jet deposited (MUSIC_2). It writes the **pair file** (both hydro evolutions), the **particlize file** (both freeze-out surfaces and the final partons), and the job record (`.json`, `.xml`).
1. **Stage 2, on the CPU** (`hadronize.py`): Cooper–Frye sampling of each freeze-out surface and hadronization of the jet partons. It writes the **hadron files**: `bulk_jet` (the medium with the jet's wake), `bulk_bg` (the medium alone) and `jet_frag` (the jet's own hadrons). `run_h5toROOT.py` then copies them into a **ROOT file**.

Stage 2 can be repeated any number of times from the particlize file, with more oversamples or other settings, without rerunning the hydro.

All files of a job share its *stem*. The files of this set:

```python
for name, size in te.files(SET).items():
    print(f"{size / 1e6:9.1f} MB  {name}")
```

```
    835.7 MB  AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0101.h5
      0.0 MB  AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0101.json
      0.0 MB  AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0101.xml
    263.2 MB  AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0101_hadrons.root
     45.5 MB  AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0101_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5
    229.2 MB  AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0101_hadrons_bulk_jet.h5
      0.2 MB  AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0101_hadrons_jet_frag.h5
    540.3 MB  AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0101_particlize.h5
      0.0 MB  campaign_campaign.root
```

## 2. The job record

`<stem>.json` summarises the job: its seed, what was simulated, how many events were written, and the cross section of the p̂T window.

```python
import json
job = json.loads(te.read_text(SET, STEM + ".json"))
for key in ["seed", "hard", "reuse", "events_written", "droplets_total", "wall_s",
            "pthat_bins", "pthat_bin_sigma_gen_mb", "events_hit_edge"]:
    print(f"{key:24s} {job[key]}")
```

```
seed                     101
hard                     PythiaGun pTHat 30.0-40.0 GeV, partons |y| < 0.6 (leading)
reuse                    5
events_written           5
droplets_total           88
wall_s                   42.3
pthat_bins               [[30.0, 40.0]]
pthat_bin_sigma_gen_mb   [2.093149017109464e-06]
events_hit_edge          {'bg': 0, 'jet': 0}
```

- **`reuse` 5**: the five jets share **one** background. The initial state and MUSIC_1 run once, and each jet is followed through the same medium. This saves time, and it makes the five events directly comparable.
- **`pthat_bin_sigma_gen_mb`**: PYTHIA's cross section for this p̂T window, in mb. Results from several windows are combined with these weights (tutorial 05).
- **`wall_s`**: the whole stage 1 took 42 s on an Apple M3 Max.

`<stem>.xml` is the complete X-SCAPE input of the job, verbatim. Every physics setting is there. Some of the most important ones:

```python
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
xml = ET.fromstring(te.read_text(SET, STEM + ".xml"))

def setting(path):
    """The text of the first element at an XPath-like path, stripped."""
    el = xml.find(path)
    return el.text.strip() if el is not None and el.text else "-"

settings = {
    "collision":              f"{setting('.//MCGlauber/projectile')}+{setting('.//MCGlauber/target')} at "
                              f"{setting('.//MCGlauber/sqrts')} GeV, b = {setting('.//MCGlauber/b_min')}-"
                              f"{setting('.//MCGlauber/b_max')} fm (centrality {setting('.//MCGlauber/cenMin')}-"
                              f"{setting('.//MCGlauber/cenMax')} %)",
    "hard scattering":        f"PYTHIA pTHat {setting('.//PythiaGun/pTHatMin')}-{setting('.//PythiaGun/pTHatMax')} GeV, "
                              f"partons |y| < {setting('.//PythiaGun/partonYMax')}",
    "hydro start tau_0":      setting(".//MUSIC/Initial_time_tau_0") + " fm/c",
    "eta/s at the kink":      f"{setting('.//MUSIC/shear_viscosity_3_at_kink')} at T = "
                              f"{setting('.//MUSIC/shear_viscosity_3_T_kink_in_GeV')} GeV",
    "zeta/s maximum":         f"{setting('.//MUSIC/bulk_viscosity_3_max')} at T = "
                              f"{setting('.//MUSIC/bulk_viscosity_3_T_peak_in_GeV')} GeV",
    "freeze-out temperature": setting(".//MUSIC/freezeout_temperature") + " GeV",
    "MATTER / LBT switch Q0":  setting(".//Matter/Q0") + " GeV",
    "alpha_s (MATTER, LBT)":  f"{setting('.//Matter/alphas')}, {setting('.//Lbt/alphas')}",
    "liquefier tau_delay":    setting(".//CausalLiquefier/tau_delay") + " fm/c",
}
for k, v in settings.items():
    print(f"{k:24s} {v}")
```

```
collision                Au+Au at 200 GeV, b = 0.0-4.7 fm (centrality 0.0-10.0 %)
hard scattering          PYTHIA pTHat 30.0-40.0 GeV, partons |y| < 0.6
hydro start tau_0        0.424 fm/c
eta/s at the kink        0.108 at T = 0.206 GeV
zeta/s maximum           0.092 at T = 0.180 GeV
freeze-out temperature   0.15 GeV
MATTER / LBT switch Q0   2.0 GeV
alpha_s (MATTER, LBT)    0.25, 0.25
liquefier tau_delay      1.0 fm/c
```

In order: the **initial state** is a 3D MC-Glauber model with strings (0–10 % central Au+Au). The **hard scattering** comes from PYTHIA. The **fluid** is MUSIC with temperature-dependent shear and bulk viscosities, which ends where the temperature falls below 150 MeV. The **jet** loses energy with MATTER at high virtuality and LBT below `$Q_0 = 2$` GeV. The **CausalLiquefier** turns the energy and momentum the jet loses into *droplets* that the fluid absorbs after a delay. Each step is explained in [The physics](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/about/physics/).

## 3. The pair file: two hydro evolutions

`<stem>.h5` holds the energy density and flow velocity of **both** hydro runs on a fixed grid in `$(x, y, \eta_s, \tau)$`: `arr` is the jet leg (MUSIC_2), `arr_bg` the background (MUSIC_1). Both start from the same initial condition, so `arr - arr_bg` is exactly what the jet did to the fluid. Tutorial 06 looks at that difference. Here we look at the layout and the per-event diagnostics.

The file is streamed: opening it and reading the diagnostics fetches a few MB of its 836 MB.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

with te.h5(SET, STEM + ".h5") as f:
    A = dict(f.attrs)                    # a copy: the attributes stay readable after closing
    print("arr:", f["arr"].shape, "= (event, channel, x, y, eta_s, tau);",
          "channels", list(A["feature_names"]))
    print(f"grid: x, y in {A['nx']} cells of {A['dx']} fm, eta_s in {A['neta']} cells of {A['deta']},"
          f" tau from {A['tau_min']} fm/c every {A['dtau']} fm/c")
    print("chunks:", f["arr"].chunks, "-> read one event and one tau frame at a time")
    cols = ["pthat", "parton_pt_lead", "parton_pt_sub", "n_droplets", "E_droplets",
            "frames_identical", "ntau_jet", "ntau_bg"]
    diag = pd.DataFrame({c: f["diag"][c][:] for c in cols})

diag["tau_identical"] = A["tau_min"] + A["dtau"] * diag["frames_identical"]   # fm/c
diag["tau_fo_jet"] = A["tau_min"] + A["dtau"] * diag["ntau_jet"]
diag["tau_fo_bg"] = A["tau_min"] + A["dtau"] * diag["ntau_bg"]
diag.round(2)
```

```
arr: (5, 4, 64, 64, 32, 131) = (event, channel, x, y, eta_s, tau); channels ['energy_density', 'vx', 'vy', 'vz']
grid: x, y in 64 cells of 0.3875 fm, eta_s in 32 cells of 0.3125, tau from 0.5 fm/c every 0.1 fm/c
chunks: (1, 4, 64, 64, 32, 1) -> read one event and one tau frame at a time
```

|     | pthat | parton_pt_lead | parton_pt_sub | n_droplets | E_droplets | frames_identical | ntau_jet | ntau_bg | tau_identical | tau_fo_jet | tau_fo_bg |
| --- | ----- | -------------- | ------------- | ---------- | ---------- | ---------------- | -------- | ------- | ------------- | ---------- | --------- |
| 0   | 31.60 | 31.92          | 31.60         | 24.0       | 54.14      | 6.0              | 131.0    | 103.0   | 1.1           | 13.6       | 10.8      |
| 1   | 34.00 | 35.84          | 32.41         | 14.0       | 34.45      | 9.0              | 103.0    | 103.0   | 1.4           | 10.8       | 10.8      |
| 2   | 30.16 | 30.32          | 30.06         | 22.0       | 27.86      | 6.0              | 109.0    | 103.0   | 1.1           | 11.4       | 10.8      |
| 3   | 34.73 | 34.85          | 34.74         | 11.0       | 15.77      | 7.0              | 123.0    | 103.0   | 1.2           | 12.8       | 10.8      |
| 4   | 30.71 | 33.96          | 29.40         | 17.0       | 19.40      | 6.0              | 114.0    | 103.0   | 1.1           | 11.9       | 10.8      |

**What to notice.**

- **`E_droplets`**: the energy the jet handed to the fluid, from 16 to 54 GeV. The two hard partons together carry about `$2\hat p_T \approx$` 60–70 GeV, so in 0–10 % central Au+Au a large part of the jets' energy ends up in the medium. How much depends on the path through the fireball.
- **`tau_identical`**: the two legs stay bit-identical until the first droplet arrives, about 1.1–1.4 fm/c. That is the jet's start (`$\tau = 0.5$` fm/c) plus the liquefier's delay.
- **`tau_fo_jet` vs `tau_fo_bg`**: the jet leg freezes out later, by up to 2.8 fm/c. The deposited energy reheats the fluid, so its last part takes longer to cool to 150 MeV. This is why `arr - arr_bg` is only a "wake" while **both** legs still exist.

## 4. The particlize file: the input of hadronization

`<stem>_particlize.h5` holds what stage 2 needs:

- the **freeze-out surface** of each leg: a list of hypersurface cells with their position, normal vector `$d\Sigma_\mu$`, flow `$u^\mu$`, temperature and viscous corrections (32 columns per cell)
- the **final partons** of the jet
- the **shower initiators**: the partons that started the jet showers

The background's surface is stored once, and every event points to it through `events/bg_unit`.

```python
with te.h5(SET, STEM + "_particlize.h5") as f:
    print("legs:", list(f.attrs["legs"]), "| T_fo =", f.attrs["T_fo"], "GeV",
          "| file_uuid", f.attrs["file_uuid"])
    print("surface cells: jet leg", f["surface/jet/cells"].shape,
          "(all events), background", f["surface/bg/cells"].shape, "(once)")
    ev = pd.DataFrame({c: f["events"][c][:] for c in ["bg_unit", "n_cells_jet", "n_cells_bg", "n_partons"]})
    # one event's surface: the cells of event 0
    o = f["surface/jet/offsets"][:]
    cells = f["surface/jet/cells"][o[0]:o[1]]
    columns = list(f["surface/jet/cells"].attrs.get("columns", []))
ev
```

```python
from jetscape.particlize_h5 import SURFACE_COLUMNS
T = cells[:, SURFACE_COLUMNS.index("T")]
tau = cells[:, SURFACE_COLUMNS.index("tau")]
at_fo = np.abs(T - 0.15) < 5e-4
print(f"event 0: {len(cells):,} surface cells, tau = {tau.min():.2f} .. {tau.max():.2f} fm/c")
print(f"  {at_fo.mean():.1%} at T = T_fo; the others: T = {T[~at_fo].min():.3f} .. {T[~at_fo].max():.3f} GeV,"
      f" all at tau = {np.unique(tau[~at_fo].round(2))} fm/c")
```

```
event 0: 1,165,243 surface cells, tau = 0.46 .. 13.38 fm/c
  98.9% at T = T_fo; the others: T = 0.120 .. 0.149 GeV, all at tau = [0.46] fm/c
```

**What to notice.**

- **Almost every cell sits at `$T = T_\text{fo} = 0.15$` GeV:** the surface is where the fluid cools through the freeze-out temperature.
- **About 1 % of the cells are colder, all at the very start of the hydro (`$\tau \approx 0.46$` fm/c).** They are fluid that was already below 150 MeV when the hydro began, at the dilute edges of the fireball (large radius or large `$|\eta_s|$`). MUSIC freezes them out at once (`Do_FreezeOut_lowtemp` in the XML), so their energy is not lost.
- **The jet leg has about 1 % more cells than the background,** from the reheated, slightly larger fluid. A leg with very different numbers would point to a broken hydro run.

## 5. The hadron files

Each hadron file holds one *tag*. The hadrons are in one flat table; the offsets mark the **units** (an event, or for `bulk_bg` a background) and their **samples** (Cooper–Frye oversamples or fragmentations):

| tag        | from                     | unit       | samples per unit here             |
| ---------- | ------------------------ | ---------- | --------------------------------- |
| `bulk_jet` | the jet leg's surface    | event      | 100                               |
| `bulk_bg`  | the background's surface | background | 500 = 100 × the 5 events using it |
| `jet_frag` | the final partons        | event      | 20                                |

Each hadron file records the `file_uuid` of the particlize file it came from, as its `source_uuid`. The readers refuse a hadron file that does not match, which catches files renamed or mixed up between runs.

```python
with te.h5(SET, STEM + "_particlize.h5") as f:
    uuid = f.attrs["file_uuid"]
for tag in ["bulk_jet", "bulk_bg", "jet_frag"]:
    with te.h5(SET, f"{STEM}_hadrons_{tag}.h5") as f:
        n_units = int(f.attrs["nunits_written"])
        samples = f["units/n_samples"][:]
        n = len(f["hadrons/pid"])
        same = f.attrs["source_uuid"] == uuid
    print(f"{tag:9s} {n_units} unit(s), samples per unit {samples.tolist()},"
          f" {n:>9,} hadrons, {n / samples.sum():7.1f} per sample, source_uuid matches: {same}")
```

```
bulk_jet  5 unit(s), samples per unit [200, 200, 200, 200, 200], 8,401,278 hadrons,  8401.3 per sample, source_uuid matches: True
bulk_bg   1 unit(s), samples per unit [200], 1,676,110 hadrons,  8380.5 per sample, source_uuid matches: True
jet_frag  5 unit(s), samples per unit [20, 20, 20, 20, 20],     2,626 hadrons,    26.3 per sample, source_uuid matches: True
```

**What to notice.** A sample of the bulk has about 8,400 hadrons, all species and charges in the full rapidity range: this is what one central Au+Au collision looks like. A jet's own fragmentation gives about 26 hadrons per sample. The jet leg's bulk has slightly *more* hadrons than the background, because the deposited energy is also turned into hadrons. That excess is the hadronic wake of tutorial 07.

## 7. Before combining files: the settings

Files can look alike and still differ in how they were made. Before you combine files from different jobs or campaigns, compare their settings. All of them are recorded in the attributes of the pair and particlize files:

```python
import yaml

def production_settings(h5file):
    """The settings that must agree between files you combine."""
    A = h5file.attrs
    xml = ET.fromstring(A["prod_user_xml"])
    late = xml.findtext(".//Hydro/MUSIC/late_delta_tau")
    grid = yaml.safe_load(A["prod_grid_yaml"])["grid"]
    return {
        "hard process": A["prod_hard"],
        "background reuse": int(A["prod_reuse"]),
        "MUSIC late time step": late.strip() if late else "absent (constant step)",
        "output grid x": grid["x"],
        "EoS": A["eos_kind"],
        "build": te.short(A["prod_build"]),
    }

with te.h5(SET, STEM + ".h5") as f:
    mine = production_settings(f)
for k, v in mine.items():
    print(f"{k:22s} {v}")
```

```
hard process           PythiaGun pTHat 30.0-40.0 GeV, partons |y| < 0.6 (leading)
background reuse       5
MUSIC late time step   0.05
output grid x          {'min': -12.20625, 'max': 12.20625, 'n': 64}
EoS                    hotqcd (MUSIC EOS 91)
build                  ~/JetScape/X-SCAPE/build_gpu
```

# 05 · Hadrons: spectra, dN/dη, oversamples and weights

**Time:** 45 minutes · **Needs:** any setup · **Data:** `auau_stats`: the hadron files (0.2 GB, downloaded once)

A campaign of jet events is many files, many events, and for each event many samples of its hadrons. Reading them is easy. Combining them correctly takes some care: which average is the right one, how a background shared by several events counts, and how events from different p̂T windows are put together. This tutorial reads a small campaign of 120 central Au+Au events and:

- explains what a unit, a sample and an oversample are, and why each event is the mean over its oversamples;
- measures the charged-hadron `$dN/d\eta$` and the identified spectra of π, K and p, for the background and for the jet events;
- combines three p̂T windows with their cross sections, and shows what goes wrong without them;
- looks at how well a window's cross section is known;
- checks the campaign for bad runs.

Reference pages: [Hadrons](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/analysis/hadrons/), [What a production writes](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/analysis/files/#4-hadron-files).

> **Work in progress: examples, not vetted physics.** The tutorials show how to run the simulation and use its outputs. The data sets are small, so the statistics are low, and the analyses have not been checked to the standard of a publication: treat every number and figure as an illustration, not as a physics result.

> **The outputs shown** were produced on an Apple Silicon Mac, in the environment the xscape wheel 0.2.0 is built in, with the hydro on the GPU through Metal.
