```
rho (bkg): mean 61.3, spread over samples 8.4 GeV
random cones:  <dpT> = +0.99 +- 0.23 GeV, width 5.55 GeV
embedded jets: <dpT> = +0.18 +- 0.34 GeV, width 5.43 GeV (99% of 252 reference jets matched in both events)
  fragments' pT the matched embedded jet keeps: 98.6%
  the jet raises rho a little: rho(bkg + jet) - rho(bkg) = +0.61 GeV per unit area
full events:   <dpT> = +1.02 GeV, width 5.93 GeV
full - embedded, jet by jet: +0.83 +- 0.49 GeV
```

**What to notice.**

- **The width is the jet resolution: about 5.5 GeV** for random cones and embedded jets alike. It is the fluctuation of the 30 GeV of background in a cone of radius 0.4, and every jet in central Au+Au is smeared by it. The distributions have a longer tail to positive `$\delta p_T$`: upward fluctuations of soft hadrons are larger than downward ones.
- **The subtraction is right on average, within about 1 GeV.** Random cones come out +1 GeV high: the median ρ is a little below the mean density, because the `$p_T/A$` of the `$k_T$` jets has a tail to high values. Embedded jets come out lower, near zero: the jet itself raises ρ a little (printed), and their error is ±0.3 GeV.
- **The jet is not lost in the background**: the matched jet keeps about 99 % of its fragments' `$p_T$`.
- **The full event gives about 0.8 GeV more than the embedding**, jet by jet, with an error of 0.5 GeV: the same fragments, but in the background with the jet's wake. Section 7 measures this medium response directly.
- **ρ changes from background to background**, from about 45 to 77 GeV per unit area: the 20 collisions differ in multiplicity (tutorial 05). Every event needs its own ρ.

## 4. Fake jets

The background alone makes jets too. After subtraction they scatter around zero with the width of the random cones, and their upper tail reaches about 20 GeV, rarely beyond. Per event, in the highest p̂T window, compare the subtracted jets of the three events with the reference jets of the fragments alone:

```python
edges = np.arange(-20, 61, 5.0)
win2 = aa.pthat_bin_events(2)
def per_event_spectrum(rec, events):
    """Subtracted anti-kT jets per event (each event: the mean over its N_OS oversamples)."""
    sel = np.isin(rec[:, 0].astype(int), events)
    h = hist.Hist(hist.axis.Variable(edges, label=r"$p_T - \rho A$ [GeV]"), storage=hist.storage.Weight())
    h.fill(rec[sel, 2] - rec[sel, 4] * rec[sel, 3], weight=np.full(sel.sum(), 1.0 / (N_OS * len(events))))
    return h

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.3))
for leg, label, ls in (("full", "bkg + wake + jet", "-"), ("emb", "bkg + jet", "--"), ("bkg", "bkg alone: fake jets", ":")):
    mh.histplot(per_event_spectrum(jets_rec[leg], win2) / np.diff(edges), ax=ax, label=label, flow="none", ls=ls)
ref_pt = matched.loc[np.isin(matched["event"], win2), "pt_ref"]
ax.stairs(np.histogram(ref_pt, edges)[0] / (N_OS * len(win2)) / np.diff(edges), edges, color="k", lw=1.5,
          label="reference jets (fragments alone, > 10 GeV)")
ax.set(yscale="log", ylabel="jets per event per GeV", title=r"$\hat p_T$ 30-50 GeV, per event")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
fake = per_event_spectrum(jets_rec["bkg"], win2).values()
real = per_event_spectrum(jets_rec["full"], win2).values()
for lo in (10, 15, 20, 25):
    i = np.searchsorted(edges, lo)
    print(f"pT - rho A {edges[i]:.0f}-{edges[i + 1]:.0f} GeV: fake jets per event {fake[i]:.3f}, "
          f"all jets of the full event {real[i]:.3f}")
```

```
pT - rho A 10-15 GeV: fake jets per event 1.145, all jets of the full event 1.365
pT - rho A 15-20 GeV: fake jets per event 0.160, all jets of the full event 0.390
pT - rho A 20-25 GeV: fake jets per event 0.020, all jets of the full event 0.265
pT - rho A 25-30 GeV: fake jets per event 0.000, all jets of the full event 0.145
```

**What to notice.**

- **Below 15 GeV, most jets are fake.** At 10–15 GeV there are about 1.4 jets per event in the full event, and 1.1 of them come from the background alone. At 15–20 GeV the fakes are still about 40 %; above 20 GeV they are below 10 %, and above 25 GeV none appear in these 600 background samples.
- **Above 20 GeV the full event has more jets than the reference.** The ±5.5 GeV fluctuations move jets up and down, but the spectrum falls steeply, so more jets move up from below than down from above. A measurement corrects for this by unfolding with the `$\delta p_T$` response.
- **The three events agree with each other**: the background, not the wake, makes the fakes and the smearing.

A measurement has to remove the fakes statistically (for example by subtracting a mixed-event spectrum, or by requiring a hard constituent in the jet) and unfold the smearing. Here the model gives the truth directly. And it gets worse in a cross-section-weighted sample: 99 % of the hard scatterings come from the lowest window, whose jets are mostly below 20 GeV, while every event brings its fakes. So section 5 compares the jets of the fragments alone.

## 5. The jet spectrum, Au+Au against p+p

Now the spectrum that a p̂T-inclusive sample would have, as in tutorial 05: per window `$k$` the jets **per event** (each event: the mean over its fragmentations), weighted by the window's cross section `$\sigma_k$`, and summed. In both systems every event is exactly one hard scattering, so the ratio

`$R = \frac{\sum_k \sigma_k \langle N_\text{jet}\rangle_k^\text{Au+Au}}{\sum_k \sigma_k \langle N_\text{jet}\rangle_k^\text{p+p}}$`

is the jet suppression *per hard scattering*: 1 if the medium did nothing. (In a measurement the Au+Au yield per collision is divided by the number of binary collisions `$N_\text{coll}$`; in the model each event has one hard scattering by construction.)

We take the jets of the **jet's own fragments**, in Au+Au and in p+p, with the array interface: no background, so no fakes and no fluctuations; what changes is only what the medium did to the partons.

**Which cross sections?** The hard scattering is the same PYTHIA process in both systems, so the two campaigns estimate the same `$\sigma_k$`, with very different precision (tutorial 05, section 7). We use the p+p ones for both:

```python
for k, (lo, hi) in enumerate(pp.pthat_bins):
    (s_aa, e_aa), (s_pp, e_pp) = aa.pthat_bin_sigma(k), pp.pthat_bin_sigma(k)
    print(f"window {lo:.0f}-{hi:.0f} GeV: sigma Au+Au {s_aa:.3e} +- {e_aa / s_aa:.0%}, p+p {s_pp:.3e} +- {e_pp / s_pp:.1%}"
          f"  -> difference {(s_aa - s_pp) / np.hypot(e_aa, e_pp):+.1f} standard deviations")
SIGMA = np.array([pp.pthat_bin_sigma(k)[0] for k in range(3)])
```

```
window 10-20 GeV: sigma Au+Au 2.853e-03 +- 12%, p+p 2.290e-03 +- 2.2%  -> difference +1.6 standard deviations
window 20-30 GeV: sigma Au+Au 3.731e-05 +- 13%, p+p 4.244e-05 +- 2.0%  -> difference -1.1 standard deviations
window 30-50 GeV: sigma Au+Au 2.570e-06 +- 11%, p+p 2.198e-06 +- 1.8%  -> difference +1.3 standard deviations
```

```python
def frag_samples(reader):
    """Every jet_frag sample of a campaign as one awkward array (samples * particles * {px, py, pz, E}),
    the accepted particles only, and the global event of each sample."""
    arrays, event_of = [], []
    for i, stem in enumerate(reader.stems):
        with HadronFile(f"{stem}_hadrons_jet_frag.h5") as hf:
            so, uo = hf.sample_offsets, hf.unit_offsets
            p = hf.f["hadrons/p"][:].astype(np.float64)
            pid = hf.f["hadrons/pid"][:]
        keep = accepted(p, pid)
        counts = np.diff(np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(keep)])[so])     # accepted per sample
        rec = ak.zip({"px": p[keep, 1], "py": p[keep, 2], "pz": p[keep, 3], "E": np.linalg.norm(p[keep, 1:], axis=1)})
        arrays.append(ak.unflatten(rec, counts))
        event_of.append(reader.global_event(i, 0) + np.repeat(np.arange(len(uo) - 1), np.diff(uo)))
    return ak.concatenate(arrays), np.concatenate(event_of)

t0 = time.time()
FJ = {}
for name, rd in (("Au+Au", aa), ("p+p", pp)):
    arr, event_of = frag_samples(rd)
    cs = fj.ClusterSequence(arr, JET_DEF)                 # every sample at once
    jets, cons = cs.inclusive_jets(min_pt=5.0), cs.constituents(min_pt=5.0)
    pt = np.sqrt(jets.px**2 + jets.py**2)
    inside = abs(np.arcsinh(jets.pz / pt)) < JET_ETA
    FJ[name] = {"pt": ak.flatten(pt[inside]).to_numpy(),
                "event": np.repeat(event_of, ak.num(pt[inside]).to_numpy()),
                "cons": ak.flatten(cons[inside], axis=1), "samples": len(arr), "reader": rd}
    print(f"{name}: {len(arr)} fragmentation samples -> {len(FJ[name]['pt'])} jets above 5 GeV")
print(f"clustered in {time.time() - t0:.1f} s")
```

```
Au+Au: 1200 fragmentation samples -> 970 jets above 5 GeV
```

```
p+p: 45000 fragmentation samples -> 67196 jets above 5 GeV
clustered in 0.5 s
```

```python
pt_edges = np.array([10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40.0])

def window_spectra(name, edges=pt_edges):
    """Per window: jets per event (mean over each event's samples), and the error from the spread
    of the events. -> list of hist.Hist (Weight storage), one per window."""
    d, rd = FJ[name], FJ[name]["reader"]
    out = []
    for k in range(3):
        g = rd.pthat_bin_events(k)
        per_event = np.zeros((len(g), len(edges) - 1))
        row = {int(e): i for i, e in enumerate(g)}
        sel = np.isin(d["event"], g)
        for e, x in zip(d["event"][sel], d["pt"][sel]):
            j = np.searchsorted(edges, x, side="right") - 1
            if 0 <= j < len(edges) - 1:
                per_event[row[int(e)], j] += 1.0 / rd.n_frag(int(e))
        h = hist.Hist(hist.axis.Variable(edges, label=r"$p_{T,\mathrm{jet}}$ [GeV]"), storage=hist.storage.Weight())
        h.view().value = per_event.mean(axis=0)
        h.view().variance = per_event.var(axis=0, ddof=1) / len(g)
        out.append(h)
    return out

W = {name: window_spectra(name) for name in FJ}
S = {name: sum((W[name][k] * SIGMA[k] for k in range(3)), start=W[name][0] * 0) for name in FJ}
width = np.diff(pt_edges) * 2 * JET_ETA                        # per GeV and per unit of eta

fig, (ax, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(7, 6.5), sharex=True, height_ratios=[2, 1])
for c, name in enumerate(FJ):
    for k in range(3):
        mh.histplot(W[name][k] * SIGMA[k] / width, ax=ax, flow="none", color=f"C{c}", ls=":", lw=1)
    mh.histplot(S[name] / width, ax=ax, flow="none", color=f"C{c}", lw=2, label=f"{name}: sum of the windows (dotted)")
ax.set(yscale="log", ylabel=r"$d\sigma/dp_T\,d\eta$ [mb/GeV]", title=r"jets of the jet's own fragments, anti-$k_T$ $R=0.4$, charged")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ratio = S["Au+Au"].values() / S["p+p"].values()
ratio_err = ratio * np.sqrt(S["Au+Au"].variances() / S["Au+Au"].values()**2 + S["p+p"].variances() / S["p+p"].values()**2)
ax2.errorbar(S["p+p"].axes[0].centers, ratio, ratio_err, xerr=np.diff(pt_edges) / 2, fmt="o", color="k")
ax2.axhline(1, color="0.5", lw=0.6)
ax2.set(ylim=(0, 1.2), ylabel="Au+Au / p+p", xlabel=r"$p_{T,\mathrm{jet}}$ [GeV]")
sig_aa = np.array([aa.pthat_bin_sigma(k)[0] for k in range(3)])
ratio_own = sum(W["Au+Au"][k].values() * sig_aa[k] for k in range(3)) / S["p+p"].values()
share_pp = np.array([W["p+p"][k].values() * SIGMA[k] for k in range(3)]) / S["p+p"].values()
for i in range(len(ratio)):
    print(f"{pt_edges[i]:.0f}-{pt_edges[i + 1]:.0f} GeV: Au+Au / p+p = {ratio[i]:.2f} +- {ratio_err[i]:.2f}"
          f"   (with Au+Au's own cross sections {ratio_own[i]:.2f});  p+p windows' shares {share_pp[:, i].round(2)}")
```

```
10-15 GeV: Au+Au / p+p = 0.12 +- 0.06   (with Au+Au's own cross sections 0.14);  p+p windows' shares [0.92 0.07 0.  ]
15-20 GeV: Au+Au / p+p = 0.06 +- 0.01   (with Au+Au's own cross sections 0.05);  p+p windows' shares [0.68 0.3  0.02]
20-25 GeV: Au+Au / p+p = 0.14 +- 0.06   (with Au+Au's own cross sections 0.15);  p+p windows' shares [0.25 0.62 0.13]
25-30 GeV: Au+Au / p+p = 0.36 +- 0.23   (with Au+Au's own cross sections 0.36);  p+p windows' shares [0.   0.53 0.47]
30-40 GeV: Au+Au / p+p = 0.09 +- 0.07   (with Au+Au's own cross sections 0.11);  p+p windows' shares [0.  0.1 0.9]
```

**What to notice.**

- **Each window dominates its own range of jet `$p_T$`**, as the hadrons did in tutorial 05: the lowest below 20 GeV, the middle one at 20–30 GeV, the highest above 30 GeV (the shares are printed).
- **The jets of the fragments are suppressed about tenfold in Au+Au.** The ratio scatters between about 0.06 and 0.36, with errors of the same size as the scatter, around a typical value of 0.1. The jets lose a large part of their energy to the fluid: about 40 GeV per event (tutorial 05, section 5). On a spectrum that falls by almost an order of magnitude every 5 GeV, a shift of several GeV removes most of the jets at a fixed `$p_T$`.
- **The cross sections matter at the level of up to 20 %.** With Au+Au's own, imprecise cross sections the ratio moves by up to 0.02 (printed). With the same cross sections in numerator and denominator, the ratio depends only on the yields per event.

**Why only illustrative.** Each window has 40 Au+Au events, and at a given jet `$p_T$` only a few of them have a jet. The ten fragmentations of an event are not independent, so the errors above come from the spread of the events. This is also not the measurable jet suppression: the jets here have no medium response (it adds back about 1 GeV in the cone, section 7), and no background fluctuations or fakes. With these statistics the full-event version (section 4) would be dominated by fakes. The ratio says how strongly the model's jets lose energy, not what an experiment would see.

## 6. Substructure: the SoftDrop `$z_g$`

SoftDrop looks inside a jet. It reclusters the jet's constituents with the Cambridge/Aachen algorithm (ordered in angle) and undoes the clustering from the top. At each step the two branches have the momentum fraction `$z = \min(p_{T,1}, p_{T,2})/(p_{T,1}+p_{T,2})$`. Branches with `$z < z_\text{cut} = 0.1$` are dropped, and the first pair that passes defines `$z_g$` (and its angle `$R_g$`). `$z_g$` is close to the splitting function of the hardest splitting of the parton. Energy loss can change it: a medium that removes soft, wide branches, or resolves the two prongs separately, shifts `$z_g$`.

The array interface wraps fjcontrib's SoftDrop. We give it the constituents of each jet above 20 GeV (jets of the fragments alone, as in section 5) as one entry, reclustered with C/A and asked for one exclusive jet.

**One window, not the sum.** In p+p, about 10 of the jets above 20 GeV come from the lowest window. Weighted with `$\sigma_k$`, each would count about 1,000 times as much as a jet of the highest window, and these few jets would decide the weighted mean, like the single hadron of the spike in tutorial 05. So we compare the jets of one window, p̂T 30–50 GeV, where Au+Au has almost all its jets above 20 GeV. Within a window every jet has the same weight. The error of the mean comes from leaving out one event at a time (jackknife): the jets of one event's fragmentations are not independent.

```python
CA = fj.JetDefinition(fj.cambridge_algorithm, 1.0)
zg_edges = np.linspace(0.1, 0.5, 9)

def jackknife_mean(x, event):
    """Mean of x and its error from leaving out one event at a time."""
    ids, inv = np.unique(event, return_inverse=True)
    s, n = np.bincount(inv, weights=x), np.bincount(inv)
    loo = (s.sum() - s) / (n.sum() - n)                     # the mean without each event
    return x.mean(), np.sqrt((len(ids) - 1) / len(ids) * np.sum((loo - loo.mean()) ** 2))

ZG = {}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4))
for name in FJ:
    d, rd = FJ[name], FJ[name]["reader"]
    sel = (d["pt"] > 20.0) & np.isin(d["event"], rd.pthat_bin_events(2))
    cs = fj.ClusterSequence(ak.to_packed(d["cons"][sel]), CA)
    zg = cs.exclusive_jets_softdrop_grooming(njets=1, beta=0.0, symmetry_cut=0.1, R0=R).symmetrysoftdrop.to_numpy()
    h = hist.Hist(hist.axis.Variable(zg_edges, label=r"$z_g$"), storage=hist.storage.Weight())
    h.fill(zg)                                     # ungroomed jets (z_g = -1) fall outside the axis
    mh.histplot(h / len(zg) / np.diff(zg_edges), ax=ax, label=name, flow="none")
    groomed = zg > 0
    ZG[name] = jackknife_mean(zg[groomed], d["event"][sel][groomed])
    print(f"{name}: {sel.sum()} jets above 20 GeV from {len(np.unique(d['event'][sel]))} events; "
          f"groomed {groomed.mean():.0%}; <z_g> = {ZG[name][0]:.3f} +- {ZG[name][1]:.3f}")
ax.set(ylabel=r"$\frac{1}{N_\mathrm{jet}}\,dN/dz_g$",
       title=r"SoftDrop $z_\mathrm{cut}=0.1$, $\beta=0$; $\hat p_T$ 30-50 GeV, jets of the fragments, $p_T>20$ GeV")
ax.legend();
```

```
Au+Au: 110 jets above 20 GeV from 33 events; groomed 95%; <z_g> = 0.229 +- 0.010
p+p: 9946 jets above 20 GeV from 1469 events; groomed 94%; <z_g> = 0.244 +- 0.001
```

**What to notice.**

- **In p+p, `$z_g$` falls from the cut at 0.1 towards 0.5.** The hardest splitting of a parton is mostly asymmetric: the QCD splitting function grows like `$1/z$` at small `$z$`.
- **Au+Au has the same shape within its errors.** The means differ by 0.015 ± 0.010, 1.5 standard deviations: with 110 jets from 33 events no change of `$z_g$` can be seen. (The error bars of the bins count jets as independent, which they are not; for Au+Au they are too small.)
- **Selection matters.** At the same jet `$p_T$` in the same window, the Au+Au jets come from the partons that lost the least energy, which biases any comparison at fixed jet `$p_T$`.

In a measurement, the background would have to be removed particle by particle before grooming (for example with fjcontrib's ConstituentSubtractor, which the Python bindings do not wrap). The jets of the fragments alone avoid that here.

## 7. The medium response inside the jet

The energy a jet loses does not disappear: the fluid picks it up (tutorial 06), and it comes out as extra soft hadrons around the jet (tutorial 07). A jet finder does not know which hadrons are which, so part of this **medium response** ends up inside the jet. Here it is ``` $\langle$``bulk_jet ``` `$-$` ``` bulk_bg``$\rangle$ ```: the charged `$p_T$` at a distance `$\Delta R$` from the leading parton, per event, next to that of the jet's own fragments. The reader averages all oversamples of all 120 events; we go out to `$\Delta R = 0.9$`, where the cone around a parton at `$|y| < 0.6$` still lies inside `$|\eta| < 1.5$`.

```python
def lead_axis(info):
    """eta and phi of the event's hardest shower initiator."""
    ini = info.initiators()
    px, py, pz = ini[np.argmax(np.hypot(ini[:, 3], ini[:, 4])), 3:6]
    return np.arcsinh(pz / np.hypot(px, py)), np.arctan2(py, px)

def dR_lead(ev, info):
    eta0, phi0 = lead_axis(info)
    return np.hypot(ev.eta - eta0, np.mod(ev.phi - phi0 + np.pi, 2 * np.pi) - np.pi)

clustered = lambda ev, info: ev.charged & (np.abs(ev.eta) < ETA_MAX) & (ev.pt > PT_MIN)
r_edges = np.linspace(0, 0.9, 10)
t0 = time.time()
wake, wake_err = aa.jet_minus_background(dR_lead, r_edges, mask=clustered, weights="pt")
frag, frag_err = aa.hist("jet_frag", dR_lead, r_edges, mask=clustered, weights="pt")
print(f"{time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4))
dr = np.diff(r_edges)
for vals, errs, label in ((frag, frag_err, "jet fragments"), (wake, wake_err, "medium response: bulk_jet - bulk_bg")):
    h = hist.Hist(hist.axis.Variable(r_edges, label=r"$\Delta R$ to the leading parton"), storage=hist.storage.Weight())
    h.view().value, h.view().variance = vals / dr, (errs / dr) ** 2
    mh.histplot(h, ax=ax, label=label, flow="none")
ax.axvline(R, color="0.5", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.axhline(0, color="0.5", lw=0.6)
ax.set(ylabel=r"$dp_T/d\Delta R$ per event [GeV]", title=r"charged hadrons, $p_T > 0.15$ GeV, $|\eta| < 1.5$")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
inside = r_edges[1:] <= R + 1e-9
print(f"inside Delta R < {R}: medium response {wake[inside].sum():.2f} +- {np.sqrt((wake_err[inside]**2).sum()):.2f} GeV,"
      f" jet fragments {frag[inside].sum():.2f} GeV")
print(f"inside Delta R < {r_edges[-1]}: medium response {wake.sum():.2f} +- {np.sqrt((wake_err**2).sum()):.2f} GeV,"
      f" jet fragments {frag.sum():.2f} GeV")
drho = rho_rec["full"] - rho_rec["emb"]          # the same fragments: the wake's effect on rho
print(f"the wake raises rho: rho(full) - rho(bkg + jet) = {drho.mean():+.2f} +- {drho.std() / np.sqrt(len(drho)):.2f}"
      f" GeV per unit area -> {drho.mean() * np.pi * R**2:+.2f} GeV more subtracted from a jet of area pi R^2")
print(f"jets (section 3): full - embedded = {diff.mean():+.2f} +- {diff.std() / np.sqrt(len(diff)):.2f} GeV")
```

```
2 s
inside Delta R < 0.4: medium response 1.12 +- 0.19 GeV, jet fragments 6.32 GeV
inside Delta R < 0.9: medium response 3.05 +- 0.43 GeV, jet fragments 7.35 GeV
the wake raises rho: rho(full) - rho(bkg + jet) = +0.74 +- 0.15 GeV per unit area -> +0.37 GeV more subtracted from a jet of area pi R^2
jets (section 3): full - embedded = +0.83 +- 0.49 GeV
```

**What to notice.**

- **The fragments sit in the core, the medium response does not.** The fragments' `$p_T$` falls steeply with `$\Delta R$`. The medium response is spread out: per unit of `$\Delta R$` it is roughly flat from 0.1 to 0.9, small only in the very core.
- **The cone of a jet with `$R = 0.4$` catches only part of it**: about 1.1 GeV, on top of about 6.3 GeV of charged fragments of the leading parton. Out to `$\Delta R = 0.9$` it is about 3 GeV. Larger jets get back more of the lost energy, so jet suppression depends on `$R$`.
- **ρA subtraction removes some of it.** The wake is spread over the whole event, so it also raises ρ, by about 0.7 GeV per unit area: about 0.4 GeV more is subtracted from each jet as if it were background. What remains in a subtracted jet, about 1.1 − 0.4 = 0.7 GeV, agrees with the 0.8 ± 0.5 GeV that the jets of section 3 gained between the embedding and the full event.

The errors here are those of independent sampling. Tutorial 07 measures the same difference with correlated sampling, about 8 times more precisely, and maps its shape around the jet.

### Check your result

FastJet places its ghosts with a small random jitter, and the Python bindings cannot set its seed. A fresh kernel repeats the same sequence, but clustering in another order, or another FastJet build, gives slightly different areas and ρ. Those checks have tolerances; the rest is exact.

```python
import json
exp = json.load(open("expected/08_jets_fastjet.json"))
np.testing.assert_allclose([len(FJ["Au+Au"]["pt"]), len(FJ["p+p"]["pt"])], exp["n_frag_jets"])
np.testing.assert_allclose(ratio, exp["ratio_aa_pp"], rtol=1e-6)
np.testing.assert_allclose([ZG["Au+Au"][0], ZG["p+p"][0]], exp["mean_zg"], rtol=1e-6)
np.testing.assert_allclose(wake[inside].sum(), exp["medium_pt_in_cone"], rtol=1e-6)
np.testing.assert_allclose(rho_rec["bkg"].mean(), exp["rho_bkg"], rtol=0.01)
np.testing.assert_allclose(cones.std(), exp["random_cone_width"], rtol=0.05)
np.testing.assert_allclose(d_emb.mean(), exp["dpt_emb_mean"], atol=0.5)
print("All checks pass.")
```

# 09 · ROOT files from Python: uproot and RDataFrame

**Time:** 40 minutes · **Needs:** any setup · **Data:** `auau_stats` and `pp_ref`: the ROOT files and the jet_frag HDF5 files (0.3 GB, downloaded once)

Most analyses in heavy-ion physics are written in ROOT. The production writes HDF5, so `run_h5toROOT.py` copies the hadrons and the event record of every job into a ROOT file, plus one campaign file with the cross sections. This tutorial reads those files from Python, without ROOT, with [uproot](https://uproot.readthedocs.io) and [awkward arrays](https://awkward-array.org). It:

- shows what the converter writes, and why one entry is one oversample;
- reads the event record, the p̂T windows, the campaign's cross sections and the provenance;
- handles the hadrons of every sample as jagged (awkward) arrays;
- makes a cross-section-weighted spectrum with `hist`, and checks it against the HDF5 reader;
- shows the same with RDataFrame, for readers who have PyROOT.

The data are 120 Au+Au events (0–10 %, 200 GeV) in three p̂T windows, and their p+p reference (4,500 events in vacuum, the same windows). Tutorial 10 reads the same files in C++.

Reference pages: [ROOT and C++](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/analysis/root/), [What a production writes](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/analysis/files/).

> **Work in progress: examples, not vetted physics.** The tutorials show how to run the simulation and use its outputs. The data sets are small, so the statistics are low, and the analyses have not been checked to the standard of a publication: treat every number and figure as an illustration, not as a physics result.

> **The outputs shown** were produced on an Apple Silicon Mac, in the environment the xscape wheel 0.2.0 is built in, with the hydro on the GPU through Metal.

## 1. What `run_h5toROOT.py` writes, and why

A production job writes its hadrons into three HDF5 files, one per *tag*: `bulk_jet` (the medium with the jet's wake, sampled from the jet leg's freeze-out surface), `bulk_bg` (the medium alone, from the background's surface) and `jet_frag` (the jet's own hadrons). `run_h5toROOT.py` turns each job into **one** ROOT file, `<stem>_hadrons.root`:

| object                            | one entry per | content                                                                                                                                       |
| --------------------------------- | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `bulk_jet`, `bulk_bg`, `jet_frag` | sample        | `event`, `unit`, `sample`, `bg_unit`, and per hadron `pid`, `pstat`, `E`, `px`, `py`, `pz` (and `t`, `x`, `y`, `z` if the job kept positions) |
| `events`                          | event         | the event record: p̂T window, background, parton and droplet summaries, the shower initiators `ini_*`                                          |
| `windows`                         | p̂T window     | this job's cross-section estimate of each window                                                                                              |
| `provenance`                      | –             | a JSON string: every setting, seed and input behind the file                                                                                  |

It also writes one **campaign file** for all jobs together, with the combined cross sections.

**Why one entry per sample?** A sample (an *oversample* of the bulk, or one fragmentation of the jet) is a complete set of hadrons, like one Monte Carlo event. One entry per event would hold all samples of an event at once, millions of hadrons at a few hundred oversamples. One entry per hadron would lose the event. So an entry reads like an event, and the columns `event`, `unit` and `sample` say which event and which sample it is. Keep in mind that the samples of one event share one fluid: they are not independent events.

The files are **RNTuples**, ROOT's new columnar format (ROOT ≥ 6.34 reads them; `--format ttree` writes classic TTrees for older ROOT). The sizes of this set, per job:

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

pd.set_option("display.float_format", "{:.4g}".format)   # 4 significant digits in tables
SET, PP = "auau_stats", "pp_ref"
CAMPAIGN = {SET: "stats_campaign.root", PP: "ppref_campaign.root"}

sizes = te.files(SET)
rows = []
for name in sorted(n for n in sizes if n.endswith("_hadrons.root")):
    stem = name[: -len("_hadrons.root")]
    h5 = sum(sizes[f"{stem}_hadrons_{tag}.h5"] for tag in ["bulk_jet", "bulk_bg", "jet_frag"])
    rows.append((stem, h5 / 1e6, sizes[name] / 1e6, sizes[name] / h5))
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["job", "3 HDF5 hadron files [MB]", "ROOT file [MB]", "ROOT / HDF5"]).round(2)
```

## 2. Open a file: on disk, or streamed

`uproot.open` reads a ROOT file in pure Python. It takes a local path or a URL. `te.data` gives the local copy when there is one, and with `stream=True` the file's `osdf://` URL on the OSDF, which uproot reads through pelicanfs (without pelicanfs: its HTTPS address at an OSDF cache):

```python
import uproot

STEM = "AuAu_0_10_jet_stats_seed0201"
f = uproot.open(te.data(SET, STEM + "_hadrons.root"))
for name, cls in f.classnames().items():
    n = f[name].num_entries if cls == "ROOT::RNTuple" else ""
    print(f"{name:14s} {cls:14s} {n}")
```

```
events;1       ROOT::RNTuple  30
windows;1      ROOT::RNTuple  3
provenance;1   TObjString     
bulk_jet;1     ROOT::RNTuple  300
bulk_bg;1      ROOT::RNTuple  100
jet_frag;1     ROOT::RNTuple  300
```

```python
url = te.data(SET, STEM + "_hadrons.root", stream=True)
print(url)
with uproot.open(url) as remote:
    first = remote["events"].arrays(["event", "pthat_bin", "pthat"])
    src = remote.file.source
    print(f"{len(first)} events streamed: {src.num_requests} requests, "
          f"{src.num_requested_bytes / 1e3:.0f} kB of the {src.num_bytes / 1e6:.0f} MB file")
```

```

```


**What to notice.** Streaming reads only the columns asked for: the events table took a few kB of a 53 MB file. That makes it cheap to look into files you have not downloaded. For an analysis that reads every hadron, download the files once (as `te.fetch` did) and read them from disk.

## 3. The event record: the `events` table

Each row is one event. The columns are those of the production's event record, plus each event's number of samples per tag and its shower initiators:

```python
import awkward as ak

events = f["events"].arrays()                    # an awkward array of records
print(len(events), "events,", len(events.fields), "columns")
cols = ["event", "pthat_bin", "pthat", "bg_unit", "parton_pt_lead", "E_droplets",
        "n_samples_jet", "n_samples_bg", "n_samples_frag", "sigma_file_mb"]
table = ak.to_dataframe(events[cols])
table.head(8)
```

| 7     | 7     | 1         | 22.91 | 1       | 23.76          | 30.93      | 10            | 20           | 10             | 4.975e-05     |

**What to notice.**

- **Three windows, one background.** The job made 5 backgrounds (hydro without a jet) and put 6 jets into each: 2 in each p̂T window 10–20, 20–30 and 30–50 GeV (`pthat_bin` 0, 1, 2). Events 0–5 share background 0 (`bg_unit`), events 6–11 background 1, and so on.
- **The samples:** 10 oversamples of the jet leg per event (`n_samples_jet`), 20 of each background (`n_samples_bg`), 10 fragmentations of the jet (`n_samples_frag`).
- **`sigma_file_mb`** is this job's estimate of the window's cross section. It is only an estimate from one job; the campaign value (section 4) is the one to use.

The initiators (the partons that started the showers) are **jagged** columns: each event has its own number of them. awkward arrays hold such data directly, and numpy functions work on them element by element:

```python
ini_pt = np.hypot(events.ini_px, events.ini_py)       # var * float64: per event, per initiator
print("initiators per event:", ak.num(ini_pt)[:10].tolist(), "...")
print("leading initiator pT, events 0-5 [GeV]:", np.round(ak.max(ini_pt, axis=1)[:6].to_numpy(), 1))
try:
    f["events"].arrays(library="np")                  # numpy cannot hold jagged columns
except ValueError as e:
    print("library='np':", type(e).__name__, "-", str(e).split("(")[0].strip())
```

```
initiators per event: [4, 3, 5, 9, 3, 3, 6, 2, 5, 4] ...
leading initiator pT, events 0-5 [GeV]: [13.4 21.3 36.3 17.5 22.4 32. ]
library='np': ValueError - cannot convert to RegularArray because subarray lengths are not regular
```

**A pitfall:** read `events` as awkward (the default). With `library="np"` uproot tries to turn the jagged `ini_*` columns into regular numpy arrays and fails. Flat tables such as `windows` read fine either way.

## 4. The p̂T windows and the campaign's cross sections

A jet campaign generates its hard scatterings in p̂T windows: equal numbers of events per window, so the rare high-p̂T jets get the same statistics as the common low-p̂T ones. To combine windows, each event is weighted by its window's cross section σ_k over the number of events N_k in that window. PYTHIA estimates σ_k while it generates; each job writes its own estimate in its `windows` table:

```python
folder = folders[SET]
per_job = {}
for path in sorted(folder.glob("*_hadrons.root")):
    with uproot.open(path) as rf:
        per_job[path.name.split("_seed")[1][:4]] = pd.DataFrame(rf["windows"].arrays(library="np"))
wins = pd.concat(per_job, names=["job", "row"])
wins[["window", "pthat_lo", "pthat_hi", "sigma_mb", "sigma_err_mb", "n_tried", "n_accepted", "n_kept"]]
```

|      |     | window | pthat_lo | pthat_hi  | sigma_mb  | sigma_err_mb | n_tried | n_accepted | n_kept |
| ---- | --- | ------ | -------- | --------- | --------- | ------------ | ------- | ---------- | ------ |
| job  | row |        |          |           |           |              |         |            |        |
| 0201 | 0   | 0      | 10       | 20        | 0.003465  | 0.0008282    | 19      | 19         | 10     |
| 1    | 1   | 20     | 30       | 4.975e-05 | 1.125e-05 | 16           | 16      | 10         |        |
| 2    | 2   | 30     | 50       | 2.27e-06  | 5.385e-07 | 15           | 15      | 10         |        |
| 0202 | 0   | 0      | 10       | 20        | 0.002373  | 0.0006315    | 24      | 24         | 10     |
| 1    | 1   | 20     | 30       | 3.525e-05 | 8.823e-06 | 20           | 20      | 10         |        |
| 2    | 2   | 30     | 50       | 2.125e-06 | 4.396e-07 | 12           | 12      | 10         |        |
| 0203 | 0   | 0      | 10       | 20        | 0.003087  | 0.0006692    | 14      | 14         | 10     |
| 1    | 1   | 20     | 30       | 3.947e-05 | 1.015e-05 | 21           | 21      | 10         |        |
| 2    | 2   | 30     | 50       | 3.291e-06 | 7.359e-07 | 12           | 12      | 10         |        |
| 0204 | 0   | 0      | 10       | 20        | 0.002691  | 0.0006858    | 21      | 21         | 10     |
| 1    | 1   | 20     | 30       | 2.883e-05 | 7.676e-06 | 24           | 24      | 10         |        |
| 2    | 2   | 30     | 50       | 2.654e-06 | 6.105e-07 | 14           | 14      | 10         |        |

Each job tried only 12–24 PYTHIA events per window (`n_tried`), so each estimate has an error of 20–27 %. Of those, `n_kept` passed the cut on the partons' rapidity (`$|y| < 0.6$`); the fraction is the `acceptance`, and the cross sections include it. The campaign file combines the estimates, weighting each job by its accepted PYTHIA events (`n_accepted`), `$\sigma_k = \sum_i n_i \sigma_{k,i} / \sum_i n_i$`, and stores the weight per event `weight_mb` `$= \sigma_k / N_k$`:

```python
camp = {s: uproot.open(folders[s] / CAMPAIGN[s]) for s in (SET, PP)}
cw = pd.DataFrame(camp[SET]["windows"].arrays(library="np"))
print(cw[["window", "pthat_lo", "pthat_hi", "sigma_mb", "sigma_err_mb", "acceptance", "n_events", "weight_mb"]].to_string(index=False))

n = wins["n_accepted"].unstack("job").to_numpy()
s = wins["sigma_mb"].unstack("job").to_numpy()
np.testing.assert_allclose(cw["sigma_mb"], (n * s).sum(1) / n.sum(1), rtol=1e-12)
np.testing.assert_allclose(cw["weight_mb"], cw["sigma_mb"] / cw["n_events"], rtol=1e-12)
print("sigma = sum(n sigma) / sum(n) and weight_mb = sigma / n_events: confirmed")
```

```
 window  pthat_lo  pthat_hi  sigma_mb  sigma_err_mb  acceptance  n_events  weight_mb
      0        10        20  0.002853     0.0003563      0.5128        40  7.131e-05
      1        20        30 3.731e-05     4.667e-06      0.4938        40  9.327e-07
      2        30        50  2.57e-06     2.948e-07      0.7547        40  6.425e-08
sigma = sum(n sigma) / sum(n) and weight_mb = sigma / n_events: confirmed
```

The campaign file also lists its files, with the offset that numbers the events of all files in one sequence (global event = `event_offset` + `event`, as the HDF5 reader `HadronFileReader` numbers them):

```python

```

|     | file_index | n_events | event_offset | prod_seed | n_backgrounds |
| --- | ---------- | -------- | ------------ | --------- | ------------- |
| 0   | 0          | 30       | 0            | 201       | 5             |
| 1   | 1          | 30       | 30           | 202       | 5             |
| 2   | 2          | 30       | 60           | 203       | 5             |
| 3   | 3          | 30       | 90           | 204       | 5             |

The p+p reference generated the same windows with the same parton cut, so it estimates the **same** cross sections, from many more tries (`n_tried` ~ 700–1200 per window and job):

```python
pw = pd.DataFrame(camp[PP]["windows"].arrays(library="np"))
pd.DataFrame({
    "window": cw["pthat_lo"].astype(int).astype(str) + "-" + cw["pthat_hi"].astype(int).astype(str) + " GeV",
    "Au+Au sigma [mb]": cw["sigma_mb"], "Au+Au error": cw["sigma_err_mb"],
    "p+p sigma [mb]": pw["sigma_mb"], "p+p error": pw["sigma_err_mb"],
    "difference / error": (cw["sigma_mb"] - pw["sigma_mb"]) / np.hypot(cw["sigma_err_mb"], pw["sigma_err_mb"]),
})
```

|     | window    | Au+Au sigma [mb] | Au+Au error | p+p sigma [mb] | p+p error | difference / error |
| --- | --------- | ---------------- | ----------- | -------------- | --------- | ------------------ |
| 0   | 10-20 GeV | 0.002853         | 0.0003563   | 0.00229        | 4.936e-05 | 1.564              |
| 1   | 20-30 GeV | 3.731e-05        | 4.667e-06   | 4.244e-05      | 8.284e-07 | -1.083             |
| 2   | 30-50 GeV | 2.57e-06         | 2.948e-07   | 2.198e-06      | 3.974e-08 | 1.252              |

**What to notice.** The two campaigns agree within their errors (at most 1.6 standard deviations apart), and the p+p values are about six times more precise. The cross section belongs to the hard scattering, which is a p+p collision in PYTHIA for both. So when the two are compared (section 6), it is better to weight both with the p+p values.

## 5. The provenance

Every ROOT file carries a JSON string, `provenance`, with what made it: the converter's settings, and the attributes of the HDF5 files it came from (production settings, seeds, XML, hadronization). It is the record to check before combining files:

```python
import json

prov = json.loads(str(f["provenance"]))           # a TObjString: str() gives the JSON
print("keys:", list(prov))
print("converter settings:", prov["settings"])
print("layout:", prov["layout"])
had = prov["hadrons"]
for tag in had:
    print(f"{tag:9s} {had[tag]['generator']:40s} samples per unit: {had[tag]['n_samples']}")
for key in ["system", "prod_hard", "hydro", "jet", "eos", "T_fo", "prod_seed", "positions"]:
    print(f"  {key:10s} {had['bulk_jet'][key]}")
print("  built in ", te.short(had["bulk_jet"]["prod_build"]))
```

**What to notice.**

- **`bulk_bg` has `n_samples` 0:** its number of samples is not one fixed number in its attributes (`oversample_bg` is `per-pthat-bin`). The `events` table has the actual number, 20 per background.
- **`layout`** says how the tags pair up: fragmentation `k % n_samples_frag` goes with jet-leg sample `k`. For files made with correlated sampling (tutorial 07), background sample `k` also pairs with jet-leg sample `k`; these files were sampled independently.

Before combining jobs, check that they agree in everything but their seeds. Here we compare the settings that matter across the four jobs, and their uuids with the campaign file's list:

```python
def fingerprint(p):
    """What must agree between files that are combined (all but the seeds)."""
    h = p["hadrons"]["bulk_jet"]
    return {"system": h["system"], "hard": h["prod_hard"], "eos": h["eos"], "T_fo": h["T_fo"],
            "oversample": h["n_samples"], "frag": p["hadrons"]["jet_frag"]["n_samples"],
            "correlated": h["correlated_sampling"], "music_input": hash(h["music_input"]),
            "hadronize_xml": hash(h["hadronize_xml"]), "converter": json.dumps(p["settings"])}

camp_prov = json.loads(str(camp[SET]["provenance"]))
uuids = {x["root_file"]: x["uuid"] for x in camp_prov["files"]}
rows = []
for path in sorted(folder.glob("*_hadrons.root")):
    with uproot.open(path) as rf:
        p = json.loads(str(rf["provenance"]))
    rows.append({"file": path.name, "seed": p["hadrons"]["bulk_jet"]["prod_seed"],
                 "uuid in campaign": uuids[path.name] == p["hadrons"]["bulk_jet"]["source_uuid"],
                 "same settings as the first": fingerprint(p) == fingerprint(prov)})
pd.DataFrame(rows)
```

## 6. The hadrons: one entry per sample

The three hadron ntuples of this job:

```python
for tag in ["bulk_jet", "bulk_bg", "jet_frag"]:
    a = f[tag].arrays(["event", "unit", "sample"], library="np")
    units = np.unique(a["unit"])
    print(f"{tag:9s} {f[tag].num_entries:4d} entries = {len(units):2d} units x "
          f"{f[tag].num_entries // len(units)} samples;  the first entries' (unit, sample):",
          list(zip(a["unit"][:3].tolist(), a["sample"][:3].tolist())))
```

```
bulk_jet   300 entries = 30 units x 10 samples;  the first entries' (unit, sample): [(0, 0), (0, 1), (0, 2)]
bulk_bg    100 entries =  5 units x 20 samples;  the first entries' (unit, sample): [(0, 0), (0, 1), (0, 2)]
jet_frag   300 entries = 30 units x 10 samples;  the first entries' (unit, sample): [(0, 0), (0, 1), (0, 2)]
```

For `bulk_jet` and `jet_frag` a unit is an event. For `bulk_bg` a unit is a background: 5 backgrounds × 20 samples, each used by 6 events (its `event` column holds the first of them).

The hadrons of each entry come as jagged arrays: one list per sample, of different lengths. Everything below works on all samples at once, without a Python loop over hadrons. Two details: `np.isin` does not take jagged arrays, so the charged-hadron mask is built on the flattened list and unflattened again; and `$\eta = \sinh^{-1}(p_z/p_T)$`.

```python
from jetscape.hadrons_h5 import CHARGED            # |pid| of the charged hadrons and leptons

def charged(pid):
    """A jagged mask: True for charged hadrons."""
    return ak.unflatten(np.isin(np.abs(ak.flatten(pid)), CHARGED), ak.num(pid))

def multiplicities(tag):
    """Per sample: all hadrons, and charged hadrons at |eta| < 1."""
    a = f[tag].arrays(["event", "unit", "sample", "pid", "px", "py", "pz"])
    pt = np.hypot(a.px, a.py)
    eta = np.arcsinh(a.pz / pt)
    mid = charged(a.pid) & (np.abs(eta) < 1)
    return pd.DataFrame({"event": a.event.to_numpy(), "unit": a.unit.to_numpy(),
                         "all": ak.num(a.pid).to_numpy(), "charged |eta|<1": ak.sum(mid, axis=1).to_numpy()})

jet = f["bulk_jet"].arrays(["pid", "px", "py", "pz"])
print("bulk_jet as awkward:", jet.type)
mult = {tag: multiplicities(tag) for tag in ["bulk_jet", "bulk_bg", "jet_frag"]}
pd.DataFrame({tag: d[["all", "charged |eta|<1"]].mean() for tag, d in mult.items()}).T.round(1)
```

```
bulk_jet as awkward: 300 * {pid: var * int32, px: var * float32, py: var * float32, pz: var * float32}
```

| | all | charged |eta|\<1 | | --- | --- | --- | | bulk_jet | 8844 | 1484 | | bulk_bg | 8814 | 1477 | | jet_frag | 28.2 | 7.5 |

A sample of the bulk has about 8,800 hadrons in all; about 1,480 of them are charged and at midrapidity. A fragmentation of the jet has 28 hadrons, 7.5 of them charged at `$|\eta| < 1$`.

How much do the samples of one event differ, and how much do events differ? Below, each event's 10 jet-leg samples (mean and spread), coloured by the background the event used, and the 20 samples of each background as a band:

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

d = mult["bulk_jet"]
bg_of = table.set_index("event")["bg_unit"]
per_event = d.groupby("event")["charged |eta|<1"].agg(["mean", "std"])
per_bg = mult["bulk_bg"].groupby("unit")["charged |eta|<1"].agg(["mean", "std"])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.8))
for b in per_bg.index:
    evs = per_event.index[bg_of[per_event.index] == b]
    m, s = per_bg.loc[b]
    ax.fill_between([evs.min() - 0.4, evs.max() + 0.4], m - s, m + s, color=f"C{b}", alpha=0.2, lw=0)
    ax.errorbar(evs, per_event.loc[evs, "mean"], per_event.loc[evs, "std"], fmt="o", color=f"C{b}",
                label=f"background {b}")
ax.set(xlabel="event", ylabel=r"charged hadrons at $|\eta|<1$ per sample",
       title="jet leg: mean $\\pm$ spread of 10 samples; bands: the background's 20 samples")
ax.legend(fontsize=7, ncol=5, loc="lower right")
within = d.groupby("event")["charged |eta|<1"].std().mean()
between = per_bg["mean"].std()
print(f"spread between the samples of one event: {within:.0f};  Poisson would give "
      f"{np.sqrt(d['charged |eta|<1'].mean()):.0f};  spread between the 5 backgrounds: {between:.0f}")
```

```
spread between the samples of one event: 43;  Poisson would give 39;  spread between the 5 backgrounds: 52
```

**What to notice.**

- **Events cluster by background.** The six events that share a background have about the same multiplicity as that background: the medium (its initial state and size) sets the number of hadrons, and a jet adds only a few.
- **The samples of one event spread by about ±43.** That is Cooper–Frye sampling of one fluid, somewhat wider than a Poisson distribution (±39); one reason is that a resonance decaying into two charged hadrons adds both at once.
- **The backgrounds differ by about as much** (±52 between the five), from fluctuations of the initial state within the 0–10 % class.
- So the 300 entries of `bulk_jet` are **not** 300 independent events: they are 30 events, from 5 media. Averages and errors must be taken per event (each event the mean over its samples), never per entry.

## 7. A cross-section-weighted spectrum with `hist`

Now the whole campaign: the `$p_T$` spectrum of charged hadrons at `$|\eta| < 1$`, summed over the three windows with their cross sections. Every event is the mean over its samples, so an entry (one sample of event `$e$` in window `$k$`) weighs

`$w = \frac{\sigma_k}{N_k}\,\frac{1}{n_\text{samples}(e)},$`

which makes the result `$d\sigma/dp_T$` in mb/GeV. The weight is per entry; `ak.broadcast_arrays` copies it to each of the entry's hadrons. We fill a [hist](https://hist.readthedocs.io) histogram with `Weight` storage, which keeps the sum of squared weights for the errors:

```python
import hist

EDGES = np.geomspace(0.2, 50, 25)                 # 24 log bins, as tutorial 10
N_SAMPLES = {"bulk_jet": "n_samples_jet", "bulk_bg": "n_samples_bg", "jet_frag": "n_samples_frag"}

def xsec_spectrum(set_name, tag, sigma=None):
    """dsigma/dpT [mb/GeV] of charged hadrons at |eta| < 1 of one hadron ntuple (bulk_jet or
    jet_frag: one unit per event), over all files of a set.  sigma: the cross section per
    window (default: the campaign's)."""
    win = camp[set_name]["windows"].arrays(["sigma_mb", "n_events"], library="np")
    per_event = (win["sigma_mb"] if sigma is None else sigma) / win["n_events"]   # sigma_k / N_k
    h = hist.Hist(hist.axis.Variable(EDGES, name="pt", label=r"$p_T$ [GeV]"),
                  storage=hist.storage.Weight())
    for path in sorted(folders[set_name].glob("*_hadrons.root")):
        with uproot.open(path) as rf:
            ev = rf["events"].arrays(["pthat_bin", N_SAMPLES[tag]], library="np")
            a = rf[tag].arrays(["event", "pid", "px", "py", "pz"])
        pt = np.hypot(a.px, a.py)
        eta = np.arcsinh(a.pz / pt)
        sel = charged(a.pid) & (np.abs(eta) < 1)
        w_entry = per_event[ev["pthat_bin"][a.event]] / ev[N_SAMPLES[tag]][a.event]
        w = ak.broadcast_arrays(w_entry, pt)[0]               # the entry's weight, per hadron
        h.fill(pt=ak.flatten(pt[sel]), weight=ak.flatten(w[sel]))
    return h

width = np.diff(EDGES)
aa_frag = xsec_spectrum(SET, "jet_frag")
aa_full = xsec_spectrum(SET, "bulk_jet") + aa_frag            # the whole jet event
pp_frag = xsec_spectrum(PP, "jet_frag")
sigma_pp = camp[PP]["windows"].arrays(["sigma_mb"], library="np")["sigma_mb"]
aa_frag_ppsigma = xsec_spectrum(SET, "jet_frag", sigma=sigma_pp)   # for the ratio
for name, h in [("Au+Au jet event", aa_full), ("Au+Au jet fragments", aa_frag), ("p+p jet fragments", pp_frag)]:
    print(f"{name:20s} sigma x <N_ch(|eta|<1, pT > 0.2 GeV)> = {h.sum().value:.4g} mb")
bulk = aa_full.values() - aa_frag.values()
print(f"the jet fragments outnumber the bulk above pT = {EDGES[np.argmax(aa_frag.values() > bulk)]:.1f} GeV")
for lo, hi in [(0.2, 2), (2, 5), (5, 50)]:
    b = (EDGES[:-1] >= lo) & (EDGES[1:] <= hi * 1.001)
    print(f"Au+Au / p+p jet fragments at {lo}-{hi} GeV: "
          f"{aa_frag_ppsigma.values()[b].sum() / pp_frag.values()[b].sum():.2f}")
```

```
Au+Au jet event      sigma x <N_ch(|eta|<1, pT > 0.2 GeV)> = 3.584 mb
Au+Au jet fragments  sigma x <N_ch(|eta|<1, pT > 0.2 GeV)> = 0.01132 mb
p+p jet fragments    sigma x <N_ch(|eta|<1, pT > 0.2 GeV)> = 0.0241 mb
the jet fragments outnumber the bulk above pT = 4.0 GeV
Au+Au / p+p jet fragments at 0.2-2 GeV: 0.41
Au+Au / p+p jet fragments at 2-5 GeV: 0.26
Au+Au / p+p jet fragments at 5-50 GeV: 0.18
```

```python
import mplhep as mh

fig, (ax, rx) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(7, 6.5), sharex=True, gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [3, 1.3]})
mh.histplot(aa_full / width, ax=ax, label="Au+Au: jet event (bulk_jet + jet_frag)", flow="none", color="k", lw=2.5)
mh.histplot(aa_frag / width, ax=ax, label="Au+Au: jet fragments", flow="none", color="C3")
mh.histplot(pp_frag / width, ax=ax, label="p+p: jet fragments", flow="none", color="C0", ls="--")
ax.set(xscale="log", yscale="log", ylim=(1e-10, 50), ylabel=r"$d\sigma/dp_T$ [mb/GeV]", xlabel="",
       title=r"charged hadrons, $|\eta|<1$, $\hat p_T$ 10-50 GeV")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
a, p = aa_frag_ppsigma, pp_frag
ok = a.values() > 0                               # bins with Au+Au hadrons
ratio = np.where(ok, a.values() / p.values(), np.nan)
ratio_err = ratio * np.sqrt(a.variances() / np.where(ok, a.values(), 1) ** 2 + p.variances() / p.values() ** 2)
c = aa_frag.axes[0].centers
rx.errorbar(c, ratio, ratio_err, xerr=[c - EDGES[:-1], EDGES[1:] - c], fmt="o", ms=3, color="C3")
rx.axhline(1, color="0.5", lw=0.8)
rx.set(xscale="log", ylim=(0, 1.6), xlabel=r"$p_T$ [GeV]", ylabel="Au+Au / p+p\njet fragments");
```

**What to notice.**

- **The bulk dominates below 4 GeV,** by more than two orders of magnitude at low `$p_T$`. Above 4 GeV the jet event is the jet's own fragments: the fluid makes no hadrons that hard.
- **The jet's own hadrons are suppressed in Au+Au** at every `$p_T$` (the ratio panel; both weighted with the p+p cross sections): to about 0.4 below 2 GeV, 0.26 at 2–5 GeV, and mostly below 0.1 above 7 GeV (one bin at 14 GeV has a large error). The hard partons lost energy on their way through the medium, so their fragments are softer. The soft part of each shower was handed to the fluid (the droplets of tutorial 06): those hadrons are now in the bulk, as the wake of tutorial 07, not in `jet_frag`.
- **The Au+Au fragments are lumpy** above 10 GeV: 40 events per window are few. The p+p reference, with 1,500 per window, is smooth.
- **Only jets of p̂T 10–50 GeV are in here.** Softer jets, which were not generated, would add hadrons at low `$p_T$`, and harder ones at high `$p_T$`. The ratio compares the hadrons of the same jets with and without the medium.

## 8. The same numbers from the HDF5 files

The ROOT files are a copy of the HDF5 files, and the weighting is the HDF5 reader's: each event the mean over its samples, each window weighted with its cross section. So `HadronFileReader` on the `jet_frag` HDF5 files must give the same spectrum, bin for bin, and the same errors:

```python
from jetscape.hadrons_h5 import HadronFileReader

mid_charged = lambda ev, info: ev.charged & (np.abs(ev.eta) < 1)

def h5_spectrum(set_name):
    """sum_k sigma_k <dN/dpT>_k with the HDF5 reader -> (values, errors) per bin."""
    r = HadronFileReader(str(folders[set_name] / "*_hadrons_jet_frag.h5"))
    val, var = np.zeros(len(EDGES) - 1), np.zeros(len(EDGES) - 1)
    for k in range(len(r.pthat_bins)):
        sigma, _ = r.pthat_bin_sigma(k)
        v, e = r.hist("jet_frag", "pt", EDGES, mask=mid_charged, events=r.pthat_bin_events(k))
        val, var = val + sigma * v, var + (sigma * e) ** 2
    return val, np.sqrt(var), r.n_events

for name, h, s in [("Au+Au", aa_frag, SET), ("p+p", pp_frag, PP)]:
    val, err, n = h5_spectrum(s)
    dv = np.max(np.abs(h.values() - val) / np.where(val > 0, val, 1))
    de = np.max(np.abs(np.sqrt(h.variances()) - err) / np.where(err > 0, err, 1))
    print(f"{name:6s} {n:5d} events: largest relative difference ROOT/uproot vs HDF5 reader: "
          f"values {dv:.1e}, errors {de:.1e}")
    np.testing.assert_allclose(h.values(), val, rtol=1e-10)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(np.sqrt(h.variances()), err, rtol=1e-10)
```

```
Au+Au    120 events: largest relative difference ROOT/uproot vs HDF5 reader: values 8.4e-15, errors 4.6e-15
```

```
p+p     4500 events: largest relative difference ROOT/uproot vs HDF5 reader: values 7.9e-13, errors 3.2e-13
```

**What to notice.** The two agree to rounding (`$10^{-15}$` to `$10^{-12}$`): the same hadrons, the same cross sections, the same per-event normalisation. The errors also agree: the sum of squared weights is the compound-Poisson error per event that the reader computes. (For `bulk_bg`, where one background is used by several events, the reader adds a background's weights before squaring; a plain `fill` per event would not.)

## 9. RDataFrame, if you have PyROOT

With ROOT ≥ 6.34 and its Python bindings, RDataFrame reads the same RNTuples and fills the histogram in C++, on several threads. The analysis environment here has no PyROOT, so the code below is **not executed**; it is the same computation as `xsec_spectrum`, and tutorial 10 runs the C++ version of it and checks it against the reader.

```
# needs PyROOT (ROOT >= 6.34 for RNTuple) -- not run in this notebook
import ROOT
ROOT.EnableImplicitMT(4)
folder = folders["auau_stats"]
weight_mb = ROOT.RDataFrame("windows", str(folder / "stats_campaign.root")).AsNumpy(["weight_mb"])["weight_mb"]
model = ROOT.RDF.TH1DModel("h", ";p_{T} [GeV];d#sigma/dp_{T} [mb/GeV]", len(EDGES) - 1, EDGES)
total = None
for path in sorted(folder.glob("*_hadrons.root")):
    ev = ROOT.RDataFrame("events", str(path)).AsNumpy(["pthat_bin", "n_samples_frag"])
    w = weight_mb[ev["pthat_bin"]] / ev["n_samples_frag"]         # per event of this file
    table = "ROOT::RVecD{" + ",".join(f"{x:.17g}" for x in w) + "}"
    h = (ROOT.RDataFrame("jet_frag", str(path))
         .Define("pt", "sqrt(px * px + py * py)")
         .Define("eta", "asinh(pz / pt)")
         .Define("ch", "abs(pid) == 211 || abs(pid) == 321 || abs(pid) == 2212 || abs(pid) == 3222"
                       " || abs(pid) == 3112 || abs(pid) == 3312 || abs(pid) == 3334"
                       " || abs(pid) == 11 || abs(pid) == 13")
         .Define("pt_sel", "pt[ch && abs(eta) < 1]")
         .Define("w", f"{table}[event]")                             # the entry's weight
         .Histo1D(model, "pt_sel", "w"))
    if total is None:
        total = h.GetValue().Clone("h_frag")
    else:
        total.Add(h.GetPtr())
total.Scale(1.0, "width")                                            # dsigma/dpT [mb/GeV]
```

- `RDataFrame("jet_frag", file)` opens a TTree or an RNTuple alike.
- Per file, the weights come from that file's `events` table: `event` is the event number *inside* the file.
- `Histo1D` with a collection (`pt_sel`) and one weight per entry fills every element with that weight.
- The C++ version (with a lambda instead of the string) is `rdf_spectrum.C` in tutorial 10.

# 10 · ROOT C++ macros and FastJet in C++

**Time:** 45 minutes · **Needs:** ROOT ≥ 6.34 (C++); FastJet's C++ library for section 7 · **Data:** `auau_stats` and `pp_ref`: the ROOT files (0.25 GB, downloaded once)

Tutorial 09 read the ROOT files of `run_h5toROOT.py` from Python. Most analyses in the field are C++ programs and ROOT macros, so this tutorial does the same in C++. It writes small macros, compiles them with ACLiC and runs them from the notebook:

- `HadronFileReader.h`, the header-only C++ reader: an event's hadrons as vectors;
- a loop over events and samples that fills histograms with the right normalisation;
- the macros that come with js-contrib, `read_hadrons.C` and `hadron_distributions.C`;
- RDataFrame in C++ on the RNTuples, checked against the reader;
- anti-`$k_T$` jets with FastJet's C++ library, with the background subtracted.

The data are those of tutorial 09: 120 Au+Au events (0–10 %, 200 GeV) in three p̂T windows, and their p+p reference.

Reference pages: [ROOT and C++](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/analysis/root/), [Jets with FastJet](https://jhputschke.github.io/js-contrib/analysis/jets/).

> **Work in progress: examples, not vetted physics.** The tutorials show how to run the simulation and use its outputs. The data sets are small, so the statistics are low, and the analyses have not been checked to the standard of a publication: treat every number and figure as an illustration, not as a physics result.

> **The outputs shown** were produced on an Apple Silicon Mac, in the environment the xscape wheel 0.2.0 is built in, with the hydro on the GPU through Metal. ROOT 6.36 and FastJet 3.4.3 (C++) came from Homebrew.

## 1. ROOT from a Python notebook

This is a Python notebook: Jupyter has no C++ kernel here. (ROOT has its own, `root --notebook`; the C++ notebook `read_hadrons.ipynb` in js-contrib uses it.) Instead, each macro is written to a file with `%%writefile`, and ROOT runs it in batch mode, the way it runs on a cluster: `root -l -b -q 'macro.C+(arguments)'`.

| option     |                                                                                                                                                       |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-l`       | no splash screen                                                                                                                                      |
| `-b`       | batch: no graphics windows (figures are saved as files)                                                                                               |
| `-q`       | quit when the macro is done                                                                                                                           |
| `macro.C+` | compile the macro with **ACLiC** (the system compiler) instead of interpreting it with Cling: full C++ speed and compiler errors before anything runs |

First, which ROOT is there? The ROOT files are RNTuples, which need ROOT 6.34 or later:

```python
import re
import subprocess

def sh(*cmd):
    return subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout.strip()

version = sh("root-config", "--version")
features = sh("root-config", "--features").split()
print("ROOT", version, "| RDataFrame:", "dataframe" in features, "| multithreading:", "imt" in features)
major, minor = (int(x) for x in re.split(r"[./]", version)[:2])
assert (major, minor) >= (6, 34), "RNTuple needs ROOT >= 6.34 (or convert with run_h5toROOT.py --format ttree)"
```

```
ROOT 6.36.06 | RDataFrame: True | multithreading: True
```

A shell command works too, with `!`:

```python
!root -l -b -q -e 'std::cout << "hello from ROOT " << gROOT->GetVersion() << std::endl;'
```

```
hello from ROOT 6.36.06
```

For the macros we use a small helper, `root()`. It runs one macro call in batch mode in the folder `out/10_root_cpp/`, where the macros and their outputs go, adds include paths and libraries first, prints ROOT's output (with the paths shortened), and raises an error when ROOT fails. A macro call that compiles and returns gives exit code 0; a compiler error or an uncaught C++ exception gives another code.

```python
import os
import time
from pathlib import Path
from IPython.display import Image, display

HERE = Path.cwd()
OUT = Path("out/10_root_cpp")                       # macros and outputs (out/ is git-ignored)
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

def root(call, includes=(), libraries=()):
    """Run ROOT in batch on one macro call; print its output; raise if it fails."""
    setup = "".join(f'gSystem->AddIncludePath("-I{Path(p).resolve()}");' for p in includes)
    setup += "".join(f'gSystem->Load("{lib}");' for lib in libraries)
    cmd = ["root", "-l", "-b", "-q"] + (["-e", setup] if setup else []) + [call]
    t0 = time.time()
    p = subprocess.run(cmd, cwd=OUT, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT, text=True)
    for line in p.stdout.splitlines():
        if not line.strip() or line.startswith("#"):          # (FastJet's banner)
            continue
        if "ACLiC>: creating shared library" in line:
            line = "ACLiC: compiled " + os.path.relpath(line.split()[-1], OUT)
        print(te.short(line.replace(str(OUT.resolve()) + "/", "")))
    if p.returncode != 0:
        raise RuntimeError(f"ROOT failed (exit code {p.returncode})")
    print(f"[{time.time() - t0:.0f} s]")
```

`HadronFileReader.h` and the example macros live in js-contrib, in `contribs/PyJetscape/example/analysis_root/`. We copy the ones we need next to our macros: from your js-contrib (a checkout or the installed tree), or else from GitHub. Copies, because ACLiC writes its compiled library next to the macro, and an installed tree may be read-only.

```python
import shutil
import urllib.request

ANALYSIS_ROOT = ("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jhputschke/js-contrib/main/"
                 "contribs/PyJetscape/example/analysis_root/")

def analysis_root_file(name):
    """Copy analysis_root/<name> into OUT: from the local js-contrib, else from GitHub."""
    try:
        from jetscape import paths
        src = Path(paths.examples_dir()) / "analysis_root" / name
    except Exception:
        src = None
    if src is not None and src.is_file():
        shutil.copy(src, OUT / name)
        return "js-contrib"
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(ANALYSIS_ROOT + name, OUT / name)
    return "GitHub"

for name in ["HadronFileReader.h", "read_hadrons.C", "hadron_distributions.C"]:
    print(f"{name:24s} from", analysis_root_file(name))
```

```
HadronFileReader.h       from js-contrib
read_hadrons.C           from js-contrib
hadron_distributions.C   from js-contrib
```

`HadronFileReader.h` is the C++ counterpart of the Python `HadronFileReader` of tutorial 07. It reads all `*_hadrons.root` files of a directory (and the campaign file), numbers the events over all files, and returns the hadrons of one sample of one event as a `std::vector<Hadron>`:

| call                   | ntuple     | the hadrons of                                                           |
| ---------------------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `r.bkg(e, k)`          | `bulk_bg`  | sample k of the background of event e (MUSIC_1, no jet)                  |
| `r.bkg_dep(e, k)`      | `bulk_jet` | oversample k of the jet leg: background + the jet's deposition (MUSIC_2) |
| `r.frag(e, j)`         | `jet_frag` | fragmentation j of the jet's partons                                     |
| `r.bkg_dep_frag(e, k)` | both       | the whole jet event: `bkg_dep(e, k)` + fragmentation k mod `n_frag(e)`   |

A `Hadron` has `pid`, `E`, `px`, `py`, `pz` and `pt()`, `eta()`, `phi()`, `charged()`, `p4()`. `r.info(e)` is the event's row of the `events` table (`EventInfo`: window, background, initiators, sample counts, `flagged()`).

## 3. A first macro, compiled with ACLiC

The macro opens the campaign, prints the windows and their cross sections, and looks at one event: its record and the hadrons of its first sample from each source.

```python
%%writefile out/10_root_cpp/first_look.C
// first_look.C: open a campaign with HadronFileReader.h and look at one event
#include "HadronFileReader.h"

#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>

void first_look(const char *dir, long e = 0) {
  using namespace hadrons_root;
  HadronFileReader r(dir);                       // every *_hadrons.root + the campaign file
  std::printf("%d files, %ld events; cross sections from the %s\n", r.n_files(),
              r.n_events(), r.sigma_source().c_str());
  for (int k = 0; k < r.n_windows(); ++k)
    std::printf("  window %d: pTHat %2.0f-%2.0f GeV, sigma = %.3e mb, %ld events,"
                " weight_mb = %.3e mb\n", k, r.pthat_lo(k), r.pthat_hi(k), r.sigma_mb(k),
                r.n_window_events(k), r.weight_mb(k));

  const EventInfo &info = r.info(e);             // the event's row of the events table
  const Initiator *lead = info.leading();        // its hardest shower initiator
  std::printf("event %ld: file %d (event %d there), window %d, pTHat %.1f GeV, background %d,"
              " vacuum %s, flagged %s\n", e, info.file_index, info.local_event,
              info.pthat_bin, info.pthat, info.bg_unit, info.vacuum ? "yes" : "no",
              info.flagged() ? "yes" : "no");
  std::printf("  %zu shower initiators; the leading one: pT %.1f GeV, eta %.2f, phi %.2f\n",
              info.initiators.size(), lead->pt(), lead->eta(), lead->phi());
  std::printf("  samples: jet leg %d, background %d, fragmentations %d\n",
              r.n_oversamples(e), r.n_bg_samples(e), r.n_frag(e));

  // the hadrons of sample 0 of each source, as std::vector<Hadron>
  auto count = [](const Hadrons &hs) {
    int n = 0;
    for (const Hadron &h : hs) n += h.charged() && std::fabs(h.eta()) < 1;
    return n;
  };
  std::printf("  sample 0:          all hadrons   charged, |eta| < 1\n");
  const Hadrons frag = r.frag(e, 0);
  std::printf("    frag            %9zu   %9d\n", frag.size(), count(frag));
  if (info.vacuum) return;                       // p+p: no medium, no bulk
  const Hadrons bkg = r.bkg(e, 0), dep = r.bkg_dep(e, 0), full = r.bkg_dep_frag(e, 0);
  std::printf("    bkg             %9zu   %9d\n", bkg.size(), count(bkg));
  std::printf("    bkg_dep         %9zu   %9d\n", dep.size(), count(dep));
  std::printf("    bkg_dep_frag    %9zu   %9d\n", full.size(), count(full));
}
```

```
Writing out/10_root_cpp/first_look.C
```

**What to notice.**

- **The cross sections** are the campaign file's, as in tutorial 09; `weight_mb` is σ_k / N_k, the weight of one event of window k.
- **Event 0** is a 10–20 GeV jet (p̂T = 12.1 GeV) in background 0. Its leading parton has 13.4 GeV, and its fragmentation 0 has only 20 hadrons, 2 of them charged at `$|\eta| < 1$`: the event's droplets carried 26 GeV into the fluid (`E_droplets` in tutorial 09's events table).
- **Sample 0 of the jet leg has fewer** charged hadrons at midrapidity (1,452) than sample 0 of the background (1,533), although the jet added energy. Single samples fluctuate by about ±43 (tutorial 09), and these files were sampled independently. Only averages over many samples show what the jet did.

ACLiC compiled the macro into a shared library next to it, with a few helper files:

```python
print(sorted(p.name for p in OUT.glob("first_look*")))
root(f'first_look.C+("{PP}")', includes=[OUT])          # unchanged: not compiled again
```

```
['first_look.C', 'first_look_C.d', 'first_look_C.so', 'first_look_C_ACLiC_dict_rdict.pcm']
```

```
Processing first_look.C+("../../data/pp_ref")...
3 files, 4500 events; cross sections from the campaign file ../../data/pp_ref/ppref_campaign.root
  window 0: pTHat 10-20 GeV, sigma = 2.290e-03 mb, 1500 events, weight_mb = 1.527e-06 mb
  window 1: pTHat 20-30 GeV, sigma = 4.244e-05 mb, 1500 events, weight_mb = 2.830e-08 mb
  window 2: pTHat 30-50 GeV, sigma = 2.198e-06 mb, 1500 events, weight_mb = 1.465e-09 mb
event 0: file 0 (event 0 there), window 0, pTHat 13.0 GeV, background -1, vacuum yes, flagged no
  6 shower initiators; the leading one: pT 13.4 GeV, eta -0.33, phi 2.51
  samples: jet leg 0, background 0, fragmentations 10
  sample 0:          all hadrons   charged, |eta| < 1
    frag                   72          18
[1 s]
```

- `first_look_C.so` is the compiled macro, `first_look_C.d` its dependencies (to know when to recompile), `first_look_C_ACLiC_dict_rdict.pcm` ROOT's dictionary for it. js-contrib's `.gitignore` ignores all of them (`*.so`, `*_C.d`, `*.pcm`). `.C+` recompiles only when the macro or a header it includes has changed; `.C++` always recompiles.
- The second call reused the library, so it took a second instead of the compilation.
- **The p+p files** have no bulk: `vacuum` is set, every event has only its 10 fragmentations, and the macro returned before asking for a background. On a vacuum file `r.bkg(e, k)` throws a `std::runtime_error`, which ends ROOT with an error.

## 4. Loop over events and samples, with the right normalisation

The core of every analysis of these files is one loop. The rules (tutorial 09, and the reader's README):

- **Each event is the mean over its own samples.** A hadron of oversample k of event e weighs `$w_e / n$`, with n the number of samples of that source for that event.
- **Each event weighs** `$w_e = \sigma_k / N_k$` (mb) for a cross-section-weighted result over the windows, or `$w_e = 1/N$` for a result per event.
- **A background serves several events** (here 6). It counts once for each of them. The macro reads it once and gives it the sum of its events' weights; filling it once per event would give the same values but too small errors, since the same hadrons would enter as independent fills.

The macro fills the `$p_T$` spectra of charged hadrons at `$|\eta| < 1$` for each source, and the jet fragments of each window separately. It writes the histograms to a ROOT file and draws them into a PNG:

```python
%%writefile out/10_root_cpp/spectra.C
// spectra.C: cross-section-weighted pT spectra of charged hadrons at |eta| < 1, per source,
// with HadronFileReader.h.  Every event is the mean over its own samples: a hadron of event
// e weighs w_e / n_samples, with w_e = sigma_k / N_k of its pTHat window k [mb], or 1 / N.
#include "HadronFileReader.h"

#include <TCanvas.h>
#include <TFile.h>
#include <TH1D.h>
#include <TLegend.h>
#include <TStopwatch.h>
#include <TStyle.h>

#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>
#include <map>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

void spectra(const char *dir, const char *out, bool xsec = true) {
  using namespace hadrons_root;
  TStopwatch clock;
  HadronFileReader r(dir);
  r.set_charged_eta(1.0);                        // keep charged hadrons at |eta| < 1 only

  // 24 logarithmic pT bins from 0.2 to 50 GeV (those of tutorial 09)
  const int nb = 24;
  std::vector<double> edges(nb + 1);
  for (int i = 0; i <= nb; ++i) edges[i] = 0.2 * std::pow(50 / 0.2, double(i) / nb);
  auto book = [&](const char *name, const char *title) {
    auto *h = new TH1D(name, title, nb, edges.data());
    h->SetDirectory(nullptr);
    h->Sumw2();                                  // errors from the sum of squared weights
    return h;
  };
  TH1D *h_bkg = book("h_bkg", "background (bulk_bg)");
  TH1D *h_dep = book("h_bkgdep", "background + deposition (bulk_jet)");
  TH1D *h_frag = book("h_frag", "jet fragments (jet_frag)");
  TH1D *h_full = book("h_full", "the jet event (bulk_jet + jet_frag)");
  std::vector<TH1D *> h_win;                     // the jet fragments of each pTHat window
  for (int k = 0; k < r.n_windows(); ++k)
    h_win.push_back(book(Form("h_frag_w%d", k), Form("jet fragments, window %d", k)));

  // the event weights: sigma_k / N_k [mb], or 1 / N [per event]
  const std::vector<long> events = r.select_events();      // hadronized, not flagged
  std::map<int, long> n_window;
  for (long e : events) ++n_window[r.info(e).pthat_bin];
  auto weight = [&](long e) {
    const int k = r.info(e).pthat_bin;
    return xsec ? r.sigma_mb(k) / n_window[k] : 1.0 / events.size();
  };
  auto fill = [](TH1D *h, const Hadrons &hs, double w) {
    for (const Hadron &x : hs) h->Fill(x.pt(), w);
  };

  // the backgrounds: read once per (file, background), weighted with the sum of the weights
  // of the events using it -- it counts once for each of them, and its errors come out right
  std::map<std::pair<int, int>, std::pair<long, double>> backgrounds;   // -> (an event, sum w)
  for (long e : events) {
    const EventInfo &info = r.info(e);
    if (info.vacuum) continue;                   // p+p: no medium
    auto &b = backgrounds[{info.file_index, info.bg_unit}];
    if (b.second == 0) b.first = e;
    b.second += weight(e);
  }
  for (const auto &[key, b] : backgrounds) {
    const int n = r.n_bg_samples(b.first);
    for (int k = 0; k < n; ++k) fill(h_bkg, r.bkg(b.first, k), b.second / n);
  }

  // the jet events: the jet leg's oversamples, and the fragmentations
  for (long e : events) {
    const double w = weight(e);
    const int nj = r.n_oversamples(e), nf = r.n_frag(e);
    for (int k = 0; k < nj; ++k) fill(h_dep, r.bkg_dep(e, k), w / nj);
    for (int j = 0; j < nf; ++j) {
      const Hadrons frag = r.frag(e, j);
      fill(h_frag, frag, w / nf);
      if (xsec) fill(h_win[r.info(e).pthat_bin], frag, w / nf);
    }
  }
  h_full->Add(h_dep, h_frag);                    // the jet event = bkg_dep + frag
  for (TH1D *h : {h_bkg, h_dep, h_frag, h_full}) h->Scale(1.0, "width");   // -> per GeV
  for (TH1D *h : h_win) h->Scale(1.0, "width");

  std::printf("%zu events, %zu backgrounds; integrals [%s]:\n", events.size(),
              backgrounds.size(), xsec ? "mb" : "per event");
  for (TH1D *h : {h_bkg, h_dep, h_frag, h_full})
    std::printf("  %-8s %10.4g\n", h->GetName() + 2, h->Integral("width"));

  // the figure: the spectra, and the windows' contributions to the jet fragments
  gStyle->SetOptStat(0);
  TCanvas c("c", "", 1100, 450);
  c.Divide(2, 1);
  c.cd(1);
  gPad->SetLogx();
  gPad->SetLogy();
  TLegend leg(0.15, 0.15, 0.40, 0.40);
  const std::vector<std::pair<TH1D *, int>> style = {
      {h_full, kBlack}, {h_dep, kRed + 1}, {h_bkg, kBlue + 1}, {h_frag, kOrange + 1}};
  for (const auto &[h, color] : style) {
    h->SetLineColor(color);
    h->SetLineWidth(2);
    h->SetTitle(";p_{T} [GeV]");
    h->GetYaxis()->SetTitle(xsec ? "d#sigma/dp_{T} [mb/GeV]" : "dN/dp_{T} per event [1/GeV]");
    h->Draw(h == h_full ? "hist e" : "hist e same");
    leg.AddEntry(h, h->GetName() + 2, "l");
  }
  leg.SetBorderSize(0);
  leg.Draw();
  c.cd(2);
  gPad->SetLogx();
  gPad->SetLogy();
  TLegend leg2(0.55, 0.70, 0.89, 0.89);
  h_frag->Draw("hist e");
  leg2.AddEntry(h_frag, "jet fragments, sum", "l");
  const int wcolor[] = {kGreen + 2, kAzure + 1, kMagenta + 1};
  for (int k = 0; k < (xsec ? r.n_windows() : 0); ++k) {
    h_win[k]->SetLineColor(wcolor[k % 3]);
    h_win[k]->SetLineStyle(2);
    h_win[k]->Draw("hist same");
    leg2.AddEntry(h_win[k], Form("#hat{p}_{T} %.0f-%.0f GeV", r.pthat_lo(k), r.pthat_hi(k)), "l");
  }
  leg2.SetBorderSize(0);
  leg2.Draw();
  c.SaveAs(Form("%s.png", out));

  TFile f(Form("%s.root", out), "RECREATE");
  for (TH1D *h : {h_bkg, h_dep, h_frag, h_full}) h->Write();
  for (TH1D *h : h_win) h->Write();
  std::printf("-> %s.root, %s.png (%.1f s)\n", out, out, clock.RealTime());
}
```

**What to notice.**

- **Left:** the bulk (`bkg`, `bkgdep`) dominates the jet event (`full`) up to 4 GeV, the jet's fragments (`frag`) above. The bulk ends near 6 GeV: the fluid makes no harder hadrons.
- **Right: how the windows add up.** Up to about 8 GeV, the 10–20 GeV window (with by far the largest cross section) gives almost all fragments. Above, its jets have no more energy to give, and the harder windows take over, each at its own range of `$p_T$`. That is why campaigns are generated in windows: the rare hard jets get the same number of events as the common soft ones, and the cross sections put each in its place.
- **The integrals** are `$\sigma \times \langle N_{ch} \rangle$` in mb, for `$0.2 < p_T < 50$` GeV.

The fragments' spectrum is the one tutorial 09 made in Python with uproot and `hist`, from the same files. ROOT histograms read with uproot, so we compare bin by bin with tutorial 09's stored result:

```python
import json

widths = np.diff(h_cpp["h_frag"].axes[0].edges)

      f"{np.max(np.abs(h_cpp['h_frag'].values() - py09)[nz] / py09[nz]):.1e};",
```

## 5. The macros that come with js-contrib

`analysis_root/` has two complete macros, documented in its `README.md`:

- **`read_hadrons.C`** is the reader by example, a larger `spectra.C`: per source the `$p_T$` spectrum and the azimuth `$\Delta\phi$` to the event's leading initiator, and the wake (`bkgdep − bkg`). `read_hadrons.ipynb` is the same macro in ROOT's C++ notebook kernel, one step per cell (it needs `pip install metakernel` in the ROOT environment).
- **`hadron_distributions.C`** fills `$\eta$`, `$\phi$` and `$p_T$` of every source and of the wake with RDataFrame, on several threads, and draws them on one page.

Their arguments are listed at the top of each file. Both run on our campaign as they are, cross-section weighted (`xsec = true`):
